teile.einleitung: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure was a naturalist from Geneva in the 18th century. He explored the Alps with measuring instruments and is regarded as one of the founders of mountaineering. In 1787 he himself stood on the summit of Mont Blanc.
wichtigste: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure came from Geneva and lived from 1740 to 1799.
In 1760 he offered a reward for the first ascent of Mont Blanc.
In 1787 he himself stood on the summit of the highest mountain in the Alps.
He developed the hair hygrometer for measuring humidity.
With his cyanometer he measured the blueness of the sky.
His main work about his mountain journeys is called Voyages dans les Alpes.
He appeared on the 20-franc note of the sixth series of banknotes.

abschnitte.text: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure was born in **Geneva** in 1740. At only 22 he became professor of philosophy at the Academy of Geneva, where he mainly taught natural sciences. He was interested in rocks, plants, weather and glaciers. He preferred to do his research not indoors but outside in the mountains.

In 1760 the young Saussure travelled to Chamonix and saw **Mont Blanc**. He offered a **reward** to whoever found the way to the summit. Only in 1786 did Jacques Balmat and the doctor Michel-Gabriel Paccard become the first to reach the top. Saussure paid the reward to Balmat.

On 3 August 1787 Saussure himself stood on Mont Blanc, accompanied by Balmat and many porters. At the top he carried out scientific **measurements**, for example of air pressure and temperature, and used them to work out the height of the mountain. In 1788 he spent more than two weeks in a tent on the Col du Géant. Because of such expeditions he is regarded as a co-founder of **mountaineering**.

Saussure developed the **hair hygrometer**, which measures humidity with a human hair. This is because a hair becomes slightly longer in damp air. With the **cyanometer**, a disc with many shades of blue, he compared the blueness of the sky. He also built a box with glass lids that trapped the sun's heat, a forerunner of today's solar collectors.

Saussure wrote down his observations in the four-volume work **Voyages dans les Alpes**, which appeared between 1779 and 1796. In it he describes rocks, glaciers, weather and the life of people in the mountains. He also travelled through Valais and in 1792 reached the Klein Matterhorn near Zermatt. The work made the Alps known throughout Europe as a field of research.

Saussure appeared on the **20-franc note** of the sixth series. In Chamonix there is a statue showing Balmat pointing out the way up Mont Blanc to Saussure. The mineral saussurite is named after him. The famous linguist Ferdinand de Saussure also came from his family.

begriffe.erklaerung: Climbing in high mountains, especially in the Alps.
An instrument that measures how damp the air is.
A colour disc for measuring how blue the sky is.
A person who closely observes and studies nature, rocks, animals or the weather.

gewusst: During Saussure's ascent of Mont Blanc, around 18 companions carried the instruments, tent and supplies.
On the summit of Mont Blanc, water boils at only about 85 degrees because of the low air pressure.
For his research on the Col du Géant, Saussure had tents and instruments carried up to over 3300 metres.

teile.einleitung: The brain is the control centre of our body. It steers our movements, processes everything we see, hear and feel, and makes thinking, learning and remembering possible. Well protected in the skull, it works day and night, even during sleep.
wichtigste: The brain controls the whole body and is the seat of thinking and feelings.
The bone of the skull protects the brain from knocks.
The cerebrum consists of two halves and has a surface full of folds.
Nerve cells pass messages on as electrical and chemical signals.
Commands travel through the nerves from the brain to the muscles.
The left half of the brain controls the right side of the body and the other way round.
The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy.

abschnitte.text: An adult's brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, roughly as much as a large pineapple. The largest part is the **cerebrum**, which consists of two halves and has a surface full of folds. At the back underneath lies the **cerebellum**, which is important for balance and finely tuned movements. The **brainstem** connects the brain with the spinal cord and controls vital things such as breathing and the heartbeat.

The brain consists of about 86 billion **nerve cells**, which are also called neurons. Each nerve cell is connected to thousands of others. The messages travel as tiny electrical signals through the cells and are passed on chemically at the contact points, the **synapses**. Through the nerves in the spinal cord and throughout the body, the commands reach the muscles.

The two halves of the cerebrum are joined by a thick bridge of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**. What is astonishing is that each half controls the opposite side of the body. So the left half of the brain moves the right hand, and the right half the left hand. In most people the speech centre lies in the left **half of the brain**.

The brain is very delicate and is therefore protected in several ways. On the outside it is surrounded by the hard **bone of the skull**. Underneath lie the membranes of the brain and a fluid, the **cerebrospinal fluid**, which cushions knocks like a pillow. All the same, a heavy fall can injure the brain, which is why you should always wear a **helmet** when cycling, skiing or inline skating.

Although the brain makes up only about two per cent of body weight, it uses about a fifth of the body's **energy**. It gets this energy mainly from sugar and oxygen brought by the blood. Just a few minutes without oxygen can damage nerve cells. During **sleep** too the brain is active; it then sorts out what has been experienced and stores what has been learned in memory.

When we learn something new, new connections form between the nerve cells, or existing ones become stronger. This ability of the brain to change constantly is called **plasticity**. That is why you get better by practising, whether at reading, arithmetic or playing the piano. Enough sleep, exercise and healthy food help the brain to work well.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a nerve cell, which can receive and pass on signals.
The contact point at which a nerve cell passes its message on to another cell.
The largest part of the brain, responsible for thinking, language, sight and conscious movements.
The part of the brain that fine-tunes movements and helps with balance.
The ability of the brain to change through learning and experience.

gewusst: If you spread the folds of the cerebral cortex out flat, it would be about as big as a double page of a newspaper.
The brain itself feels no pain, because there are no pain sensors in it.
Nerve signals can shoot through the body at more than 100 metres per second.

teile.einleitung: Lascaux Cave in France is famous for its beautiful paintings from the Stone Age. Around 17,000 years ago, people painted hundreds of animals on its walls and ceilings there. That is why it is sometimes called the “Sistine Chapel of prehistory”.
wichtigste: Lascaux Cave lies in south-western France.
Its paintings are around 17,000 years old.
The animals painted most often are horses and aurochs.
The Ice Age people painted with earth pigments and charcoal.
Since 1963 the real cave has been closed, because the pictures were being damaged.
Today visitors can view a faithful replica.
Since 1979 the cave has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Lascaux lies in the **Dordogne** region in south-western France, near the small town of Montignac in the Vézère valley. The cave was discovered in September 1940 by four teenagers. One of them had investigated a hole in the ground beneath a fallen tree. With lamps, the boys climbed down and discovered the painted walls.

The cave contains around 600 painted pictures and about 1500 engraved figures. The most common are **horses**, along with deer, ibex, bison and **aurochs**. In the famous “Hall of the Bulls”, one aurochs is around five metres long. People, on the other hand, are almost never shown, and there are many mysterious signs such as dots and grids.

The people of the **Palaeolithic** painted with colours from nature. They obtained red, yellow and brown from **earth pigments** such as ochre, and black from **charcoal** and manganese earth. They applied the colours with their fingers, with brushes made of animal hair or by blowing through small tubes. For the high ceilings they probably built scaffolding, and they worked by the light of fat lamps.

After the war, Lascaux was opened to visitors in 1948, and many hundreds of people came every day. Their breath brought warmth, moisture and carbon dioxide into the cave. Algae and deposits formed on the walls and **damaged** the pictures. That is why the cave was closed in 1963, and only a few experts are still allowed to enter it.

So that everyone can still see the pictures, **faithful replicas** were built. Lascaux II opened in 1983, and since 2016 there has been the large visitor centre Lascaux IV in Montignac. Since 1979 the cave, together with other sites in the Vézère valley, has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. The pictures show how closely the people of the Ice Age observed animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The oldest period of human history, in which tools were made of stone.
An extinct wild ox, the ancestor of our domestic cattle.
A natural yellow to red earth pigment.
An exact copy of an original.

gewusst: When they made their discovery, the four teenagers were accompanied by a dog called Robot.
Some animals in Lascaux are painted so that, thanks to the curve of the rock wall, they stand out almost three-dimensionally.
Works of art from the Ice Age have also been found in Switzerland, for example in the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen.

teile.einleitung: The Gulf Stream is a powerful, warm ocean current in the Atlantic. It carries warm water from the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico northwards and on towards Europe. Without this huge hot-water heating system, winters in northern Europe would be much colder.
wichtigste: The Gulf Stream gets its name from the Gulf of Mexico.
It is a warm ocean current.
It flows from south to north along the east coast of North America.
Its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, makes the climate in Europe milder.
Thanks to the warm current, ports on the coast of Norway usually stay free of ice in winter.
In the 18th century, Benjamin Franklin had a map of the Gulf Stream printed.
Researchers are watching whether meltwater could weaken the current in the Atlantic.

abschnitte.text: The **Gulf Stream** is one of the strongest ocean currents on Earth. It begins near Florida, where warm water from the **Gulf of Mexico** and the Caribbean flows into the Atlantic. From there it flows north along the east coast of North America and then turns east. It carries many times the amount of water of all the world's rivers put together. Its surface is noticeably warmer than the surrounding sea, which can be seen clearly on satellite images.

Off the coast of Canada, the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold **Labrador Current**, which comes from the north. There, near Newfoundland, thick fog often forms, and there are rich fishing grounds. After that the current continues across the Atlantic as the **North Atlantic Current**. It reaches the British Isles, Ireland and the coast of Norway. On the way the water gives off a lot of heat to the air, which the westerly wind carries to Europe.

Without the North Atlantic Current, the climate in western and northern Europe would be considerably colder. On the coast of Norway, many ports such as **Hammerfest** usually stay free of ice in winter, even though they lie north of the Arctic Circle. At the same latitude in Canada or Siberia, the sea freezes over in winter. In Ireland and south-west England, palm trees even grow in sheltered gardens. Switzerland also benefits indirectly from the milder westerly winds, even though the weather here is strongly shaped by the Alps.

Spanish sailors noticed the strong current off the coast of Florida as early as 1513. Later, sailing ships used the Gulf Stream to reach Europe faster. Around 1770 the American statesman **Benjamin Franklin** had a map of the Gulf Stream printed. He had noticed that mail ships travelling from England to America were slower when they sailed against the current. Today satellites, buoys and underwater robots measure the current precisely.

abschnitte.titel: The Gulf Stream and climate change
abschnitte.text: The Gulf Stream is part of a large circulation in the Atlantic, the **Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation**. In the far north the water cools, becomes heavier and sinks into the depths, from where it flows back south. When Greenland's ice melts, a lot of light **fresh water** gets into the sea. This could slow down the sinking of the water and weaken the whole overturning circulation. How fast and how strongly this could happen is disputed among researchers, which is why the current is closely watched.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lasting movement of seawater in a particular direction.
The continuation of the Gulf Stream, which brings warm water to Europe.
A cold ocean current that flows south off Canada.
A large circulation in the sea in which water at the surface and in the depths flows in opposite directions.

gewusst: Drifting seeds and fruits from the Caribbean are sometimes carried by the Gulf Stream all the way to the beaches of Ireland or Norway.
A drop of water takes many centuries to complete one round of the entire worldwide system of ocean currents.

teile.einleitung: With our senses we take in the world around us. At school, five senses are usually listed: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. For each sense there is a special sense organ that takes in stimuli and passes them on to the brain.
wichtigste: The five classic senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
With your eyes you see, for example what colour an apple is.
With your nose you smell, and with your tongue you taste.
The skin is the largest sense organ of the human body.
Blind people read braille with their sense of touch.
When you have a cold, food tastes bland, because you cannot smell properly.
Dogs can smell much better than people.

abschnitte.text: The **eye** takes in light and creates an image on the retina. The retina contains sensory cells for brightness and for colours. In this way we can tell whether an apple is red, yellow or green. The brain puts the signals from both eyes together into a three-dimensional picture, which is why we can judge distances.

The **ear** catches sound waves and passes them through the eardrum and the tiny bones of the ear into the inner ear. In the **cochlea** the vibrations are turned into nerve signals. People hear high and low sounds, but some animals such as bats hear much higher sounds. The inner ear also houses the **sense of balance**, which is often counted as a sixth sense.

In the **nose** there are smell cells that can tell thousands of different scents apart. The **tongue**, with its taste buds, recognises the basic tastes sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. The full flavour of a dish only arises when nose and tongue work together. That is why food often tastes bland when you have a cold.

At about two square metres in adults, the **skin** is the largest sense organ. It senses touch, pressure, warmth, cold and pain. There are especially many touch receptors in the fingertips and on the lips. Blind people use them to read **braille**, which consists of raised dots.

Many animals have senses that are much sharper than ours. A **dog** has many times more smell cells and can recognise people by their trail. Birds of prey see very sharply, and bees even see **ultraviolet light**. Some birds sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.

The division into five senses goes back to the Greek philosopher **Aristotle**. Today we know that people have other senses too. These include the sense of balance, the sense of temperature, the sense of pain and the feeling for the position of your own body parts. All the senses send information to the **brain**, which puts together a picture of the world from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body that takes in stimuli such as light, sound or scent.
Something from the environment that a sense organ can detect.
A tiny group of sensory cells on the tongue that detects taste.
A script of raised dots that blind people read with their fingers.

gewusst: Braille was invented by Louis Braille, who had himself gone blind as a child.
If you hold your nose, you can hardly tell an apple and a raw potato apart by taste.
Our brain fills in missing information, which is why we can also be fooled by optical illusions.

teile.einleitung: Hermann von Helmholtz was one of the most versatile researchers of the 19th century. He was a doctor and a physicist and studied how the eye, the ear and the nerves work. He also formulated one of the most important laws of physics, the conservation of energy.
wichtigste: Helmholtz was born in Potsdam in 1821 and died in 1894.
He paid for his medical studies by committing himself to work as an army doctor.
In 1847, in “On the Conservation of Force”, he formulated the principle of the conservation of energy.
In 1850 he invented the ophthalmoscope, with which you can examine the back of the eye.
He was the first to measure how fast signals travel in nerves.
The Young-Helmholtz theory explains colour vision with three types of receptors.
From 1888 he was the first president of the Imperial Physical Technical Institute in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: **Hermann Helmholtz** was born on 31 August 1821 in Potsdam. His family had little money, so he studied medicine at a school for army doctors and then worked for several years as an **army doctor**. Alongside this, he did research eagerly. Later he became a professor in Königsberg, Bonn, Heidelberg and finally Berlin, where he taught physics. In 1883 he was ennobled and was allowed to call himself “von Helmholtz”.

In 1847 Helmholtz published the paper **“On the Conservation of Force”**. In it he showed that energy is never lost and never comes from nothing, but is only changed from one form into another. When you brake on a bicycle, for example, energy of motion turns into heat. Today this principle is called the **conservation of energy**, and it is regarded as one of the most important laws of physics.

In 1850 Helmholtz invented the **ophthalmoscope**, with which doctors can look through the pupil at the back of the eye. The instrument changed eye medicine greatly. He also explained that the lens curves more when we focus on nearby objects. With the **Young-Helmholtz theory** he described how colour vision depends on three kinds of receptors, roughly for red, green and blue.

Around 1850 Helmholtz measured how fast a signal travels in a frog's nerve. He arrived at about **30 metres per second**, much slower than people thought at the time. In 1863 his work “On the Sensations of Tone” appeared, which is about hearing and music. In it he investigated how sounds are made up of many individual tones, using small hollow spheres that are now called **Helmholtz resonators**.

In 1887 the **Imperial Physical Technical Institute** was founded in Berlin, and from 1888 Helmholtz led it as its first president. Precise units of measurement and measuring methods were developed there. Helmholtz died on 8 September 1894. Today the Helmholtz Association, one of the largest research organisations in Germany, is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law that energy does not disappear but only changes its form.
An instrument with which you can look inside the eye.
A sensory cell that picks up a particular stimulus such as light or sound.
A hollow body that vibrates especially strongly at a particular tone.

gewusst: According to Helmholtz's measurement, a nerve signal in a frog's nerve is about as fast as a car on the motorway.
Helmholtz was so famous that he was sometimes called the “Chancellor of Physics”.
Helmholtz built his first ophthalmoscope from cardboard, glue and small glass plates.

teile.einleitung: The house dust mite is a tiny arachnid that lives in almost every home. It is so small that you cannot see it with the naked eye. For most people it is harmless, but in some it triggers an allergy.
wichtigste: House dust mites are related to spiders.
They are too small to see with the naked eye.
Especially large numbers of house dust mites live in beds.
They eat flakes of skin, which people lose every day.
House dust mites like it warm and damp.
They do not bite or sting people.
An allergy is mainly triggered by the mites' droppings.
Washing bedding often at a high temperature helps against mites.

abschnitte.text: House dust mites are only about 0.1 to 0.5 millimetres in size, smaller than a grain of sand. Their body is roundish, whitish and almost transparent. Like spiders, adult mites have **eight legs**, because they belong to the **arachnids**. They have no eyes and find their way with sensory hairs. The most common species in Europe has the scientific name Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, which means roughly “skin eater”.

House dust mites live in homes, especially in **mattresses**, pillows, duvets, carpets and upholstered furniture. In bed they find everything they need: warmth, moisture and food. They feel most at home at about 25 degrees and high **humidity**. When the air is dry, as in heated rooms in winter, many of them die. In the high mountains, too, there are hardly any house dust mites because of the dry air.

House dust mites mainly eat **flakes of skin**, which people and pets are constantly shedding. A person loses about one to two grams of skin flakes every day, enough food for a great many mites. They often let moulds pre-digest the flakes first. House dust mites do not bite or sting and do not suck blood. They do not transmit diseases either.

In some people the immune system reacts to proteins in the mites' **droppings**. These tiny pellets break down, mix with house dust and are breathed in. Typical signs are a blocked or runny nose, sneezing and itchy eyes, especially in the morning after waking up. Sometimes this also leads to **asthma**. A doctor can use a test to find out whether someone is allergic to house dust mites.

You can never get rid of house dust mites completely, but you can reduce their numbers. Bedding should be washed often and at at least 60 degrees, because **heat** kills the mites. Regular airing lowers the humidity in the bedroom. For allergy sufferers there are special mite-proof covers for mattresses and pillows. Cuddly toys can also be washed or put in the freezer for a day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with eight legs that includes spiders, scorpions and mites.
An exaggerated defence reaction of the body to substances that are actually harmless.
Tiny dead bits of skin that we are constantly losing.
How much water vapour the air contains.

gewusst: Hundreds of thousands to millions of house dust mites can live in a single mattress.
House dust mites do not drink; instead they take in water directly from the damp air.

teile.einleitung: Green algae are a large group of mostly small living things that, like plants, make food using sunlight. There are tiny single-celled ones, balls made of many cells and long green threads. Our land plants developed from green algae many millions of years ago.
wichtigste: Green algae make their food using light and release oxygen into the water as they do so.
There are single-celled and multicellular green algae.
Without light, green algae cannot grow.
The green coating on tree trunks often consists of tiny green algae.
The globe alga rolls through the water as a green ball.
Filamentous algae float in ponds like green cotton wool.
Certain algae can turn snow in the mountains red.
Our land plants are descended from green algae.

abschnitte.text: **Green algae** are living things that, like plants, have the green pigment **chlorophyll**. With it they capture sunlight and make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. During this **photosynthesis** they release oxygen; on sunny days you can sometimes see little bubbles on the algae in a pond. Many thousands of species are known worldwide. Most are so small that you can only see them individually under a microscope.

Some green algae consist of just a single cell, such as Chlamydomonas, which swims through the water with two flagella. Others live in colonies, like the **globe alga** Volvox, a hollow ball of hundreds to thousands of cells that moves by rolling. Still others form long chains, known as **filamentous algae**, which float in ponds like cotton wool. Sea lettuce, a green alga from the sea, even looks like a green lettuce leaf. So green algae range from tiny dots to structures the size of a hand.

Most green algae live in **fresh water**, that is, in lakes, ponds, streams and puddles. Some grow in the sea, others on land in damp places. The green coating on the weather side of tree trunks, fences and walls often consists of tiny green algae. Some species even live in snow and turn it reddish in summer; this is called **watermelon snow** and can also be seen in the Swiss Alps. Many lichens are a partnership of fungi and green algae.

Green algae are at the start of many **food chains** in water. Small crustaceans eat them, and these in turn are eaten by fish. With their oxygen, algae help animals in the water to breathe. But if too much fertiliser gets into a lake, the algae grow excessively. When they then die, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen breaking them down, which can become dangerous for fish.

Around 450 to 500 million years ago, descendants of green algae conquered the land. Mosses, ferns and later all flowering plants developed from them. That is why green algae and **land plants** have the same green pigment and similar cells. Today some green algae are also farmed for food supplements, such as chlorella. Researchers are also investigating whether fuel could be made from algae in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green pigment that plants and algae use to capture sunlight.
The process in which sugar and oxygen are made from light, water and carbon dioxide.
A living thing that consists of only one single cell.
A group of identical cells or living things that live together.

gewusst: Red snow sometimes smells slightly of watermelon, which is why it is also called watermelon snow.
The fur of sloths is often greenish because algae grow in it, camouflaging them in the rainforest.

teile.einleitung: “Eureka” (in German “Heureka”) is an Ancient Greek exclamation that means “I have found it”. The famous scientist Archimedes is said to have shouted it when the solution to a difficult puzzle came to him in the bath. Today people shout “Eureka” when they suddenly have a good idea or solution.
wichtigste: Eureka comes from Ancient Greek and means “I have found it”.
According to legend, Archimedes shouted the word in the bath.
King Hiero II of Syracuse wanted to know whether his crown was made of pure gold.
Archimedes compared the amount of water displaced by the crown with that of pure gold.
The story was written down by the Roman architect Vitruvius.
The US state of California has “Eureka” as its motto.
A sudden flash of inspiration is also called a eureka moment.

abschnitte.text: **Eureka** is a word from **Ancient Greek** and means “I have found it”. In German it is written “Heureka”, in English and many other languages “Eureka”. It is used when you suddenly arrive at the solution after thinking for a long time. Such moments are also called **eureka moments** or flashes of inspiration.

According to legend, **King Hiero II** of Syracuse in Sicily had a crown made of gold. He suspected that the goldsmith had replaced some of the gold with cheaper silver. **Archimedes**, the city's most famous scholar, was asked to find out. But the crown was not to be damaged in the process.

When Archimedes climbed into a full bathtub, water ran over the edge. Then he realised that a body **displaces** exactly as much water as the space it takes up itself. Silver is lighter than gold, so silver of the same weight takes up more space. Archimedes dipped the crown and a lump of gold of the same weight into water. The crown displaced more water, so it was not made of pure gold.

The story does not come from Archimedes himself. It was written down about 200 years later by the Roman architect **Vitruvius** in his work on architecture. Whether everything happened exactly like that is not known. Archimedes lived in **Syracuse** in the 3rd century BC and was an important mathematician and inventor.

The US state of **California** has “Eureka” as its motto, a reference to the discoveries of gold in the 19th century. Many places, companies and competitions bear the name. In physics, **Archimedes' principle** recalls the scholar: it explains why ships float and stones sink. A body in water becomes lighter by exactly as much as the displaced water weighs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The language spoken in ancient Greece more than 2000 years ago.
When a body is dipped into water and pushes the water aside.
How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
A story passed down over time, where it is not certain whether it is true.

gewusst: A piece of gold is almost twice as heavy as a piece of silver of the same size.
In Europe there is a research programme also called Eureka, in which Switzerland takes part too.
Archimedes is said to have been so excited that he leapt out of the bath and ran straight home.

teile.einleitung: Goose bumps are the little bumps that suddenly appear on the skin when we feel cold. The fine body hairs stand up at the same time. Strong feelings such as fear, emotion or beautiful music can also give you goose bumps.
wichtigste: Goose bumps often arise when we feel cold.
Tiny muscles at the hair roots pull the hairs up.
In animals with fur, raised fur keeps them warm.
Goose bumps hardly warm people, because we have only a few body hairs.
Strong feelings can also give you goose bumps.
The name comes from the skin looking like the skin of a plucked goose.
In English goose bumps are also called gooseflesh.

abschnitte.text: With goose bumps, many small raised spots form on the skin and the hairs stand up. You see them most often on arms and legs. The skin then looks like that of a **plucked goose**, which is where the name comes from. In technical language it is called **piloerection**, which means the raising of the hairs.

At every hair root there is a tiny muscle, the **hair-raising muscle**. When it contracts, the hair stands up and the skin around the hair bulges upwards. This is controlled by the **autonomic nervous system**, which we cannot influence consciously. That is why you cannot simply produce or stop goose bumps by willpower.

In animals with thick fur, goose bumps are very useful. The raised **fur** traps a thick layer of air that **insulates** like a jacket. Birds fluff up their feathers in winter for the same reason. We humans have only a few fine body hairs left, so goose bumps hardly warm us.

Goose bumps also help animals when they are afraid or feel threatened. Faced with a strange dog, a cat raises its **fur** and arches its back so that it looks bigger and more dangerous. The **porcupine** raises its quills when in danger, and these are modified hairs. In this way the animals frighten attackers off without having to fight.

Many people get goose bumps from **strong feelings**. That can happen during an exciting film, from fear, from being moved or from especially beautiful **music**. The body then releases the messenger substance adrenaline, which also activates the hair muscles. People then say that something is so beautiful or so eerie that it sends a shiver down their spine.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical term for the raising of the hairs in goose bumps.
A tiny muscle at every hair root that can make the hair stand up.
A messenger substance the body releases when excited or afraid.
To hold warmth in so that it is not lost.

gewusst: Goose bumps are a leftover from a time when our ancestors had far more body hair.
You can get goose bumps even on parts of the body with no visible hair, because fine hairs grow there.
Many people get goose bumps when they hear a sound such as chalk on a blackboard.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Schliemann was a German merchant and archaeologist who searched for the legendary city of Troy in the 19th century. Inspired by Homer's “Iliad”, he dug in what is now Turkey and in Greece. His finds made him world-famous, but his excavation methods are still controversial today.
wichtigste: Heinrich Schliemann was born in Germany in 1822 and died in Naples in 1890.
He made his fortune as a merchant in trade.
Homer's “Iliad” inspired him to search for Troy.
From 1871 he dug on the hill of Hisarlik in what is now Turkey.
In 1873 he found a gold treasure, which he called “Priam's Treasure”.
In 1876 he discovered the famous gold Mask of Agamemnon in Mycenae.
He is regarded as one of the founders of archaeology in Greece and Asia Minor.

abschnitte.text: Heinrich Schliemann was born on 6 January 1822 in Neubukow in Mecklenburg, in the north of what is now **Germany**. He grew up as the son of a pastor and heard stories from ancient Greece from an early age. Later he said that, as a child, he had been gripped by a picture of Troy burning. Experts today doubt whether this story is true. What is certain is that Homer's heroic poem, the **Iliad**, fascinated him all his life.

Schliemann had to leave school early and worked as an apprentice in a grocery shop. Later he became a **merchant** and moved to St Petersburg in Russia, where he traded in goods such as the dye indigo. He earned a great deal of money and became a rich man. He taught himself many languages, including English, Russian and Ancient Greek. At about 40 he gave up trading to devote himself entirely to the study of antiquity.

At that time many scholars thought Troy was an invented city. Schliemann suspected it lay in the hill of **Hisarlik** in the north-west of today's Turkey and began large excavations there in 1871. He found the remains of several cities lying one on top of another. In 1873 he discovered a treasure of gold, silver and jewellery, which he called **Priam's Treasure**, after the legendary king of Troy. It later turned out that the treasure is around a thousand years older than the Troy of Homer's story.

In 1876 Schliemann dug in **Mycenae** in Greece, the city of the legendary King Agamemnon. In ancient shaft graves he found gold, weapons and several death masks made of gold sheet. He called the finest one the **Mask of Agamemnon**. Today we know that it too is older than the Trojan War and does not belong to Agamemnon. The mask is on display in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

Schliemann showed that real places can lie behind old legends, and he made **archaeology** popular with many people. However, he dug very quickly and carelessly, destroying valuable layers in the process. A deep trench right across the hill of Troy is still called Schliemann's Trench today. He also smuggled the treasure out of the country, which broke the agreement with the Ottoman Empire. The treasure later went to Berlin and after the Second World War was taken to Moscow, where it is today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies ancient cultures through finds in the ground.
An Ancient Greek heroic poem by Homer about the war over Troy.
Carefully uncovering old walls and objects from the ground.
A stratum in the ground that comes from a particular time.

gewusst: For a photograph, Schliemann had his wife Sophia wear the jewellery from Priam's Treasure.
At Troy, experts today distinguish more than nine settlement layers one on top of another.
Schliemann is buried in a magnificent tomb in Athens that looks like a Greek temple.

teile.einleitung: The geocentric view of the world is the idea that the Earth stands still at the centre of the universe. The Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars are supposed to move around it. This teaching was regarded as correct for about 1400 years, until it was replaced by the heliocentric view of the world.
wichtigste: In the geocentric view of the world the Earth stands at the centre of the universe.
People believed in it for a long time, because the Sun and the stars seem to move around the Earth.
The philosopher Aristotle imagined the Earth surrounded by celestial spheres.
Ptolemy of Alexandria summed up this view of the world in the 2nd century after Christ.
His main work is known under the name Almagest.
With small extra circles, the epicycles, he explained the paths of the planets.
Copernicus put the Sun at the centre in 1543, and Galileo found the moons of Jupiter in 1610.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek **gē** for Earth and the word **centre** for middle. In the geocentric view of the world the Earth stands still in the middle. Around it circle the Moon, the Sun, the planets and, right on the outside, the **fixed stars**. For people in earlier times this was quite logical, because that is how it looks in the sky.

Every day the **Sun** rises in the east and sets in the west. The stars too seem to turn around us during the night. At the same time you cannot feel the Earth moving. That is why for many centuries people took a **motionless Earth** for granted.

In the 4th century before Christ the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** imagined that the heavenly bodies are fixed to transparent **celestial spheres**. In the 2nd century after Christ **Ptolemy** in Alexandria summed up the knowledge about the sky. His main work is known under the Arabic name **Almagest**. With his calculations the positions of the planets could be predicted quite well.

Some planets seem at times to run backwards in the sky, which is called **retrograde motion**. To explain this, Ptolemy made the planets run on small extra circles, the **epicycles**. These small circles in turn moved on big circles around the Earth. That made the model very complicated, but it worked surprisingly well.

In 1543 the book of **Nicolaus Copernicus** appeared, in which the Sun stands at the centre. In 1610 **Galileo Galilei** discovered with the telescope four moons circling Jupiter, so not everything turned around the Earth. He also observed that Venus shows phases like the Moon. Johannes Kepler found out in addition that the planets run on ellipses around the Sun.

The geocentric view of the world was replaced by the **heliocentric view of the world**. This change was so far-reaching that people speak of the **Copernican revolution**. Today we know that the Sun too is only one star among many in the Milky Way. All the same, in everyday life we still say that the Sun rises and sets.

begriffe.erklaerung: With the Earth at the centre.
With the Sun at the centre.
A small extra circle on which a planet moves in Ptolemy's model.
The idea of how the universe is built up.

gewusst: As early as the 3rd century before Christ the Greek Aristarchus of Samos suspected that the Earth turns around the Sun, but hardly anyone believed him.
The name Almagest means roughly “the greatest work”.
The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe designed a mixed form in which the planets circle the Sun and the Sun circles the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Memory is the ability to remember things and to recall them later. It stores names, experiences, knowledge and even movements such as riding a bicycle. Without memory we could not learn, nor would we know who we are.
wichtigste: Memory is the ability to remember things.
In short-term memory you keep things only briefly, for example a telephone number.
In long-term memory, knowledge stays stored for many years.
Memory aids are little sayings that help you to remember.
You often learn better using several senses.
You remember experiences with strong feelings especially well.
Most people have their first memories from about the age of 3.

abschnitte.text: **Memory** is not a single box in your head but the interplay of many areas in the **brain**. When we learn something, nerve cells make new connections or strengthen their connections. The **hippocampus**, a part of the brain shaped like a seahorse, plays an important part. It helps to move new memories into long-term memory.

In **short-term memory** you keep things only for seconds to minutes, such as a telephone number until you have typed it in. It can hold only a few things at once, often about seven. What is important or often repeated moves into **long-term memory**. There it can stay stored for many years or a whole lifetime.

In long-term memory there are different areas. **Factual memory** stores facts, such as that Bern is the federal city of Switzerland. Memory for experiences stores your own experiences, for example your last birthday. In **movement memory**, skills such as swimming or cycling are stored, and these are almost never forgotten.

A **memory aid** is a saying that helps you to remember. The sentence “My very educated mother just served us nachos” helps with the order of the planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. If you learn with several senses, by reading, listening, drawing and explaining out loud, you remember more. Enough **sleep** is important too, because during sleep the brain fixes what you have learned.

Forgetting is normal and even useful; otherwise our heads would be crammed with unimportant things. In 1885 the researcher **Hermann Ebbinghaus** showed that without repetition you quickly forget new things again. Experiences with **strong feelings**, such as great joy or a fright, on the other hand, often stick especially well. Most people have no memories at all from their first two to three years of life.

begriffe.erklaerung: The store for things you keep only briefly
The store for knowledge and experiences you keep for a long time
A part of the brain that helps to store new memories
A saying or trick that helps you to remember
A diagram showing how quickly you forget what you have learned without repetition

gewusst: Memories are not fixed like a photo; the brain puts them together again each time you remember and can change them in the process.
There are memory championships in which people memorise the order of a whole pack of cards in a few minutes.
If you go over what you have learned after a day, a week and a month, you remember it much longer.

teile.einleitung: A hypothesis is a reasoned guess that can be tested with observations or experiments. It stands at the start of almost every piece of research, whether in a laboratory or in an experiment in the classroom. Even if a hypothesis turns out to be wrong, you have learned something along the way.
wichtigste: Hypothesis is the technical word for a scientific guess.
A hypothesis must be testable.
You write it down before the experiment.
Good hypotheses are based on what you already know.
It is often worded as an “If ..., then ...” sentence.
If an experiment confirms a hypothesis, it is supported, but not finally proven.
The philosopher Karl Popper demanded that scientific statements must be capable of being refuted.

abschnitte.text: A **guess** is an idea about what might happen, for example: “I think the stone will sink.” In science, such a guess is called a **hypothesis** if it can be tested. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “supposition” or “foundation”. So a hypothesis is not yet knowledge, but a suggestion that is to be tested.

A good hypothesis is **clear, precise and testable**. A sentence with “If ..., then ...” works especially well. For example: “If cress gets more light, then it grows faster.” The statement “Cress is pretty”, on the other hand, cannot be tested and is therefore not a hypothesis. Good ideas for hypotheses come from what you have already observed or learned.

Whether a hypothesis is right is found out with an **experiment**. Nino suspects that his plant grows better in the light than in the dark. He sets up two identical plants, one in the light and one in a dark cupboard, and waters both the same. In this way he changes only one single condition, and the comparison shows whether his guess is right. The hypothesis is always written down **before the experiment**, so that you do not adjust it afterwards.

If the result matches the hypothesis, it is **supported**, but not yet finally proven. A later experiment could contradict it. If careful experiments clearly contradict the hypothesis, it is **rejected** or adjusted. In this way research moves forward step by step, even through mistakes.

The Austrian-British philosopher **Karl Popper** wrote the book “The Logic of Scientific Discovery” in 1934. In it he demanded that scientific statements must in principle be **falsifiable**, that is, capable of being shown to be wrong. The sentence “All swans are white” can never be completely proven, but a single black swan refutes it. And indeed, Europeans discovered black swans in Australia.

In 1912 the German researcher **Alfred Wegener** put forward the hypothesis that the continents move. He saw that the coasts of Africa and South America fit together like pieces of a jigsaw. Many experts rejected his idea at first. Only in the 1960s did new measurements on the sea floor confirm the hypothesis, and from this the theory of **plate tectonics** arose.

begriffe.erklaerung: A testable guess in science.
A planned test with which you check a guess.
To show that a statement is not true.
A well-tested explanation that brings together many observations.

gewusst: In statistics there is even a “null hypothesis”, which assumes the opposite of what you actually suspect.
Alfred Wegener did not live to see his hypothesis confirmed, because he died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930.
Many great discoveries began with a hypothesis that was at first thought to be crazy.

teile.einleitung: Excavation tools are the tools archaeologists use to recover traces of the past from the ground. They include large tools such as the shovel and wheelbarrow, but above all fine tools such as the trowel, brush and spatula. Almost as important are the measuring tape, camera and notebook, because every find has to be documented precisely.
wichtigste: With a small trowel, archaeologists scrape the soil away layer by layer.
With a brush they carefully sweep soil off finds.
For very delicate work on bones they use small spatulas and wooden sticks.
A measuring tape is used to record exactly where a find lies.
The excavated soil is taken away in a wheelbarrow.
A notebook and pencil are part of the equipment for writing everything down.
A metal detector beeps when there is metal in the ground.

abschnitte.text: The most important tool on an excavation is the **trowel**, a small, pointed bricklayer's trowel. With it you scrape off the soil in thin layers instead of digging roughly. For delicate spots people use **brushes**, small spatulas, wooden sticks or even tools like those of a dentist. The top layer of soil without finds is sometimes removed with a shovel, pickaxe or even a digger. The soil that is dug out goes into buckets and is taken to a heap in a **wheelbarrow**.

With a big shovel you could easily damage small finds such as beads, coins or bones. With the trowel you dig more precisely and gently and can spot changes in the soil. Often the soil is also tipped through a **sieve** so that even tiny finds such as seeds or fish bones are not lost. Some samples are even washed with water to rinse out charred plant remains. Finds made of bone or wood sometimes have to be strengthened while still in the ground before they can be lifted out.

An excavation destroys the site, because the soil cannot be put back again. That is why everything must be precisely **documented** before a find is taken out. With measuring tapes, measuring rods and modern surveying instruments, the exact position and depth of every find is determined. Archaeologists draw the layers of soil, photograph every step and write everything in an **excavation diary**. Every find goes into a labelled bag so that later it is known where it came from.

Today, devices that can look into the ground without digging also help. With **ground-penetrating radar** or magnetic surveys, people find walls and pits that are still hidden underground. Drones take aerial pictures, from which a computer creates accurate 3D models of the excavation. A **metal detector** beeps when metal such as coins or nails lies in the ground. In Switzerland, you need a permit in most cantons to search with a metal detector.

In Switzerland, the **cantonal archaeology services** are responsible for excavations. They often dig before a new house or road is built, so that traces are not lost. Under Swiss law, archaeological finds belong to the canton in which they are found. Well-known sites include the Roman town of Augusta Raurica near Basel and the **pile dwellings** on the shores of many lakes. Under water, divers work with similar tools and carefully suck away the mud.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, flat shovel with a point, used to scrape off soil in thin layers.
A place where traces of people from earlier times lie in the ground.
Precisely writing down, drawing, measuring and photographing an excavation.
A stratum of soil that was deposited at a particular time.

gewusst: Many archaeologists keep their favourite trowel with them for years, until the blade is worn down very short from scraping.
The deeper a layer of soil lies, the older it usually is, so the depth of a find often already tells you something about its age.

teile.einleitung: Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who lived from 1564 to 1642. He was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky, and in doing so he made astonishing discoveries. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern natural science.
wichtigste: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564 and died near Florence in 1642.
With a telescope he discovered four moons of Jupiter in 1610.
He also observed craters on the Moon, the phases of Venus and sunspots.
Galilei supported the teaching that the Earth goes round the sun.
For this he came into conflict with the Catholic Church.
With experiments he studied how bodies fall and move.
He is regarded as the founder of modern experimental physics.

abschnitte.text: Galileo Galilei was born on 15 February 1564 in **Pisa** in Italy. At first he studied medicine but soon became more interested in mathematics. Later he was a professor in Pisa and in **Padua**. He was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer all at once.

In 1609 Galilei heard about a new invention from the Netherlands, the **telescope**. He built better telescopes himself and pointed them at the sky. In January 1610 he discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter. Today these are called the **Galilean moons**: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

For a long time many people believed that the Earth was at the centre of the universe. Nicolaus Copernicus, by contrast, had taught that the Earth orbits the sun. Galilei's observations, such as the **phases of Venus**, supported this **heliocentric view of the world**. He defended it in a famous book that appeared in 1632.

The teaching that the Earth moves contradicted the way the Bible was then interpreted. In 1633 Galilei was brought before a church court, the **Inquisition**. He had to withdraw his teaching and afterwards lived under house arrest near Florence until his death in 1642. Only in 1992 did Pope John Paul II declare that Galilei had been wronged.

Galilei used balls on inclined planes to study how things fall. He realised that, without air resistance, all bodies fall equally fast, however heavy they are. He also worked on the **pendulum**. Because he tested ideas with measurements, he is regarded as the father of the **experiment** in physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with lenses that makes distant things look bigger.
The idea that the sun is at the centre and the Earth orbits it.
A former court of the Catholic Church that prosecuted departures from the faith.
The four largest moons of Jupiter, which Galilei discovered in 1610.

gewusst: The space probe Galileo, which studied Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, was named after him.
In 1971 the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both landed at the same time, just as Galilei had predicted.
The European satellite navigation system is also called Galileo.

teile.einleitung: The hypothetico-deductive method is an important procedure that researchers use to test their ideas. First you put forward a guess, then you derive a prediction from it and test it against reality. This is how scientists work in many subjects, from medicine to astronomy.
wichtigste: First you put forward a hypothesis, then you derive a consequence and test it against observation.
Deduction is a logical conclusion from the general to the particular.
If a prediction comes true, the hypothesis is supported, but not proven.
In the 1840s in Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis tested his idea about how a dangerous disease was being passed on in this way.
The planet Neptune was discovered in 1846 thanks to a calculated prediction.
A control group shows what happens without the influence being studied.
In statistics, the assumption that there is no effect is called the null hypothesis.

abschnitte.text: It starts with a **hypothesis**, that is, a reasoned guess. From it, through **deduction**, you derive a consequence that can be observed. Deduction means a logical conclusion from the general to the particular. Then you compare the prediction with experiments or observations. If it does not fit, the hypothesis must be changed or rejected.

In the 19th century the planet Uranus moved slightly differently from what the calculations predicted. The French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier suspected that an unknown planet was pulling it off course with its gravity. He calculated where in the sky this planet would have to be. In 1846 Johann Gottfried Galle in Berlin found the planet **Neptune** almost exactly at that spot. The prediction from the theory had been brilliantly confirmed.

In the 1840s the doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** worked in a large hospital in Vienna. He suspected that tiny particles from dead bodies on doctors' hands were passing on a deadly disease. From this he concluded: if everyone disinfects their hands, fewer people must die. He introduced handwashing with chlorinated lime, and the number of deaths really did fall sharply. This meant his hypothesis was well supported.

If a prediction comes true, the hypothesis is **supported**, but not yet finally proven. There could be another explanation for the same result. If a prediction does not come true, on the other hand, that speaks strongly against the hypothesis. That is why the philosopher **Karl Popper** stressed that good theories must be capable of being refuted. So science tests its ideas again and again.

A **control group** shows what happens without the influence being studied. In a medicine trial, for example, one group gets the medicine and another group gets a dummy pill. In statistics you often start with the **null hypothesis**, the assumption that there is no effect. Only if the data clearly speak against it do you reject it. In 1948 Carl Hempel and Paul Oppenheim used the deductive-nomological model to describe how scientific explanations are logically built.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reasoned guess that can be tested.
A logical conclusion from the general to a single case.
A comparison group that does not get the treatment being studied.
The assumption that there is no effect or difference.
Refuting a hypothesis through an observation.

gewusst: Neptune was first calculated with pencil and paper and only afterwards seen through a telescope.
Even a child testing whether a toy car rolls faster down a steeper ramp is working according to this method.
After its inventors, the deductive-nomological model is also called the Hempel-Oppenheim scheme.

teile.einleitung: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef on Earth and lies off the north-east coast of Australia. It is so huge that it can even be seen from space. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981, but it is severely threatened by the warming of the oceans.
wichtigste: The Great Barrier Reef lies in the Coral Sea off the Australian state of Queensland.
It stretches for around 2300 kilometres and consists of thousands of individual reefs.
The reef is built by tiny animals, the coral polyps.
The skeletons of reef corals are made of calcium carbonate, that is, limestone.
The reef has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.
In 1770 James Cook ran aground on the reef with his ship “Endeavour”.
Warming, ocean acidification and crown-of-thorns starfish threaten the corals.

abschnitte.text: The Great Barrier Reef lies in the **Coral Sea**, part of the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Queensland. It stretches for around 2300 kilometres, which makes it about six times as long as Switzerland from west to east. The reef consists of thousands of individual reefs and hundreds of islands. Large parts of it are protected as a **marine park**.

A coral reef is built by tiny animals, the **coral polyps**. Each polyp produces a small skeleton of **calcium carbonate**, that is, limestone. Over thousands of years, millions of these skeletons grow together into huge reefs. Inside the polyps live tiny algae, which make food from sunlight and give the corals their bright colours.

Thousands of species of fish, molluscs and corals live in the reef. Here the **clownfish**, known from the film “Finding Nemo”, swims protected among the tentacles of sea anemones. Sea turtles, sharks, rays, dugongs and humpback whales are also found. Many birds nest on the islands of the reef.

The Aboriginal peoples and the Torres Strait Islanders have known and used the reef for a very long time. In 1770 the British navigator **James Cook** ran aground on the reef with his ship “Endeavour” and only managed to repair it with difficulty. In 1981 the Great Barrier Reef was added to the list of **UNESCO World Heritage** sites. Today it is an important destination for divers, snorkellers and researchers.

If the sea becomes too warm, the corals expel their algae and turn white; this is called **coral bleaching**. If the heat lasts, the corals die. In addition, the sea absorbs a lot of carbon dioxide from the air and becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build limestone. When the **crown-of-thorns starfish** multiplies greatly, it eats large areas of coral bare. Australia is trying to preserve the reef with protected areas and water protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny sea animal that forms a limestone skeleton and builds reefs.
Corals turning pale when the water is too warm and they lose their algae.
A natural or cultural site that UNESCO protects as especially valuable for all humankind.
When seawater becomes more acidic because of absorbed carbon dioxide.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is considered the largest structure on Earth built by living things.
On some nights in early summer, many corals release tiny beads into the water at the same time, which looks like an underwater snowstorm.
Since 2016 there have been several major coral bleaching events on the reef.

teile.einleitung: The honeybee is an insect that lives in large colonies and makes honey. It is one of the most important animals that humans use, because it pollinates countless flowers while collecting nectar. Without bees there would be far fewer apples, cherries and other fruits.
wichtigste: A bee colony consists of a queen, many workers and, in summer, also drones.
The queen is the female bee that lays the eggs in the hive.
The cells of a honeycomb are hexagonal.
A person who keeps honeybees is called a beekeeper.
The home of a bee colony kept by a beekeeper is called a beehive.
In winter the bees form a warm cluster in the hive.
After stinging a person's skin, a honeybee usually dies.

abschnitte.text: The honeybee is about 12 to 15 millimetres long and brown to black in colour. Its body is covered with fine hairs, to which flower dust, the **pollen**, sticks. Like all insects, it has six legs, two antennae and two pairs of wings. In Europe the **western honeybee** is widespread; in Switzerland the dark bee is an old native subspecies.

A honeybee never lives alone, but in a **colony** that in summer often has 30,000 to 50,000 members. At its head is the **queen**, the only one that lays eggs, up to 2000 a day in summer. The workers clean, feed the larvae, build combs, guard the entrance and collect food. The drones are the male bees; they have no sting and only live in the colony in summer.

The foragers suck sweet **nectar** from flowers and carry it home in their honey stomach. In the hive they pass it on to other bees and store it in the hexagonal cells of the **combs**. There water evaporates until thick honey forms, and the cells are sealed with wax. The bees make the wax for the combs themselves from glands on their abdomen.

When a bee has found a good source of food, it shows the others with a **waggle dance**. The direction of the dance reveals the direction of the food source, and its duration the distance. The researcher Karl von Frisch decoded this bee language and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1973. In winter the bees huddle together in a warm **cluster** and heat it with their flight muscles while living on their store of honey.

While collecting, bees carry pollen from flower to flower; this is called **pollination**. Only pollinated flowers produce fruits such as apples, pears, cherries or rapeseed. The **beekeeper** keeps the bees in boxes, the beehives, and harvests honey and wax. Their sting has barbs, so it stays stuck in a person's skin, and the bee usually dies afterwards.

Honeybees are threatened by diseases and above all by the **varroa mite**, a parasite brought in from elsewhere. Pesticides and the lack of flowering meadows also harm them. In Switzerland, thousands of beekeepers look after their colonies. Anyone who plants flowers on their balcony and avoids poisons helps honeybees and wild bees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who keeps and cares for honeybees.
A sweet juice in flowers from which bees make honey.
Fine flower dust that helps plants to produce fruit.
A wall of hexagonal wax cells for honey and larvae.
Pollen is carried from flower to flower so that fruit can grow.

gewusst: For one jar of honey, bees together fly a distance that would go round the Earth several times.
In summer a worker lives for only about six weeks, whereas winter bees live for several months.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us humans.

teile.einleitung: The half-life is the time in which half of the atomic nuclei of a radioactive substance decay. For some substances this takes a fraction of a second, for others billions of years. With the half-life you can even work out the age of mummies and rocks.
wichtigste: The half-life describes the time in which half of the atomic nuclei of a radioactive substance decay.
After two half-lives only a quarter is left, after three an eighth.
Every radioactive substance has its own fixed half-life.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years.
The radiocarbon method is used to work out the age of old finds.
Because of long half-lives, nuclear waste has to be stored safely for a very long time.
The term is also used for medicines in the body.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and change by themselves into other nuclei. As they do so they give off radiation; this is called **radioactivity**. When a single nucleus will decay is pure chance. But with a very large number of nuclei you can say exactly when half of them will have decayed: this is the **half-life**.

Imagine a bar of chocolate with 64 pieces, half of which disappears after every half-life. After one half-life 32 pieces remain, after two 16 and after three 8. So the amount keeps getting smaller, but never drops to zero all at once. This pattern is called **exponential decay**.

Half-lives vary enormously. **Iodine-131**, which is used in medicine, has a half-life of about 8 days. **Uranium-238**, on the other hand, takes around 4.5 billion years, about as long as the Earth has existed. Some artificially made substances decay in tiny fractions of a second.

While they are alive, living things take in a little radioactive **carbon-14**. After death no new carbon-14 is added, and it decays with a half-life of about 5730 years. By measuring how much is still left, you know the age of bones, wood or fabrics. This is how it was found that the glacier mummy **Ötzi** is more than 5000 years old.

Waste from nuclear power stations remains dangerous for a very long time because of long half-lives. In Switzerland, **Nagra** is planning a deep geological repository for it in the Nördlich Lägern area, deep in the rock. Medicine also talks about half-life. It tells you how long it takes for the body to break down half of a **medicine**.

begriffe.erklaerung: When unstable atomic nuclei decay and give off radiation as they do so.
The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A method that uses carbon-14 to work out the age of old finds.
The change of an unstable atomic nucleus into another nucleus.

gewusst: Around 1900 the New Zealander Ernest Rutherford realised that radioactive substances decay according to fixed half-lives.
Thousands of radioactive atoms decay in your body every second too, for example from potassium in food.
After ten half-lives, only about a thousandth of the original amount is left.

teile.einleitung: A hedge is a strip of many shrubs and sometimes small trees that grows along field edges, paths or gardens. For many animals it is home, larder and hiding place all at once. That is why hedges are among the most valuable habitats in farmed landscapes.
wichtigste: A hedge consists of many shrubs.
In thorny hedges, birds' nests are well protected.
The red-backed shrike impales its prey on thorns.
The hazel bears hazelnuts in autumn.
Blackthorn flowers white very early in spring and later bears blue fruit.
In autumn and winter, birds find many berries in hedges.
Hedges slow down the wind and serve animals as sheltered routes through the landscape.

abschnitte.text: A **hedge** is a strip of densely growing shrubs, often mixed with a few trees. Natural hedges in the countryside are also called **field hedges**. Typical hedge shrubs in Switzerland are hazel, blackthorn, hawthorn, dog rose, elder and spindle. Garden hedges, by contrast, often consist of only a single plant species, for example box, privet or hornbeam. The more different native shrubs a hedge has, the more valuable it is for nature.

Hundreds of animal species can live in a species-rich hedge, from insects to mammals. Birds like to build their nests in **thorny** shrubs, because cats and martens find it hard to reach them there. A typical hedge bird is the **red-backed shrike**, which impales insects and small mice on thorns as if in a larder. Hedgehogs, dormice, lizards and common toads find shelter under the protection of the hedge. In spring, bees and butterflies buzz around the flowers.

**Blackthorn**, also called sloe, flowers white as early as March or April, even before it has leaves. Its blue fruit only becomes really mild after the first frost. The **hazel** bears hazelnuts in autumn, which squirrels and mice love to collect. Rose hips, elderberries and haws are important food for birds in autumn and winter. Many birds then spread the seeds and so help to plant new shrubs.

A hedge at the edge of a field **slows down the wind**, so that the soil dries out less and is blown away less. Many beneficial creatures that eat pests in the fields live in hedges. Hedges also connect woods and other habitats, so that animals can **move along them** safely. In the past, hedges also served as fences for grazing animals and provided firewood. In many cantons hedges are protected, and farmers receive payments for well-kept hedges as biodiversity areas.

To keep a hedge dense and full of life, it is cut back hard in sections every few years. You never cut the whole hedge at once, so that the animals can still find hiding places. Cutting is done in winter, not during the birds' **breeding season** in spring and summer. In the garden, native shrubs are much more valuable than hedges of thuja or cherry laurel. Cherry laurel spreads into woods and may no longer be sold in Switzerland since September 2024.

begriffe.erklaerung: A natural-looking hedge of different shrubs in the open countryside.
A small bird that impales its prey on thorns.
The variety of living things and habitats.
A plant or animal that occurs naturally in an area.

gewusst: In German the red-backed shrike is called “nine-killer”, because people used to believe it always killed nine animals before eating one.
An old hedge can live for several hundred years if it is cared for regularly.

teile.einleitung: Geckos are lizards that can run on walls, panes of glass and even upside down on the ceiling. Their secret is millions of fine hairs on their toes. Many species are out at night and live in warm countries all over the world.
wichtigste: Geckos belong to the lizards.
They can run upside down on the ceiling.
On their toes they have countless fine hairs.
They need no glue in order to stick.
To release their foot they roll their toes up.
Many geckos are out at night.
When in danger they can shed their tail.

abschnitte.text: Geckos are usually small to medium-sized **lizards** with large eyes. There are more than a thousand species, from the tiny dwarf gecko, which is less than two centimetres long, to the tokay gecko at more than 30 centimetres. Many species have no movable eyelids and clean their eyes with their **tongue**. Unlike most lizards, many geckos can make sounds, such as chirping or barking.

On the underside of their toes there are pads with millions of extremely fine hairs, the **setae**. Each hair splits at the end into hundreds of tiny tips. These come so close to the surface that weak attractive forces between the particles take effect, the **van der Waals forces**. Together they are so strong that a gecko sticks to a pane of glass, with no glue at all, and by rolling its toes it releases the foot again.

Geckos live in the warm regions of every continent except the Antarctic. You find them in rainforests, deserts, rocks and often on house walls too. In southern Europe, for example around the Mediterranean, the **Moorish gecko** is often seen. In the evening, geckos like sitting near lamps, because many insects fly around there.

Many geckos are **nocturnal** and hunt in the dark. They mainly eat **insects** such as mosquitoes, moths, crickets and spiders. If they are attacked, they can shed their **tail**, which goes on wriggling for a while and distracts the enemy. The tail grows back afterwards but usually looks a little different from before.

Researchers have studied gecko feet closely and copied them. This led to **adhesive tapes** that stick strongly and can still be removed again. Climbing robots and grippers also use this principle. When technology learns from nature, it is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reptile with scales, four legs and usually a long tail
Extremely fine hairs on a gecko's toes
Very weak attractive forces between particles that are close together
Out at night and resting during the day
Technology that takes ideas from nature

gewusst: The name “gecko” probably comes from the call of a species from Southeast Asia that sounds like “ge-ko”.
Geckos can even hang from a pane of glass holding on by a single toe.
A gecko's feet stay clean despite dust, because the hairs clean themselves as it walks.

teile.einleitung: The degree Celsius is the unit we use in Switzerland and most other countries to measure temperature. The scale is designed so that water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. It is abbreviated with the symbol °C.
wichtigste: The degree Celsius is a unit of temperature and is abbreviated °C.
The scale is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius.
Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees.
Temperatures below 0 degrees Celsius are called degrees below zero.
A healthy person has a body temperature of about 37 degrees Celsius.
From about 38 degrees Celsius, it is called a fever.
In a fridge it is about 5 degrees, in a freezer about minus 18 degrees Celsius.

abschnitte.text: The degree Celsius is a **unit of measurement** for temperature, meaning how warm or cold something is. It is measured with a **thermometer**. The scale has two fixed points: water freezes at 0 degrees and starts to boil at 100 degrees. The gap between them is divided into 100 equal steps.

The scale is named after **Anders Celsius**, a Swedish astronomer from Uppsala who lived from 1701 to 1744. He presented his temperature scale in 1742. Originally it was upside down: water boiled at 0 degrees and froze at 100 degrees. Shortly after his death the scale was turned round to the way we know it today.

Temperatures below 0 degrees are called **degrees below zero**, and then puddles and lakes freeze. Minus 5 degrees is colder than 5 degrees, because the bigger the number after the minus, the colder it is. In a fridge it is about 5 degrees, in a **freezer** about minus 18 degrees Celsius. On a hot summer's day in Switzerland it gets to about 30 degrees.

A healthy person has a **body temperature** of about 37 degrees Celsius. If it rises to about 38 degrees or more, it is called a **fever**. Fever helps the body fight germs. Body temperature is measured with a clinical thermometer, for example in the mouth, in the ear or under the armpit.

In the USA temperature is usually measured in **degrees Fahrenheit**; there, 32 degrees Fahrenheit is the freezing point of water. In science, the unit **kelvin** is often used, which starts at absolute zero. This lies at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, and it cannot get any colder. A difference of one degree Celsius is exactly the same size as a difference of one kelvin.

The highest temperature ever measured in Switzerland was 41.5 degrees Celsius, recorded in 2003 in Grono in the Grisons. The lowest temperature was measured in 1987 in **La Brévine** in the Neuchâtel Jura, at minus 41.8 degrees Celsius. That is why La Brévine is also called the **Siberia of Switzerland**. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss give all temperatures in degrees Celsius.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument for measuring temperature.
The temperature at which water turns to ice, namely 0 degrees Celsius.
The temperature at which water boils, 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
A scientific unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero.

gewusst: On high mountains, water boils below 100 degrees Celsius because the air pressure there is lower.
At minus 40 degrees, a Celsius and a Fahrenheit thermometer show exactly the same number.
Anders Celsius did not turn his scale round himself; that only happened after his death.

teile.einleitung: The urea synthesis is a famous experiment in the history of chemistry. In 1828 the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler made urea in the laboratory, a substance that until then had only been known from living things. In doing so, he showed that substances from living things do not need any mysterious life force.
wichtigste: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea artificially in Berlin.
In his experiment the urea was formed from the salt ammonium cyanate.
The urea synthesis shook the theory of vitalism.
Wöhler wrote enthusiastically to his teacher Jöns Jacob Berzelius about the discovery.
Urea has the chemical formula CO(NH2)2.
Today urea is made industrially from ammonia and carbon dioxide.
In 1845 Hermann Kolbe made acetic acid from the elements and weakened vitalism further.

abschnitte.text: **Urea** is a colourless, odourless substance that dissolves well in water. Its chemical formula is **CO(NH2)2**, so it consists of carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen. In the bodies of humans and many animals it is made in the liver. In this way surplus nitrogen from food, especially from protein, is made harmless. The kidneys then get rid of the urea in urine, which is also where its name comes from.

abschnitte.titel: The theory of the life force
abschnitte.text: Chemists used to divide substances into two groups: **inorganic** substances from non-living nature and **organic** substances from living things. Many researchers believed that organic substances could only be formed with the help of a special life force. This idea is called **vitalism**, after the Latin word “vita” for life. The famous Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius also believed in it. According to this theory, it was impossible to make organic substances in the laboratory from non-living substances.

In 1828 **Friedrich Wöhler** was working as a teacher at a trade school in Berlin. He actually wanted to make the salt **ammonium cyanate**, an inorganic compound. But when he heated the solution, he obtained white crystals that had exactly the properties of urea. The atoms of the salt had rearranged themselves into a new molecule, which has the same atoms but a different structure. Wöhler wrote enthusiastically to Berzelius that he could make urea “without needing kidneys to do it”.

Wöhler's experiment is regarded as the beginning of modern **organic chemistry**. Vitalism did not disappear immediately, however, because the starting material still came partly from animal substances. Only when Hermann Kolbe made acetic acid from the elements in 1845 was the theory weakened further. Today organic chemistry means the chemistry of carbon compounds, whether or not they come from living things. Chemists can now make millions of organic substances in the laboratory, from medicines to plastics.

Today urea is made in huge quantities in factories from **ammonia** and carbon dioxide. It is one of the most important **fertilisers** in the world, because it supplies plants with a lot of nitrogen. It is also used for synthetic resins, glue for chipboard and skin creams. In modern lorries and diesel cars, a urea solution helps to reduce harmful exhaust gases. This liquid is known by the name AdBlue.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance the body uses to get rid of surplus nitrogen, which is used today as a fertiliser.
The old theory that substances from living things can only be formed with a special life force.
The chemistry of carbon compounds.
Making a substance artificially from other substances.

gewusst: Wöhler was also one of the first people to produce the metal aluminium, which at that time was more valuable than gold.
Ammonium cyanate and urea consist of exactly the same atoms but are built differently; such substances are called isomers.

teile.einleitung: Gold is a shiny, yellow precious metal that has fascinated people for thousands of years. Its chemical symbol is Au, from the Latin word aurum. Gold does not rust and is rare, which is why it is very valuable.
wichtigste: Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au.
The symbol comes from the Latin word aurum.
Gold has the atomic number 79 and is a precious metal.
