It does not rust and keeps its shine for thousands of years.
Gold is very soft and can be beaten into wafer-thin sheets.
It is used for jewellery, coins, gold bars and electronics.
A large part of the world's gold is refined in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Gold is a **chemical element** with the atomic number 79. It is very heavy: a cube with sides 10 centimetres long weighs over 19 kilograms. Gold melts at about 1064 degrees Celsius. Because it does not react with air and water, it counts as one of the **precious metals**.

Gold occurs in veins in rock or as grains in rivers. Large gold mines are found, for example, in China, Australia, Russia and Canada. In Switzerland there is only a little gold, but in the Napf area and in some streams you can find tiny flakes by **panning for gold**. There was once even a small gold mine at Gondo in Valais.

The ancient Egyptians already made magnificent gold treasures, such as the death mask of the pharaoh **Tutankhamun**. For a long time, coins were made of gold. In the 19th century, the **gold rush** in California and Alaska attracted hundreds of thousands of people. Today, too, countries keep gold reserves as security.

Most of it is made into **jewellery**. Gold is also found in mobile phones and computers, because it conducts electricity well and does not rust. Dentists used it for fillings and crowns. Because pure gold is very soft, it is often mixed with other metals to make an alloy.

Switzerland is one of the most important hubs for gold in the world. Large **gold refineries**, mainly in Ticino, purify a significant share of the gold mined worldwide every year. The Swiss National Bank owns about 1040 tonnes of gold (as of 2025). Also well known is the **Goldvreneli**, an old Swiss gold coin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A valuable metal that hardly rusts or tarnishes, such as gold, silver or platinum.
A measure of the purity of gold; 24 carat means pure gold.
A mixture of two or more metals.
A plant where a raw material such as gold is purified.

gewusst: One gram of gold can be drawn into a wire several kilometres long.
All the gold that people have ever mined would fit into a cube with sides only about 22 metres long.
Gold leaf is so thin that light shines through it with a greenish glow.

teile.einleitung: Yeast dough is a dough that becomes light and airy thanks to tiny fungi, the yeasts. It is used to bake bread, Zopf, pizza and many sweet pastries. To turn out well, it needs warmth, time and vigorous kneading.
wichtigste: The base of a pizza is made of yeast dough.
Yeast dough rises best in a warm place.
While it rises, the bowl is covered with a cloth.
After rising, the dough should be about twice as big.
Long kneading makes the dough nice and elastic.
Fresh yeast is often bought as a small block.
In the fridge, yeast dough rises more slowly.
Around 6 December, people in Switzerland eat the Grittibänz made of yeast dough.

abschnitte.text: **Yeast dough** usually consists of flour, water or milk, salt and yeast. For sweet pastries, sugar, butter and eggs are often added. **Yeast** is a tiny single-celled fungus that can only be seen under a microscope. Fresh yeast is usually bought as a small block, but there is also dried yeast in sachets. Yeast dough is used to bake bread, pizza, Zopf, Gugelhopf and many other treats.

The yeast fungi feed on sugar that is in the flour or is added. This produces carbon dioxide, a gas, and a small amount of alcohol; this is called **fermentation**. The gas forms lots of little bubbles that puff up the dough like many tiny balloons. During baking the alcohol evaporates, and the bubbles remain as holes in the bread. Yeast feels most at home at about 30 degrees; if it gets too hot, it dies.

Yeast dough has to be **kneaded** for a long time and vigorously. As you do this, the protein in the flour, **gluten**, forms an elastic network. This network holds the gas bubbles, so that the dough does not collapse. Then the dough is left to rest covered with a cloth in a warm place until it is about twice as big. In the fridge it rises more slowly, which gives many breads an especially good flavour.

In Switzerland the **butter Zopf** is a popular Sunday bread made of plaited strands of dough. Around 6 December, St Nicholas' Day, people bake and eat the **Grittibänz**, a little man made of yeast dough with raisin eyes. On 6 January there is the Three Kings' cake, in which a small king figure is hidden. Whoever finds it may be king or queen for a day and wear a crown. The bread rolls and croissants from the baker's are also made from yeast dough.

People have been baking light bread for thousands of years; sourdough was already used in ancient Egypt. For a long time nobody knew why dough rises. Only in the 19th century did the French researcher **Louis Pasteur** show that living yeast fungi cause fermentation. Baker's yeast belongs to the same species as the yeast used to brew beer. Today it is grown in large tanks in factories.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny single-celled fungus that ferments sugar and produces gas as it does so.
A process in which yeasts turn sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
A protein in flour that forms an elastic network when kneaded.
A little man made of sweet yeast dough that people in Switzerland eat around 6 December.

gewusst: A block of fresh yeast contains billions of living yeast cells.
If you leave yeast dough to rise for too long, it collapses again, because the gluten network can no longer hold all the gas bubbles.

teile.einleitung: The genotype is the whole of the genetic make-up of a living thing. Often it also means just the alleles that a living thing has for a particular feature. The visible appearance, by contrast, is called the phenotype, and the two do not always match.
wichtigste: The genotype means the whole of the genetic make-up.
A human normally has two alleles of every gene in the body cells.
A genotype with two identical alleles such as AA or aa is called homozygous.
For a gene with the alleles A and a there are three possible genotypes.
You cannot always tell the genotype from the appearance, because dominant alleles can mask recessive ones.
The Punnett square is used to show the possible genotypes of the offspring.
Today the genotype can be worked out directly with a genetic test.

abschnitte.text: The **genotype** is, so to speak, the building plan that lies in the genes. The **phenotype** is what you can see or measure of it, such as flower colour, eye colour or body height. The phenotype depends on the genotype, but also on the environment. Two plants with the same genotype can grow to different sizes, for example, if one gets a lot of light and the other very little. The terms genotype and phenotype were introduced by the Danish researcher Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909.

Of most genes a human has two copies in the body cells, one from each parent. These can be the same or different, and the different versions are called **alleles**. In genetics they are often written with letters, a capital A for a dominant allele and a small a for a recessive one. With two alleles there are three possible genotypes: AA, Aa and aa. AA and aa are called **homozygous**, and Aa is called **heterozygous**.

A **dominant** allele prevails over a **recessive** one. In Mendel's peas the allele for violet flowers is dominant over the one for white flowers. So a plant with the genotype Aa flowers violet, just like one with AA. That is why you cannot always tell from the appearance which genotype a living thing has.

With the **Punnett square**, named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett, you can predict which genotypes are possible in the offspring. You write the alleles of one parent along the top and those of the other down the side and fill in the boxes. If you cross two pea plants with Aa, for example, the result is on average 25 per cent AA, 50 per cent Aa and 25 per cent aa. Three quarters of the plants then flower violet and one quarter white.

One example in humans are the **blood groups** of the ABO system. The alleles A and B are dominant over the allele O. A person with blood group A can therefore have the genotype AA or AO. With a **genetic test** in the laboratory it is possible today to find out directly which alleles someone carries.

Knowledge about genotypes helps in **plant breeding** and animal breeding to keep wanted properties such as resistance to diseases in a targeted way. In medicine a genetic test can show whether someone carries a recessive allele for a hereditary disease without being ill themselves. Such people are called **carriers**. The genotype also plays a part in how some medicines work.

begriffe.erklaerung: The visible or measurable appearance of a living thing.
Two identical alleles for a feature, for example AA or aa.
Two different alleles for a feature, for example Aa.
An allele that prevails over another one.
An allele that only becomes visible when it is present twice.

gewusst: For his rules, Gregor Mendel studied thousands of pea plants over several years in the monastery garden in Brno.
Identical twins have the same genotype but can look somewhat different through a different way of living.
In the four o'clock flower, crossing red and white plants gives pink flowers, because neither of the two alleles is dominant.

teile.einleitung: Hydrothermal vents are hot springs on the sea floor from which mineral-rich water streams out. Around them, in complete darkness, live astonishing creatures that manage without sunlight. Researchers even suspect that life on Earth could have begun in places like this.
wichtigste: Hydrothermal vents usually form at mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates drift apart.
The water at black smokers is over 300 degrees hot, but does not boil because of the high pressure.
In 1977 hydrothermal vents with communities of living things were discovered in the deep sea for the first time.
Bacteria there make food without sunlight through chemosynthesis.
As a source of energy they use, for example, hydrogen sulphide, which smells of rotten eggs.
Giant tube worms with red plumes grow over two metres long.
In 2000 the Lost City field with pale limestone towers was discovered in the Atlantic.

abschnitte.text: At the **mid-ocean ridges**, tectonic plates drift apart and magma rises close to the sea floor. Cold seawater seeps through cracks deep into the rock. There it is strongly heated and dissolves minerals out of the rock. Then it shoots out again as in a spring.

When the hot, mineral-rich water meets the ice-cold seawater, metal compounds settle out. This looks like black smoke, which is why these chimneys are called **black smokers**. The water can be over 350 degrees hot. It still does not boil, because the enormous **water pressure** in the depths prevents it from boiling.

Almost all food chains on Earth begin with plants that use sunlight. At hydrothermal vents it is different. Bacteria get energy from substances such as **hydrogen sulphide** and use it to build food; this is called **chemosynthesis**. Snails, mussels, crabs and worms live off them.

The **giant tube worm** grows over two metres long and has a red plume at the top. It has neither mouth nor gut, but is fed by bacteria inside its body. White crabs also live there, including a hairy species called the yeti crab. Many of these animals are found nowhere else in the world.

In 1977 researchers dived into the depths near the Galápagos Islands in the submersible **Alvin**. They found warm springs full of life, which nobody had expected. In 2000 the **Lost City** field was discovered in the Atlantic, with pale limestone towers, some of them more than 60 metres tall. Many researchers think such places may be where the first life was born.

Metals such as copper, zinc and sometimes gold are deposited at hydrothermal vents. That is why companies are interested in **deep-sea mining**. Experts warn, however, that unique habitats could be destroyed in the process. Mining in international waters is therefore fiercely disputed.

begriffe.erklaerung: An underwater mountain range where tectonic plates move apart and new sea floor forms.
Making food with energy from chemical substances instead of from light.
A chimney on the sea floor from which very hot, dark water streams out.
The part of the sea below about 200 metres, which sunlight no longer reaches.

gewusst: The discovery of 1977 was a surprise, because the expedition was actually only looking for warm water, not for life.
Some microbes at hydrothermal vents survive temperatures above 100 degrees.
Experts suspect that there are also hydrothermal vents under the ice of Saturn's moon Enceladus.

teile.einleitung: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes solid. When water gets very cold it turns into ice, namely at 0 degrees Celsius. Every substance has its own freezing point.
wichtigste: At the freezing point a liquid becomes a solid.
When water gets very cold it turns into ice.
Pure water freezes at normal air pressure at 0 degrees Celsius.
The freezing point and the melting point are at the same temperature.
Salt in water lowers the freezing point, which is why salt is spread on roads in winter.
Water expands as it freezes, which is why ice floats.
Other substances have quite different freezing points.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be solid, liquid or gaseous. These forms are called **states of matter**. If you cool a liquid, its smallest particles move more and more slowly. At the **freezing point** they arrange themselves firmly, and the liquid solidifies.

In the 18th century the Swedish scientist Anders Celsius set out a temperature scale. On today's **Celsius scale**, water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. In the USA, temperature is often measured in Fahrenheit, where the freezing point of water is 32 degrees. On warming, ice melts again at 0 degrees, which is the **melting point**.

If you dissolve salt in water, it only freezes at lower temperatures. That is why sea water only freezes at about minus 2 degrees. In winter, **road salt** is spread on roads and pavements so that no black ice forms. This effect is called **freezing point depression**.

Most substances contract when they freeze. Water is an exception; it expands by about 9 per cent. That is why ice is lighter than water and floats on top. In this way lakes freeze from the top down, and fish can spend the winter in the water underneath. This special property is called the **anomaly of water**.

Every substance has its own freezing point. **Mercury** solidifies at about minus 39 degrees, and alcohol only at about minus 114 degrees. Iron, on the other hand, is already solid at room temperature, because it only melts at about 1,538 degrees. For cars there is **antifreeze**, so that the cooling water does not freeze in winter.

In very cold winters, whole lakes sometimes freeze over in Switzerland. This is called a **Seegfrörni**. Lake Zurich was last completely frozen in 1963, and thousands of people walked on it. Smaller mountain lakes such as the lake of St Moritz freeze over almost every winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form of a substance: solid, liquid or gaseous.
The temperature at which a solid substance becomes liquid.
When a dissolved substance such as salt makes water freeze only at lower temperatures.
The Swiss word for a whole lake freezing over.

gewusst: Frozen water can split rocks, because it expands as it freezes.
Very pure water can be cooled carefully below 0 degrees without freezing, which is called supercooled water.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst, because the ice needs more space than the water.

teile.einleitung: Freezing is the process in which a liquid becomes solid because it cools down a great deal. The best-known example is water freezing into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. Whether ice cream, frozen peas or icicles: we meet freezing all the time in everyday life.
wichtigste: In freezing, a liquid becomes solid through cooling.
Pure water freezes at normal air pressure at 0 degrees Celsius.
Water expands as it freezes, which is why ice floats on water.
The opposite process, when frozen things become soft again, is called thawing.
Ice crystals can damage the cells of fruit, which is why thawed strawberries go mushy.
Frozen food keeps for a long time, because germs hardly grow in the cold.
Salt lowers the freezing point of water, which is why salt is spread on roads in winter.

abschnitte.text: In a liquid the tiny particles move about freely. As it gets colder they slow down and finally arrange themselves into a firm lattice. In water this forms **ice crystals**. The temperature at which this happens is called the **freezing point**. In the opposite process, melting, the lattice breaks up again.

Most substances contract as they become solid, but water expands by about a tenth. That is why **ice** is lighter than liquid water and floats on top. For that reason lakes freeze from the top down, and fish can survive underneath. But the expansion can also burst water pipes and glass bottles. In cracks in rock, freezing water even splits the rock, which is called **frost shattering**.

In a freezer it is usually about minus 18 degrees Celsius. Peas become hard as little stones there, because the water in them turns to ice. In fruit such as strawberries, the ice crystals pierce the cell walls, which is why they are soft and mushy after **thawing**. In quick **blast freezing**, smaller crystals form, which treats the food more gently. Over time a layer of ice builds up on the walls of the freezer, which should be defrosted now and then.

If you put syrup in a mould and place it in the freezer, you get a water ice. For cream ice cream you stir the mixture again and again as it freezes. In this way the ice crystals stay small and the ice cream becomes nicely creamy. Without stirring it would be hard and grainy.

In great cold a damp tongue can stick to metal, because the moisture freezes at once. Skin too can be damaged by severe cold, which is called **frostbite**. In winter, salt is spread on roads, because salt water only freezes below 0 degrees. In this way less black ice forms.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid; for water 0 degrees Celsius.
A tiny, regularly shaped structure of frozen water.
When something frozen becomes soft or liquid again.
Very quick freezing, so that only small ice crystals form.

gewusst: Every snowflake is made of ice crystals and usually has six arms.
Very pure water can be cooled below 0 degrees without freezing at once; this is called supercooled water.
In the 1920s the American Clarence Birdseye made deep-frozen food well known, after seeing how fish froze quickly in great cold.

teile.einleitung: A hygrometer is a measuring instrument that shows how damp the air is. It is found in weather stations, museums, cellars and many homes. The name comes from Greek: “hygros” means damp and “metron” means measure.
wichtigste: A hygrometer measures humidity.
It usually shows the relative humidity as a percentage.
At 100 per cent the air is saturated with water vapour.
A hair hygrometer makes use of the fact that hairs get longer in damp air.
A psychrometer compares a dry and a wet thermometer.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
When air cools down to the dew point, dew or fog forms.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains some invisible **water vapour**. How much it can hold at most depends on the temperature. A cubic metre of air can contain at most about 17 grams of water vapour at 20 °C, but only about 5 grams at 0 °C. The **relative humidity** tells you what percentage of this maximum amount is in the air at the moment. At 100 per cent the air is saturated.

A human hair becomes a tiny bit longer in damp air and shorter again in dry air. In a **hair hygrometer**, a bundle of hairs is stretched so that it moves a pointer. It was invented by the Geneva naturalist **Horace-Bénédict de Saussure** in the 18th century. Such instruments are still often seen today in old weather houses.

A **psychrometer** has two thermometers. One is dry, the other is inside a damp cloth sock. Because water uses up heat when it evaporates, the wet thermometer shows a lower reading, and the drier the air, the lower it is. Modern hygrometers usually work with electronic sensors that react to moisture.

If air is warmed without any water being added, the relative humidity falls. If the air cools down, on the other hand, it rises. When it reaches the **dew point**, the air is saturated and the water vapour turns into droplets. This is how dew forms on the grass, fog over the lake or misted-up glasses in winter.

Meteorologists measure humidity in order to forecast the weather. In homes, a humidity of about 40 to 60 per cent is considered comfortable. If the air is permanently too damp, **mould** can form. Museums and libraries pay close attention to it, so that paintings, wood and old books are not damaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: What percentage of the possible amount of water vapour is in the air at the moment.
Water in the form of a gas, which you cannot see.
The temperature at which the air is saturated and dew forms.
A humidity meter with a dry and a wet thermometer.
When water slowly turns into water vapour without boiling.

gewusst: The hair in a hair hygrometer is first degreased so that it reacts well to moisture.
In winter the air in heated rooms is often very dry, even though it is wet outside.
Some plant parts, such as pine cones, also react to moisture and open in dry weather.

teile.einleitung: The gram is a unit of measurement used to say how heavy light things are. It is abbreviated with the letter g. A thousand grams make one kilogram.
wichtigste: The gram is a unit of mass; in everyday life people usually say weight.
The abbreviation for gram is g.
1000 grams are 1 kilogram.
A paper clip weighs about 1 gram.
A bar of chocolate usually weighs 100 grams.
A hen's egg weighs about 60 grams, a medium-sized apple about 150 grams.
The gram is the right unit for the weight of a letter.

abschnitte.text: The **gram** is part of the metric system, which is also used in Switzerland. The base unit of mass is actually the **kilogram**, and a gram is one thousandth of it. Grams are used for light things such as letters, ingredients or fruit. For very heavy things, people use kilograms or tonnes.

1000 grams are 1 kilogram, and 500 grams are half a kilo. A **milligram** (mg) is one thousandth of a gram; it is needed, for example, for medicines. Calculating with grams is easy: 250 grams and 250 grams make 500 grams together. A litre of water weighs roughly 1000 grams, so about one kilogram.

A paper clip weighs roughly 1 gram. A bar of chocolate usually has 100 grams, a hen's egg about 60 grams and a medium-sized apple about 150 grams. Packaging states how many grams are inside; this is called the **net quantity**. At the post office, the weight in grams decides how much a letter costs.

The gram was introduced in France in 1795, shortly after the French Revolution. At that time it was decided that a gram is as heavy as a cubic centimetre of water. Later, a metal cylinder in Paris, the **International Prototype Kilogram**, determined exactly how heavy a kilogram is. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by a constant of nature, so it can be determined equally precisely anywhere in the world.

When baking, you have to weigh out flour, sugar and butter in grams so that the cake turns out well. For this you use **kitchen scales**. In shops, prices are often compared per 100 grams. In science and in pharmacies, too, things have to be weighed very precisely, sometimes to a thousandth of a gram.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter an object has; in everyday life people say weight.
1000 grams, the base unit of mass, abbreviated kg.
One thousandth of a gram, abbreviated mg.
A device used to measure the weight of things.

gewusst: The word gram comes from the Greek word “gramma”, which originally meant a small weight.
A hummingbird, one of the smallest birds, weighs only a few grams.
The old prototype kilogram in Paris was kept in a safe under glass bells for more than 100 years.

teile.einleitung: Advanced ceramics are an especially hard and heat-resistant kind of ceramic used in technology. Unlike cups or clay bricks, they are made from very pure, finely ground powders. They are found in hip joints, dental crowns, brake discs and watches.
wichtigste: Advanced ceramics are also called technical ceramics.
They are very hard, heat-resistant and do not rust.
A typical disadvantage is that they are brittle and can break when struck.
In sintering, powder is compacted into a solid body below its melting point.
Aluminium oxide is often used for the balls of hip replacements.
Thanks to transformation toughening, zirconium dioxide is tougher than most other ceramics.
Silicon nitride is valued for ball bearing balls because of its hardness and low density.

abschnitte.text: **Advanced ceramics** are materials made of inorganic, non-metallic substances. Important examples are **aluminium oxide**, zirconium dioxide, silicon carbide and silicon nitride. They are much harder than steel, withstand great heat and are hardly attacked by acids. Many ceramics do not conduct electricity and are therefore suitable as insulators.

It all starts with a very pure, fine **powder**. It is pressed or cast into shape. Then the part is strongly heated during **sintering**, but not melted. The tiny grains grow together, and a solid, dense body is created. Because the ceramic is so hard, it can afterwards only be ground with diamond tools.

Advanced ceramics are **brittle**, which means they hardly bend and break suddenly if they are loaded too much. Tiny flaws in the material, such as small pores, are the starting points for cracks. Because these flaws are randomly spread, the strength of similar samples varies greatly and is described with **Weibull statistics**. With zirconium dioxide a trick helps: at the tip of a crack the crystal lattice changes, expands and slows the crack down. So that this phase stays stable at room temperature, yttrium is often added.

For **hip replacements**, the joint balls are often made of aluminium oxide or mixed ceramics. They are very smooth, hardly wear and are well tolerated by the body. **Dental crowns** and implants are also often made of zirconium dioxide. It is as pale as a natural tooth and very strong.

In cars, insulators made of aluminium oxide sit in the spark plugs. Very fast sports cars have brake discs made of carbon-fibre-reinforced **silicon carbide**, which are light and withstand great heat. Ball bearing balls made of silicon nitride run in fast-spinning machines. Ceramic knives, scratch-resistant watch cases from Swiss manufacturers and the heat shield tiles of space shuttles are also among the uses.

begriffe.erklaerung: Compacting powder with heat without it melting.
A material is brittle if it does not give way but breaks suddenly.
An artificial replacement for a body part, for example a hip joint.
A material that does not conduct electric current.

gewusst: Silicon carbide is so hard that it is used as an abrasive and comes close to the hardness of diamond.
Ceramic knives stay sharp for a very long time, but they can shatter if they fall onto a hard floor.
Some ceramic parts can withstand temperatures of well over 1000 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: The hippocampus is a part of the brain that is especially important for memory. It helps to store new experiences and knowledge permanently, and it helps us find our way around in space. It gets its name because its shape is reminiscent of a seahorse.
wichtigste: Hippocampus is the Latin word for seahorse.
Every person has two hippocampi, one in each half of the brain.
The hippocampus lies deep in the temporal lobe of the cerebral cortex.
It helps to transfer new information into long-term memory.
Place cells in the hippocampus fire when you are in a particular place.
In the dentate gyrus, new nerve cells are formed even in adults.
The hippocampus is counted as part of the limbic system.

abschnitte.text: The **hippocampus** lies deep inside the brain, in the **temporal lobe** on both sides of the head. It is curved and looks like a seahorse, hence its name. A doctor gave it this name in the 16th century. It belongs to the **limbic system**, a group of brain areas that have to do with memory and emotions.

When you experience or learn something new, the hippocampus is especially active. It helps to transfer this information from short-term memory into **long-term memory**. Much of this happens during **sleep**, when the brain goes over the day once more. The memories are later stored mainly in the cerebral cortex. That is why enough sleep is so important when you are learning.

Much of what we know about the hippocampus comes from the American **Henry Molaison**, for a long time known in research only as “H. M.”. In 1953, during an operation to treat severe seizures, large parts of the hippocampus on both sides were removed. After that he could no longer form new memories. Older memories and skills, on the other hand, remained, and he could even practise new movement sequences. The researcher Brenda Milner studied him for decades.

In the hippocampus there are **place cells**, which fire when an animal is in a particular place. The researcher John O'Keefe discovered them in rats in 1971 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 2014. A well-known study showed that part of the hippocampus was enlarged in London taxi drivers. They have to remember thousands of streets, and this apparently trains this area of the brain.

abschnitte.titel: A part of the brain that changes
abschnitte.text: In the **dentate gyrus**, an area of the hippocampus, new nerve cells are formed even in adults. It was also here that **long-term potentiation** was first described, the lasting strengthening of connections between nerve cells. It is regarded as an important mechanism in learning. In Alzheimer's disease the hippocampus is often affected early on, which is why those affected forget new things first.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of memory in which memories remain stored for a long time.
A connecting point between two nerve cells.
A nerve cell that becomes active when you are in a particular location.
A group of brain areas that has to do with memory and emotions.

gewusst: In humans the hippocampus is only a few centimetres long.
John O'Keefe shared the 2014 Nobel Prize with May-Britt and Edvard Moser, who had discovered grid cells, which work like an inner coordinate grid.
After the operation, Henry Molaison still could not recognise a person he saw every day.

teile.einleitung: A brain-computer interface connects the brain directly with a computer. It measures brain activity and translates it into commands, so that devices can be controlled by thought alone. This technology can help people with paralysis in particular.
wichtigste: With a brain-computer interface, devices can be controlled by brain activity alone.
Brain activity is most often measured with electroencephalography, or EEG.
Invasive systems use implants such as the Utah array with about 100 fine needles.
In the BrainGate project, paralysed people were able to control a computer cursor.
Many systems use the imagining of movements as a control signal.
Researchers at EPFL and the CHUV in Lausanne helped a paralysed man to walk again with a “digital bridge”.
Invasive interfaces require an operation on the brain.

abschnitte.text: A **brain-computer interface** is a system that picks up signals from the brain and makes them understandable to a computer. In English it is called a brain-computer interface, **BCI** for short. So instead of using a keyboard, mouse or voice, you control a device directly with brain activity. That can be a cursor on a screen, a wheelchair, a robot arm or even an implant in the body.

In **electroencephalography**, or EEG, you wear a cap with electrodes on your scalp. These measure tiny electrical voltages that arise when many nerve cells work at the same time. The EEG was developed in the 1920s by the German doctor Hans Berger. It is harmless and needs no operation, but the signals are rather imprecise, because the skull and skin weaken them.

More precise signals come from **invasive** systems, in which electrodes are placed directly in the brain. One well-known implant is the **Utah array**, a tiny plate only a few millimetres across with about 100 fine needles. In the **BrainGate** research project in the USA, paralysed people used it from the 2000s to control a computer cursor or a robot arm. The disadvantage is that an operation on the brain is needed, which brings risks such as infections.

abschnitte.titel: How do you control things with thoughts?
abschnitte.text: Many EEG systems use **imagined movement**: if you imagine moving your left or right hand, the brain activity changes in particular places. The computer learns to recognise these patterns. In the **P300 speller**, rows and columns of letters flash on a screen. When the letter you want flashes, the brain shows a typical reaction about 300 milliseconds later, and in this way you can write letter by letter.

In Lausanne, researchers at the **EPFL** and the university hospital **CHUV** are working on aids for people with spinal cord injuries. In 2023 they presented a “digital bridge”: an implant reads the intention to move in the brain and sends it wirelessly to a stimulator on the spinal cord. With it, a man who had been paralysed after an accident was able to stand and take a few steps again. The team is led by the neuroscientist Grégoire Courtine and the neurosurgeon Jocelyne Bloch.

Brain-computer interfaces could give people who can no longer move or speak more independence again. Companies such as **Neuralink** are also developing implants and have been testing them in people since 2024. At the same time, important questions arise about **data protection**, because brain data is very personal. Experts are therefore discussing how a person's thoughts can be protected from misuse by technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: The measurement of electrical brain activity with electrodes on the scalp.
A conducting sensor that picks up or gives out electrical signals.
Means that something enters the body, for example through an operation.
A device or part that is placed inside the body.
Paralysis that arises when the spinal cord is damaged.

gewusst: With EEG caps, simple computer games can even be controlled by concentration alone in experiments.
A Utah array is smaller than the nail of your little finger.
Some systems can already produce whole sentences on a screen from the brain activity of paralysed people.

teile.einleitung: A crevasse is a deep crack in the ice of a glacier. It can be a few centimetres or several metres wide and dozens of metres deep. Because snow often hides crevasses, they are among the greatest dangers in the high mountains.
wichtigste: A crevasse is a deep crack in glacier ice.
Crevasses form when the ice flows over an edge or around a bend.
Crevasses hidden by snow are especially dangerous.
A thin layer of snow over a crevasse is called a snow bridge.
On glaciers, mountaineers protect each other with a rope.
To stop themselves slipping, they wear crampons under their boots.
The large crevasse at the top edge of a glacier is called a bergschrund.

abschnitte.text: A glacier is not a rigid block of ice; it flows slowly down the valley. The upper layers of ice, however, are as brittle as glass and cannot stretch as much as they like. When the ice flows over a **ledge in the terrain**, it is stretched and splits open. Cracks also form at bends or at the edges, where the ice flows more slowly than in the middle. Further down, the great pressure makes the ice pliable, which is why most crevasses are at most about 30 to 40 metres deep.

Depending on their direction, people distinguish between **transverse crevasses**, longitudinal crevasses and marginal crevasses. Transverse crevasses form across the direction of flow when the glacier becomes steeper. Where the ice tumbles over a steep slope, it breaks into towers and blocks called **séracs**. At the upper end of the glacier, where the moving ice pulls away from the solid rock or firn, lies the **bergschrund**. It is often especially wide and a difficult obstacle for mountaineers.

In winter and spring, snow covers many crevasses. A **snow bridge** forms over the crack, which from above looks like normal ground. If too much weight is put on it, or if it has been softened by the sun, it can suddenly collapse. Anyone who falls into a crevasse can be badly injured and suffer from hypothermia. That is why it is dangerous to cross a snow-covered glacier alone and without a rope.

On glaciers, mountaineers form a **rope team** and walk at a distance from one another on the same rope. If one person falls into a crevasse, the others hold them and pull them out again using a special technique. The equipment includes a climbing harness, ice axe, helmet and **crampons**, which are metal spikes under the boots. Anyone without experience of their own should only go onto a glacier with a trained **mountain guide**. In Switzerland there is a demanding training course for this with a federal certificate.

For glacier researchers, crevasses reveal a lot about how the ice moves. From their shape you can tell where the ice flows faster or more slowly. In the walls of a crevasse you can often see layers that show how much snow fell in earlier years. The deep ice there often glows blue, because dense ice absorbs red light and lets blue light through. Meltwater also reaches the bed of the glacier through moulins, which are vertical shafts in the ice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A layer of snow that covers a crevasse and can collapse.
The large crevasse at the upper end of a glacier between moving and stationary ice.
Towers and blocks of ice that form when a glacier flows over a steep step.
A group of mountaineers tied together on the same rope.
Metal spikes strapped to mountain boots to grip on ice.

gewusst: Some crevasses slowly open and close over the years, because the glacier is constantly moving.
Objects that fall into a crevasse can reappear further down the glacier decades later.

teile.einleitung: Glacier retreat means that glaciers are becoming smaller, shorter and thinner. In the Alps, glaciers have been melting since the 19th century, and faster and faster in recent decades. The main cause is global warming.
wichtigste: The main cause of today's glacier retreat is global warming.
In the record year 2022, Swiss glaciers lost around 6 per cent of their ice volume, according to GLAMOS.
In 2026, according to GLAMOS, the loss was around 5 per cent.
Dark dust and debris on the ice speed up melting.
At the Rhone Glacier, part of the ice is protected in summer with white fleece blankets.
In 2019 a funeral ceremony was held for the almost vanished Pizol Glacier.
In May 2025, the collapse of the Birch Glacier buried most of the village of Blatten.

abschnitte.text: A glacier grows when more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Because of **global warming**, summers today are longer and hotter, and the snow line lies higher. So glaciers lose more ice every year than they gain. Since the end of the **Little Ice Age** around 1850, Swiss glaciers have lost more than half of their ice.

The Swiss glacier monitoring network **GLAMOS** measures every year how much ice is lost. In the record year **2022**, around 6 per cent of the total ice volume melted away. The winter had little snow, and in summer Saharan dust lay on the ice. In 2026, too, the glaciers again lost around 5 per cent of their volume, according to GLAMOS.

Fresh snow is white and reflects a lot of sunlight. But if **dust**, soot or debris lies on the ice, the surface becomes dark. Dark surfaces absorb more heat from the sun; this is called a lower **albedo**. At the **Rhone Glacier**, part of the ice is therefore covered with white fleece blankets in summer to preserve the ice grotto for visitors.

In September 2019 a symbolic funeral ceremony took place on the **Pizol** in the canton of St Gallen. The Pizol Glacier had almost completely disappeared and was removed from the monitoring network. Many people hiked up to draw attention to climate change. Other small glaciers have also now become **dead ice** that no longer flows.

When the ice melts, steep mountain slopes lose their support and rock can break off. In May 2025, in the **Lötschental**, the **Birch Glacier** collapsed under the weight of masses of rock. Ice, rock and debris buried most of the village of **Blatten**, which had been evacuated in time beforehand. In addition, new glacial lakes form in the basins left behind, and these can burst.

At the **Morteratsch Glacier** in the Engadine, a nature trail leads to the glacier snout. Along the way, signs with dates show where the ice used to be. So you can see with your own eyes how far the glacier has retreated in over a hundred years. Experts expect that a large part of the Alpine glaciers will disappear by the end of the century if warming continues.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rise in the average temperature on Earth, mainly caused by greenhouse gases.
How strongly a surface reflects sunlight; snow has a high albedo.
Ice that has become separated from the glacier and no longer flows.
The Swiss monitoring network that observes the glaciers every year.

gewusst: The white fleece blankets at the Rhone Glacier can noticeably slow down melting in those spots.
Where glaciers used to be, the first plants and even young trees are often already growing today.
As glaciers retreat, objects sometimes come to light that were lost in the ice centuries ago.

teile.einleitung: Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI for short, is a method that lets you watch the brain at work. It shows which areas are active while someone is reading, calculating or listening to music, for example. To do this it measures where in the brain more oxygen-rich blood is flowing.
wichtigste: fMRI shows which parts of the brain are currently active.
It uses the BOLD signal, short for Blood Oxygen Level Dependent.
Haemoglobin low in oxygen behaves differently magnetically from haemoglobin rich in oxygen.
The Japanese researcher Seiji Ogawa described the BOLD contrast around 1990.
The images consist of three-dimensional picture points, the voxels.
Unlike PET, fMRI needs no radioactive substances.
Because blood flow only reacts after seconds, the time resolution is rather poor.

abschnitte.text: Ordinary **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI) makes precise pictures of the inside of the body without X-rays. **Functional** MRI goes one step further: it shows not only what the brain looks like but also what it is doing. The person lies in a tube and, for example, solves tasks on a screen. The computer then colours in the areas that were especially active.

When nerve cells work harder, the body sends more **oxygen-rich blood** there. The red blood pigment **haemoglobin** behaves differently magnetically depending on whether it is carrying oxygen or not. The strong magnetic field of the machine can measure this difference. This measurement signal is called the **BOLD signal**, and the Japanese researcher Seiji Ogawa described it around 1990.

An fMRI image consists of tiny cubes, the **voxels**, which are like three-dimensional pixels. Each voxel is usually only a few millimetres across and still contains hundreds of thousands of nerve cells. The **spatial resolution** is therefore good; you can see fairly precisely where something is happening. The time resolution is poorer, because blood flow only increases a few seconds after the activity.

Doctors use fMRI, for example before an operation on the brain, to spare important areas for speech or movement. In research it is used to study learning, memory, feelings and language. Unlike **positron emission tomography**, fMRI needs no radioactive substances. Because of the strong magnet, people with certain **metal implants**, such as some pacemakers, often cannot be examined without further checks.

In 2009, researchers put a dead salmon in an fMRI machine for fun and showed it pictures. Without proper statistical correction, they apparently found “active” places in its brain. That was of course impossible and showed that with so many voxels **false findings** easily arise. The study became famous and helped researchers to analyse their data more carefully today.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaging method using strong magnets and radio waves
The red blood pigment that carries oxygen
A measurement signal that depends on the oxygen content of the blood
A three-dimensional picture point, like a tiny cube
How finely a measuring device can detect differences in space or time

gewusst: An MRI machine is so loud that patients often wear ear protection.
The magnet of a typical MRI machine is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.
The study with the dead salmon received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012, a prize for research that first makes you laugh and then makes you think.

teile.einleitung: The genome is the whole of the genetic information of a living thing. It contains all the genes and also the many stretches of DNA in between. The human genome consists of about 3 billion pairs of building blocks and was decoded in the Human Genome Project.
wichtigste: The genome is the whole of the genetic information of a living thing.
The human genome consists of about 3 billion base pairs.
The Human Genome Project was declared complete in 2003.
Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 to 99 per cent of their genetic material.
Only about 1 to 2 per cent of the human genome are direct building instructions for proteins.
Reading the order of the bases is called sequencing.
In 1998 the genome of an animal, the nematode worm, was fully decoded for the first time.

abschnitte.text: The **genome** is something like the complete library of all the genetic information of a living thing. It is stored in the **DNA**, which in humans is spread over 23 pairs of chromosomes in the cell nucleus. Almost every cell of the body contains a complete copy. If you unrolled the DNA from a single human cell, the thread would be about two metres long.

The human genome consists of about 3 billion **base pairs**. If these letters were printed in books, they would fill hundreds of thick volumes. Only about 1 to 2 per cent of them are direct building instructions for proteins, that is **genes** in the narrower sense. The rest contains, for example, switches that turn genes on and off, as well as many stretches whose task is still being researched.

Reading the order of the bases is called **sequencing**. In 1998 the genome of an animal, the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, was fully decoded for the first time. The great **Human Genome Project** began in 1990, with researchers from many countries working together on it, and in 2003 it was declared complete. A few difficult gaps were only closed in 2022.

Comparing genomes shows how closely living things are related. Humans and **chimpanzees** agree in their genetic material to about 98 to 99 per cent. But the size of a genome says nothing about how complicated a living thing is. Some plants, for example wheat, and some lungfish have a much bigger genome than humans do.

Knowing the genome helps doctors to recognise hereditary diseases and to use medicines in a more targeted way. In **farming** it helps in breeding hardier plants. Viruses too can be identified quickly from their genome, which was important during the coronavirus pandemic, for example. Today the sequencing of a human genome costs only a tiny fraction of what the first one cost.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two matching building blocks of the DNA that are joined like the rungs of a ladder.
Working out the order of the building blocks in the DNA.
A coiled-up strand of DNA that lies in the cell nucleus.
An international research project to decode the human genetic material.

gewusst: Decoding the first human genome took over ten years; today modern machines manage it in about a day.
The genome of bread wheat is about five times as big as that of a human.
A genetic fingerprint is a DNA pattern from the genome that makes people distinguishable.

teile.einleitung: Good scientific practice means that researchers work honestly, carefully and in a way others can follow. It includes rules such as correctly citing other people's ideas, documenting experiments precisely and keeping data. Only if everyone sticks to these rules can research results be trusted.
wichtigste: Good scientific practice covers rules for honest and careful research.
In Switzerland, the “Code of Conduct for Scientific Integrity” of the Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences applies.
Other people's ideas and texts must be cited correctly with their source.
A carefully kept lab notebook makes experiments traceable.
According to the guidelines of the German Research Foundation, research data should normally be kept for ten years.
If they suspect misconduct, researchers can turn confidentially to an ombudsperson.
Good researchers consistently question their own results too.

abschnitte.text: Science depends on being able to trust results. That is why there are rules called **good scientific practice** or scientific integrity. They include honesty, care, openness and fairness towards others. Anyone who does research should describe results in such a way that others can check and repeat them.

In the **lab notebook**, researchers write down exactly what they did, when and how, and what the result was. This makes it possible later to understand how a result came about. Measurement data and samples are also kept, normally for ten years according to the guidelines of the German Research Foundation. It is also important not to leave out results just because they do not fit your own idea.

Anyone who uses ideas, texts or pictures by others must give the **source**. Passing off other people's work as your own is **plagiarism**. Inventing or falsifying data are also serious offences. Such misconduct can lead to losing a doctorate or a job. By the way, these rules also apply to presentations and projects at school.

In Switzerland, the **Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences** have published a “Code of Conduct for Scientific Integrity”. Universities and the Swiss National Science Foundation base their rules on it. At many universities there is an **ombudsperson** whom you can contact confidentially if you suspect misconduct. In Germany, the German Research Foundation lays down similar guidelines.

An important principle is that results can be repeated. In recent years, however, it turned out that many published studies did not give the same result when repeated, for example in psychology and medicine. This is called the **replication crisis**. In response, studies are now more often registered in advance and data are shared openly. Review by other experts, **peer review**, is also meant to spot mistakes early.

begriffe.erklaerung: Honesty and reliability, here in research.
Passing off other people's texts or ideas as your own.
An independent person of trust who helps with conflicts or suspected misconduct.
The checking of a piece of research by other experts before it is published.
Repeating an experiment to check whether the same result comes out.

gewusst: In the early 2000s it came to light that a young physicist in the USA had invented numerous celebrated measurement results; many of his articles were withdrawn.
A mistake that you discover yourself and correct openly is also part of good scientific practice.
Today software can automatically check whether passages have been copied from other works.

teile.einleitung: Handwashing is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect yourself from illness. With water and soap you remove dirt and germs that you might otherwise carry into your body through your mouth, nose or eyes. As early as the 19th century, the doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed how many lives clean hands can save.
wichtigste: Germs are tiny pathogens such as bacteria and viruses.
For thorough handwashing you need water and soap.
You should always wash your hands after going to the toilet and before eating.
The spaces between the fingers are easy to forget when washing.
After washing, it is best to dry your hands with a clean towel.
When you are out and there is no water, you can use a hand sanitiser.
Around 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis demanded that doctors in hospital disinfect their hands.

abschnitte.text: All day long our hands touch door handles, mobile phones, money and other people. **Germs** stick to our hands as we do so, that is, tiny pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. If we then touch our face, they easily get into the body. This is how colds, flu and stomach bugs spread, for example. Regular handwashing breaks this chain.

Water alone only rinses away part of the dirt, because grease and water do not mix. **Soap** consists of particles that bind to water on one side and to grease on the other. In this way it loosens greasy dirt and germs from the skin, and the water can rinse everything away. Many viruses have an envelope made of fat, which soap even destroys.

First wet your hands and lather them well with soap. Then rub your palms, the backs of your hands, fingertips, thumbs and above all the spaces **between your fingers** thoroughly. This takes about 20 to 30 seconds, as long as humming “Happy Birthday” slowly twice. After that, rinse everything off and dry your hands with a clean towel or paper towel.

You should wash your hands after going to the toilet, before eating and before cooking. It is also important after blowing your nose, sneezing or coughing, after playing outside and after contact with animals. When you come home, it is best to wash your hands straight away. When you are out without water, a hand **sanitiser** helps.

The doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** worked in a hospital in Vienna around 1847. He noticed that in one ward, where doctors treated patients straight after examining dead bodies, an especially large number of women patients died of fever. He demanded that the doctors disinfect their hands with **chlorinated lime**, and the deaths fell sharply. Many colleagues did not believe him at the time; today he is regarded as an important pioneer of **hygiene**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny pathogens such as bacteria and viruses.
All the measures that protect cleanliness and health.
A liquid that kills germs, often containing alcohol.
A cleaning product that loosens grease and dirt so that water can rinse them away.

gewusst: Global Handwashing Day takes place every year on 15 October.
Most people touch their face many times an hour without noticing.
In Semmelweis's time people did not yet know that bacteria cause disease; that was only proved a few years later.

teile.einleitung: The High Altitude Research Station Jungfraujoch is one of the highest research laboratories in Europe. It lies at around 3450 metres above sea level between the Jungfrau and the Mönch in the Bernese Oberland. Here researchers from many countries measure, for example, the air, the climate and radiation from space.
wichtigste: The station lies at around 3450 metres above sea level on the Jungfraujoch.
Since 1912 the Jungfrau Railway has been taking researchers up all year round.
It is run by the International Foundation HFSJG, which also runs a station on the Gornergrat.
The Jungfraujoch is an important station in the Global Atmosphere Watch network.
The station often lies above the planetary boundary layer and therefore measures especially clean air.
The air pressure there is only around two thirds of the pressure at sea level.
The landscape around it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001.

abschnitte.text: The **Jungfraujoch** is a saddle between the peaks of the Jungfrau and the Mönch on the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais. The research station lies at around **3450 metres above sea level**. On the south side begins the **Aletsch Glacier**, the longest glacier in the Alps. Since 2001 the area has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.

In 1912 the **Jungfrau Railway** was completed up to the Jungfraujoch, which made the place reachable all year round. In 1930 the International Foundation **HFSJG** was founded, and in 1931 it opened the research building. In 1937 the Sphinx Observatory was added on a rocky peak, which you reach by lift. The foundation also runs a research station on the Gornergrat near Zermatt.

The station often lies above the **planetary boundary layer**, the lowest layer of air, in which exhaust gases and dust from the ground collect. That is why you can measure air here that is hardly polluted by nearby sources. The Jungfraujoch is an important station in the **Global Atmosphere Watch** network of the World Meteorological Organization. It measures, for example, greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, fine particles and ozone. This makes it possible to track how the air over Europe changes in the long term.

At high altitude the layer of air above you is thinner, so more radiation from space reaches the ground. On the Jungfraujoch, a **neutron monitor** measures secondary particles of **cosmic radiation**. These particles are created when very fast particles from space hit the atmosphere. The measurements also help to study eruptions on the Sun.

The air pressure is only around **two thirds** of the pressure at sea level, so you get less oxygen with every breath. Some visitors feel a headache or dizziness; this is called altitude sickness. That is why research is also done here into how the human body reacts to high altitudes. Researchers from many countries work at the station, often for a few days or weeks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
The lowest layer of air, in which dust and exhaust gases from the ground collect.
Very fast particles that hit the Earth from space.
The weight of the air pressing down on a surface.

gewusst: Jungfraujoch railway station, at 3454 metres, is considered the highest railway station in Europe.
On the Jungfraujoch, water boils at around 88 degrees Celsius, because the air pressure is lower.
The Jungfrau Railway runs for most of its route through a tunnel inside the Eiger and the Mönch.

teile.einleitung: The Global Innovation Index, GII for short, is a ranking that shows how innovative the countries of the world are. It is published every year by the World Intellectual Property Organization in Geneva. Switzerland has been at the top every year since 2011.
wichtigste: The Global Innovation Index is published by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
It compares around 140 economies (as of 2026).
Switzerland has held first place without interruption since 2011, including in 2026.
In 2026, Sweden was in second place.
The index consists of two sub-indices, innovation input and innovation output.
It covers seven pillars and around 80 individual indicators.
Many indicators are needed because innovation takes many forms.

abschnitte.text: The **Global Innovation Index** measures how well a country produces and uses new ideas. **Innovation** means new things, such as new products, processes or ideas, that are actually put to use. The index was first published in 2007, originally by the business school INSEAD. Today it is published by **WIPO**, a specialised agency of the United Nations based in Geneva. Every year a new report appears with a ranking of all the countries studied.

The GII consists of two sub-indices: **innovation input** and **innovation output**. The input includes five pillars: institutions, education and research, infrastructure, market development and business development. They describe the conditions a country creates for new ideas. The output includes two pillars: knowledge and technology results, and creative results. These measure what new things actually come out at the end.

Altogether, around 80 different **indicators** go into the index. They include, for example, spending on research, the number of patents, universities, internet access and exports of high-tech products. Creative achievements such as films, brands or apps are also taken into account. A single number such as the quantity of patents would not show how varied innovation is. From all the values together, WIPO then calculates an overall score for each country.

Switzerland has taken **first place** every year since 2011, including in 2026. Reasons for this include strong universities such as ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. Swiss companies also invest a lot of money in research, for example in the pharmaceutical industry, mechanical engineering and the watch industry. Relative to its population, Switzerland registers a very large number of patents. Political stability and good infrastructure also contribute to the good result.

In 2026 Sweden was in second place behind Switzerland. Other countries that regularly rank near the top include the USA, Singapore, the United Kingdom and South Korea. China has risen sharply in recent years. Critics point out that every **ranking** simplifies things and depends on which indicators are chosen. Even so, governments like to use the GII to identify their country's strengths and weaknesses.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something new, for example a new product or process, that is actually used.
The World Intellectual Property Organization, a UN organisation based in Geneva.
A measurement that tells you something about a situation, for example the number of patents.
A legal right that allows an inventor to be the only one to use their invention for a certain time.

gewusst: WIPO, which publishes the index, has its headquarters in Geneva, in the very country that has led the ranking for years.
The index also compares how much innovation a country produces in relation to its wealth, so some poorer countries do surprisingly well.

teile.einleitung: Glow-worms are not worms but beetles that can glow with their abdomen. On warm summer nights you can see their little lights in meadows, gardens and at the edges of woods. Because they often glow around 24 June, in German they are also called St John's beetles.
wichtigste: Glow-worms are actually beetles and belong to the family of fireflies.
They are seen glowing mainly on warm summer nights.
The light is produced in the abdomen.
Their light is cold light and does not get hot.
The larvae eat snails.
Because they appear around 24 June, they are also called St John's beetles.
A lot of artificial light at night is especially disturbing for glow-worms.

abschnitte.text: Glow-worms belong to the family of **fireflies**. The males are usually slender brown beetles with wings and grow to about one centimetre long. In the common glow-worm, the females have no wings and look more like a larva, which is why people used to think they were worms. The **light organs** are on the underside of the abdomen.

The glow is produced by a chemical reaction. A substance called **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped by a protein called luciferase. This produces almost only light and hardly any heat, which is why it is called **cold light**. This ability of living things to produce light is called **bioluminescence**. With the light, males and females find each other in the dark.

The larvae usually live on the ground for two to three years and hunt mainly **snails**. They bite the snail and inject a digestive juice that dissolves the flesh. Then they can suck up their prey. The adult beetles live for only a few weeks and hardly eat anything at all. The larvae can already glow faintly too.

Several species of firefly live in Switzerland; the best known are the **common glow-worm** and the lesser glow-worm. They are seen mainly in June and July on warm evenings. They like natural gardens, hedges, woodland edges and meadows that are not mown too often. Because of St John's Day on 24 June, they are popularly called St John's beetles in German.

Glow-worms have become rarer in many places. Artificial light from street lamps and gardens outshines their signals, so they can no longer find each other. This is called **light pollution**. Slug pellets and overly tidy gardens also harm them. If you want to help them, switch off unnecessary lights at night and leave wild corners in the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A beetle family whose members can produce light; glow-worms belong to it.
The ability of living things to produce light themselves.
A light-producing substance that, together with oxygen, creates the light of glow-worms.
Too much artificial light at night, which disturbs animals and plants.

gewusst: The light of glow-worms is so efficient that researchers study it as a model for energy-saving lamps.
Some fungi, jellyfish and deep-sea fish can also produce their own light, just like glow-worms.
In some Asian countries, whole trees full of fireflies flash at the same time in the same rhythm.

teile.einleitung: Göbekli Tepe is an ancient archaeological site in south-eastern Turkey, near the city of Şanlıurfa. Around 11,500 years ago, people there put up huge stone pillars with pictures of animals, long before there was writing, metal or pottery. The site is considered one of the oldest known stone structures in the world.
wichtigste: Göbekli Tepe belongs to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, the New Stone Age before pottery was invented.
The structures were built around 9500 BC and are therefore about 6500 years older than Stonehenge.
The largest T-shaped pillars are over 5 metres tall.
Animals such as foxes, wild boars, snakes and vultures are shown on the pillars.
Among the bones found, gazelles are especially common.
The site was excavated by the German Archaeological Institute together with the Şanlıurfa Museum.
Göbekli Tepe has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018.

abschnitte.text: Göbekli Tepe lies on a hill about 15 kilometres north-east of **Şanlıurfa** in south-eastern Anatolia. The name is Turkish and means roughly “potbelly hill”. The oldest structures were built around 9500 BC in the **Pre-Pottery Neolithic**. This is the early New Stone Age, when people did not yet make clay vessels. For comparison: Stonehenge in England is about 6500 years younger, and the pyramids of Giza are about 7000 years younger.

Typical of Göbekli Tepe are large **T-shaped stone pillars**, which stand in a circle in round or oval enclosures. In the middle there are always two especially large pillars; the biggest are over 5 metres tall and weigh several tonnes. Many researchers interpret the pillars as highly simplified human figures, because some have carved arms, hands and belts. There are also **reliefs** of foxes, wild boars, snakes, scorpions, cranes and vultures. The stones were cut from the nearby limestone rock with stone tools.

During a first survey in 1963, researchers thought the mounds were an Islamic **cemetery** and did not recognise their importance. Only from 1995 did the German archaeologist **Klaus Schmidt** excavate the site systematically. The work was carried out by the German Archaeological Institute together with the Şanlıurfa Museum. Schmidt led the excavations until his death in 2014. So far only a small part of the hill has been uncovered, but measuring instruments have detected many more structures in the ground.

The builders were **hunter-gatherers** who did not yet practise proper farming. Among the animal bones found, gazelles are especially common, along with wild sheep, aurochs and wild asses. Klaus Schmidt interpreted Göbekli Tepe as a place of worship where people from the surrounding area gathered for celebrations. He also believed that the structures were later deliberately filled in with rubble. Newer research shows that people probably also lived here and that the burial was partly caused by landslides.

Göbekli Tepe changed our idea of how **settled life** began. People used to think that humans first had to become farmers before they could build large structures. Here it is clear that even hunter-gatherers built huge stone complexes together. Some of the earliest forms of cultivated grain were found very close by. Since 2018 Göbekli Tepe has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by many tourists.

begriffe.erklaerung: The New Stone Age, when people settled down and began farming and keeping livestock.
From the time before people made vessels from fired clay.
A picture carved out of a stone surface that stands out slightly.
People who live by hunting and gathering wild plants.

gewusst: A similar site with T-pillars, Nevalı Çori, disappeared under the reservoir of the Atatürk Dam; some pillars were taken to a museum beforehand.
In the surrounding area there are other sites with similar pillars, such as Karahan Tepe, which are studied together as “Taş Tepeler”, meaning stone hills.

teile.einleitung: Yeasts are tiny fungi made of just a single cell. They turn sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol and so make bread dough rise. People have been using yeasts for baking and for making drinks for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Yeasts belong to the fungi and consist of a single cell.
A yeast cell is only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size.
Without oxygen, yeasts break sugar down into alcohol and carbon dioxide; this is called alcoholic fermentation.
The carbon dioxide forms bubbles and makes yeast dough rise.
During baking, the alcohol evaporates almost completely in the heat of the oven.
Baker's yeast works best at a lukewarm temperature.
The yeast used for bread and many beers is called Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

abschnitte.text: Yeasts are **fungi**, but they do not form caps like ceps; they live as single cells. A yeast cell is only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size, so it can only be seen under a **microscope**. Yeasts usually multiply by forming small buds that break off; this is called budding. In nature they live, for example, on ripe fruit, on flowers and in the soil.

Yeasts feed on **sugar**. When there is no oxygen, they break the sugar down into alcohol and **carbon dioxide**. This process is called **alcoholic fermentation**. If there is enough oxygen, yeasts breathe and get even more energy from it.

In bread dough, the yeast produces carbon dioxide, which stays trapped in the dough as tiny gas bubbles. That is why the dough rises and becomes light and airy. Baker's yeast works best at a **lukewarm** temperature; if it gets too hot it dies, and in the fridge it becomes very slow. The small amount of alcohol evaporates almost completely in the hot oven. The Swiss **Zopf**, a plaited loaf, is usually baked with yeast too.

The yeast **Saccharomyces cerevisiae** is used for baking, for many beers and for wine. It is also an important subject of research, because its cells are built in a similar way to human cells. In 1996 it was the first living thing with a cell nucleus whose entire genetic material was decoded. Today genetically modified yeasts produce medicines such as insulin, for example.

Bread was already baked with yeasts in ancient Egypt, even though people did not yet know about them. Only in the 19th century did the French researcher **Louis Pasteur** show that living yeast cells cause fermentation. After that, yeast could be grown deliberately and sold as baker's yeast. Some yeasts, however, can also cause illness, for example fungal infections of the skin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The breakdown of sugar without oxygen; in yeasts this produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
A gas that also fizzes in sparkling mineral water and is produced when we breathe out.
The way yeast multiplies, in which a small daughter cell grows out of the mother cell.
A living thing that consists of only a single cell.

gewusst: A block of fresh baker's yeast contains many billions of yeast cells.
The word Saccharomyces means roughly “sugar fungus”.
Without yeasts there would be no light, airy Zopf on Sunday mornings.

teile.einleitung: Face recognition is a technology with which computers recognise people by their face. It is found in many smartphones, at airports and in some surveillance cameras. The technology is handy, but it also raises important questions about data protection and fairness.
wichtigste: Face recognition identifies people by their face.
What is measured are, for example, the distance between the eyes and the shape of the nose.
Methods that recognise people by bodily features are called biometrics.
Many people unlock their smartphone with face recognition.
Cameras with face recognition in public places are controversial, because they can be used for surveillance.
Some systems recognised people with dark skin less well, because the training pictures showed too few such faces.
In the chip of the Swiss passport, a picture of the face and fingerprints are stored.

abschnitte.text: In **face recognition** a computer compares a face in a photo or video with stored faces. It belongs to **biometrics**, that is, to the methods that recognise people by bodily features, like fingerprints or the iris. The difference from **face detection** is important: a camera that marks faces with a frame and focuses on them only finds faces. But it does not know who the person is.

First the system looks for a face in the picture. Then it measures characteristic points, such as the **distance between the eyes**, the shape of the nose, the chin and the lips. Out of these measurements a kind of number code arises, a so-called **template**. Today it is mostly artificial neural networks that learn from millions of photos which features make a face unmistakable.

Many people unlock their **smartphone** with their face. Some devices project invisible infrared dots onto the face for this and build up a three-dimensional picture, so that a simple photo is not enough. At airports, gates compare the face of travellers with the picture in the **passport**. In the chip of the Swiss passport, a picture of the face and fingerprints are stored.

Face recognition is not perfect. Studies showed that some systems recognised people with dark skin considerably less well. The reason was that the **training pictures** contained too few such faces. If a person is wrongly recognised, that can have serious consequences, for example when the police suspect the wrong person. Experts then speak of distortion, or **bias** in English.

Cameras with face recognition in public squares could follow every person's every move. That is why their use is very controversial. Critics fear that people would then no longer move about freely or take part in demonstrations. In Switzerland and in the EU there is discussion and regulation about when such systems are allowed, because face data count as especially sensitive **personal data**.

Our brain too is a master of face recognition. Even babies especially like to look at faces. In the brain there are areas that have specialised in recognising faces. Some people have an inborn **face blindness** and recognise even good acquaintances only by the voice, the hairstyle or the way they walk.

begriffe.erklaerung: Recognising people by bodily features such as the face, fingerprints or the iris.
Finding faces in a picture without recognising the person.
Examples from which a computer program learns.
The protection of personal information against misuse.
A weakness in which someone can hardly recognise faces again.

gewusst: People sometimes see faces in plug sockets, cars or clouds, partly because our brain pays such strong attention to faces.
Identical twins can fool some face recognition systems.
Face recognition is also used to recognise rare animals such as chimpanzees or bears again in photos.

teile.einleitung: A common ancestor is a living thing or a species from which two or more species of today descend. According to the theory of evolution, all living things on Earth are related to one another, as in a gigantic family tree. The more closely two species are related, the more recently their last common ancestor lived.
wichtigste: Humans and chimpanzees have a common ancestor.
It lived about 6 to 7 million years ago.
The last common ancestor of all living things today is called LUCA.
Homologous organs have the same basic design because they come from a common ancestor.
Almost all living things use the same genetic code.
Vestigial organs such as the pelvic bones of whales are traces of their ancestors.
The closest living relatives of whales today are the hippopotamuses.

abschnitte.text: The idea that all living things are related was put forward by the British naturalist **Charles Darwin** in his 1859 book “On the Origin of Species”. You can picture life as a gigantic **family tree**. Every branching stands for a common ancestor from which two different lines developed. Importantly: humans do not descend from chimpanzees; both descend from a common ancestor that was neither human nor chimpanzee.

The last common ancestor of **humans and chimpanzees** lived about 6 to 7 million years ago in Africa. Since then both lines have developed separately. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 to 99 per cent of their genetic material. Further back lie the common ancestors with gorillas, orang-utans and finally with all other **mammals**.

Right at the root of the family tree stands **LUCA**, short for “Last Universal Common Ancestor”, that is, the last common ancestor of all living things. LUCA was probably a simple single-celled organism that lived about 4 billion years ago. All bacteria, fungi, plants and animals descend from it. One important sign of this is the **genetic code**: almost all living things use the same “language” to translate genetic information into proteins.

A human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper look quite different and serve different purposes. All the same, they have the same bones in the same arrangement: upper arm, ulna, radius and finger bones. Such organs are called **homologous organs**, because they come from the same basic design of a common ancestor. **Vestigial organs** such as the small pelvic bones of whales have almost lost their original purpose and recall ancestors that still had legs.

Whales descend from land mammals that lived about 50 million years ago. One of the earliest known ancestors of whales is **Pakicetus**, an animal about the size of a wolf whose fossils were found in Pakistan. Comparisons of genetic material show that **hippopotamuses** are the closest living relatives of whales. So whales and hippopotamuses had a common ancestor that lived on land and perhaps partly in water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
A diagram showing how species are related to one another.
Short for the last common ancestor of all living things today.
Body parts with the same basic design, because they come from the same ancestor.
Body parts that have largely lost their earlier purpose.

gewusst: Fungi too are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Many human genes occur in a similar form in fruit flies and yeasts.
Some giant snakes such as pythons still have tiny remains of hind legs, visible as small spurs.

teile.einleitung: Galen of Pergamon was a Greek doctor who lived in the Roman Empire in the 2nd century AD. He was a doctor to gladiators and later to emperors. His teachings shaped medicine in Europe and the East for more than 1,300 years.
