wichtigste: Galen was a doctor from Pergamon in Asia Minor.
At the beginning of his career he treated gladiators.
Emperor Marcus Aurelius brought him to the court in Rome as a doctor.
Galen greatly developed the theory of the four humours.
Because opening human bodies was forbidden, he studied animals above all.
In the 16th century Andreas Vesalius corrected many of his errors.
The field of galenics in pharmacy is named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Galen** was born around 129 AD in **Pergamon**, a rich city in Asia Minor, today's Turkey. His father was an architect and had him well educated. Galen studied medicine, among other places in **Alexandria** in Egypt, at that time the most important place for science. He died around 200 or a little later; the exact year is not known for certain.

Back in Pergamon he became doctor to the **gladiators** around 157. He treated their wounds and watched over their food and training. Through the deep wounds he could look inside the body, and he called them “windows into the body”. Later he moved to **Rome**, where he quickly became famous.

Emperor **Marcus Aurelius** brought Galen to his court as a doctor. He also looked after the emperor's son Commodus. Galen wrote hundreds of books on anatomy, diseases and remedies. Many of them have survived to this day and are among the most extensive works of the ancient world.

Galen greatly developed the **theory of the four humours**, which went back to Hippocrates. According to this theory the body consists of four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, and illness arises when they get out of balance. Because human bodies could not be opened in Rome, he studied **animals** such as monkeys and pigs. He showed, for example, that blood flows in the arteries and not air, as many believed at the time.

In the Middle Ages, Galen was regarded in Europe and in the Arab world as the greatest authority in medicine. But because he had studied animals, his books contained errors about human beings. In 1543 the anatomist **Andreas Vesalius** published a great work that corrected many of these errors. **Galenics** is still named after Galen today: the study of how medicines are made in the form of tablets, ointments or syrups.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of the structure of the body
An old theory according to which health depends on the balance of four body fluids
The field of pharmacy concerned with making forms of medicine
An ancient city in Asia Minor, today in Turkey
A fighter who fought in the arena before an audience in ancient Rome

gewusst: Galen showed with a pig that a particular nerve is responsible for the voice: when it was cut, the animal no longer squealed.
For more than 1,300 years hardly anyone dared to contradict Galen.
Far fewer of the gladiators Galen looked after are said to have died than under his predecessor.

teile.einleitung: Paper is one of the most important inventions of humankind. It was invented in China about 2000 years ago and reached Europe by way of the Arab world. Without paper there would be no books, newspapers or school exercise books as we know them.
wichtigste: The Chinese official Cai Lun is traditionally regarded as the inventor of paper.
According to tradition, Chinese prisoners brought papermaking to Samarkand in the year 751.
Papermaking first reached Europe by way of Spain.
In medieval Europe, paper was made above all from rags.
Paper was cheaper to make than parchment.
Printing with movable type around 1450 made the need for paper rise sharply.
In Basel a museum in an old paper mill shows how paper is made by hand.

abschnitte.text: Before there was paper, people wrote on quite different materials. In Egypt they used **papyrus**, which was pressed from the pith of a marsh plant and which gave paper its name. In Europe in the Middle Ages people wrote above all on **parchment**, that is, on specially treated animal skin. Parchment was very durable but expensive, because the skins of many animals were needed for one thick book.

The Chinese official **Cai Lun**, who presented the method to the emperor around the year 105 AD, is traditionally regarded as the inventor of paper. Finds show, however, that there were simple papers in China even earlier. Cai Lun used tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets. The fibres were pounded, stirred into water and lifted out as a thin layer with a fine sieve, then dried.

For a long time the Chinese kept the method secret. According to tradition, Chinese prisoners brought the art to **Samarkand** in Central Asia in the year 751. From there it spread in the Arab world, and an important papermaking industry grew up in Baghdad. By way of North Africa the knowledge reached **Spain**, where the first paper mills in Europe were working in the 11th and 12th centuries.

In medieval Europe, paper was made above all from **rags**, that is, from old scraps of linen and hemp cloth. In **paper mills**, water wheels drove big hammers that pounded the rags into a fibre pulp. In Italy, especially in Fabriano, the **watermark** was invented in the 13th century, a mark in the paper that you see against the light. Because paper was cheaper than parchment, more people could soon afford written documents.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz invented **printing** with movable type. Now books could be printed in large numbers, and the need for paper rose sharply. Soon rags became scarce, and people looked for new raw materials. In the 19th century they learned to make paper from **wood**, and since then paper has been a cheap everyday product.

In Switzerland too the first paper mills appeared in the 15th century, among other places in the area of Fribourg and in Basel. With its printing houses, **Basel** became an important centre of book printing. In the St. Alban valley stands the **Basel Paper Mill** today, a museum where you can make paper by hand yourself and try out old printing machines. Today a large part of waste paper in Switzerland is collected and recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A writing material made from treated animal skin.
The writing material of the ancient Egyptians, made from a marsh plant.
A workshop in which paper was made with water power.
A mark in the paper that you only see well against the light.
To lift a thin layer of fibre pulp out of the water with a sieve in order to form a sheet.

gewusst: Banknotes still have watermarks today, so that forgeries can be recognised more easily.
Old rag paper is often more durable than many papers from the 19th and 20th centuries.
The word “paper” comes from the Greek word for the papyrus plant.

teile.einleitung: The Glacier Garden Lucerne is a natural monument and museum right in the middle of the city of Lucerne. There you can see huge glacier potholes that meltwater drilled into the rock at the end of the last Ice Age. Right next to it is the famous Lion Monument.
wichtigste: In the Glacier Garden Lucerne you can marvel at large glacier potholes in the rock.
The glacier potholes are about 20,000 years old.
They formed when meltwater swirled stones round and round in circles.
The Glacier Garden was discovered in 1872.
The man who discovered it actually wanted to build a wine cellar.
The Glacier Garden has a fun mirror maze.
The Lion Monument lies right next to the Glacier Garden.

abschnitte.text: The Glacier Garden lies in the north of Lucerne's old town, on Denkmalstrasse. Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne in Central Switzerland. During the last Ice Age the whole area was buried under the mighty **Reuss Glacier**. The ice here was many hundreds of metres thick.

Under the glacier, a lot of meltwater flowed with great force. Where it plunged through cracks onto the rock, it swirled stones round in circles. Like a drill, these stones ground round holes into the sandstone, which are called **glacier potholes**. In some potholes you can still see the round **grinding stones** that drilled the hole. You can also see glacial polish, rock surfaces that the ice has ground smooth.

In 1872 Josef Wilhelm Amrein-Troller wanted to build a **wine cellar** on this spot. While digging, he came across the strange round holes in the rock. Experts realised that they had been made by a glacier. Amrein-Troller uncovered the potholes and turned them into a sight for visitors.

The sandstone itself is much older than the glacier potholes. It formed around 20 million years ago, when a warm, shallow sea lay here. That is why you can find fossilised shells and even imprints of palm leaves in the rock. In the museum you learn how the landscape of Switzerland changed from a subtropical beach to the Ice Age and up to the present day.

A special attraction is the **mirror maze** in Moorish style, which is reminiscent of the Alhambra palace in Spain. Among all the mirrors you easily lose your sense of direction. Right next door is the **Lion Monument**, a dying lion carved into the rock. It commemorates the Swiss Guards who died in Paris in 1792 defending the royal palace.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round hole in the rock that meltwater has ground out with swirling stones.
A round stone that was swirled around in a glacier pothole and drilled the hole.
A long period when the Earth was much colder and glaciers covered large areas.
A rock surface ground smooth by ice and the stones it dragged along.

gewusst: Without the wish for a wine cellar, the Glacier Garden might never have been discovered.
The mirror maze was originally built for the Swiss National Exhibition of 1896 in Geneva.
In Lucerne there was once a warm sea and later a thick glacier, and you can discover both in the same place.

teile.einleitung: Garden cress is a small plant with a slightly hot taste that is eaten as a seasoning and in salads. It sprouts so quickly that you can almost watch it growing. That is why it is the most popular plant for experiments in the classroom.
wichtigste: Garden cress belongs to the cabbage family, like mustard and radishes.
Cress seeds absolutely need water in order to sprout.
You can sow cress very easily on damp cotton wool.
After 1 to 2 days you see the first seedlings.
After about a week you can harvest the cress.
Cress grows towards the light; in the dark it stays pale and yellowish.
Fresh cress is popular on a slice of bread and butter.

abschnitte.text: Garden cress has the scientific name **Lepidium sativum**. It belongs to the **cabbage family**, which also includes mustard, cabbage and radishes. If you let it grow, it reaches up to half a metre in height and forms small white flowers. But it is usually harvested as a young plant with two small leaves.

A cress seed needs above all **water** in order to sprout. It soaks itself full, swells up, and the seed coat splits. First a small **root** comes out and grows downwards. Then the stem pushes upwards with the first two little leaves, the **seed leaves**. After just 1 to 2 days you see the first seedlings.

Because cress grows so quickly, it is perfect for **experiments**. You sow it on damp cotton wool, kitchen paper or soil and watch what happens. If you put a dish on the windowsill, the little plants grow towards the **light**. In a dark cupboard they grow long and thin and stay pale and yellowish, because they lack the green **chlorophyll**. Without water, on the other hand, nothing sprouts at all.

After about a week you can harvest the cress with scissors. It tastes **slightly hot**, similar to mustard or radish. This hot taste comes from so-called **mustard oils** in the plant. Cress is especially popular on bread and butter, in salads, in quark or on eggs.

Cress contains plenty of **vitamin C** as well as minerals such as iron and calcium. It can be grown on the windowsill all year round, even in winter. You need neither a garden nor much space for it. Garden cress probably comes originally from western Asia and is now grown almost everywhere in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a young plant begins to grow out of a seed.
One of the first leaves that come out of the seed.
The green pigment of plants with which they use sunlight.
A plant family whose flowers have four petals in the shape of a cross.

gewusst: Cress even sprouts on a wet sponge or in an empty eggshell.
Cress bends towards the window because the cells on the shady side grow faster.
The ancient Greeks and Romans already knew cress as a seasoning and a medicinal plant.

teile.einleitung: Henry Dunant was a Geneva businessman who came up with the idea for the Red Cross. After seeing the suffering of thousands of wounded soldiers in 1859, he worked to make sure that all the wounded in war receive help. For this, in 1901, he was one of the first people to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva in 1828.
He was originally a businessman.
In 1859, at the Battle of Solferino in Italy, he saw thousands of wounded men.
Afterwards he wrote a book about his experiences to shake people up.
His idea led to the founding of the Red Cross.
In 1901 he received the first Nobel Peace Prize.
His birthday, 8 May, is today World Red Cross Day.

abschnitte.text: Henry Dunant was born on **8 May 1828** in Geneva. His family was devout and helped poor people, which shaped him early on. He became a **businessman** and founded a company in Algeria, which at that time belonged to France. For this business he needed permission from the French emperor Napoleon III.

To meet the emperor, Dunant travelled in 1859 to northern Italy, where France and Sardinia were fighting against Austria. On 24 June 1859 he arrived in the area after the **Battle of Solferino**. Thousands of wounded soldiers lay without help on the battlefield and in the villages. Together with women from the town of Castiglione, Dunant organised help for all the injured, no matter which side they had fought on.

In 1862 Dunant published the book “**A Memory of Solferino**”. In it he described the terrible suffering and made a proposal: in every country, volunteers should be ready to help those wounded in war. The book was read all over Europe and moved many people, including kings and governments. It was the beginning of a worldwide movement.

abschnitte.titel: The founding of the Red Cross
abschnitte.text: In 1863 Dunant and four other men founded a committee in Geneva, which became the **International Committee of the Red Cross**. As early as 1864, several states signed the first **Geneva Convention**, which regulates the protection of the wounded and of helpers in war. As a symbol they chose a red cross on a white background, the reverse of the Swiss flag. In Islamic countries a red crescent is often used.

Dunant's businesses in Algeria failed, and in 1867 he was bankrupt. He left Geneva and lived poor and almost forgotten for many years. He spent the last years of his life in **Heiden** in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, where a journalist rediscovered him. In 1901, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy, he received the first **Nobel Peace Prize**, and he died in Heiden in 1910.

begriffe.erklaerung: A worldwide organisation that helps people in wars and emergencies.
An agreement between states to protect the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war.
A famous award for people who work for peace.
Not belonging to any side, not favouring anyone.

gewusst: Dunant did not spend the Nobel Prize money on himself; he left it to charitable causes.
Today a Henry Dunant Museum in Heiden commemorates his life.
The Red Cross and Red Crescent have millions of volunteers worldwide.

teile.einleitung: The heliocentric model says that the Sun is at the centre and the Earth, like the other planets, circles around it. Today we know this is true, but for more than a thousand years most people believed something else. The switch to this view of the world is one of the greatest upheavals in the history of science.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Greek word “helios” for sun.
The older geocentric model put the Earth at the centre of the universe.
As early as the 3rd century BC, Aristarchus of Samos had placed the Sun at the centre.
Nicolaus Copernicus described the heliocentric model in a famous book in 1543.
Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei later provided important evidence and improvements.
In 1838 Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel measured the first stellar parallax and so confirmed the movement of the Earth.
A great upheaval in thinking is today called a Copernican revolution.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people thought the Earth rested at the centre and the Sun, Moon and stars turned around it. This **geocentric model** was described by the scholar Claudius Ptolemy around AD 150 in his work the **“Almagest”**. It shaped thinking in Europe and the Arab world for more than 1000 years. It also fitted everyday experience well, because we do not feel the Earth moving.

abschnitte.titel: Copernicus puts the Sun at the centre
abschnitte.text: The astronomer **Nicolaus Copernicus** lived in what is now Poland. In his book “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium”, which appeared in 1543, he placed the Sun at the centre. According to his idea, the Earth turns once a day on its own axis and once a year around the Sun. In his time six planets were known: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and **Saturn**.

abschnitte.titel: The puzzle of the Mars loop
abschnitte.text: In the sky, Mars sometimes seems to trace a loop backwards. In the old model, complicated extra circles were needed to explain this. In the heliocentric model the explanation is simple: the Earth travels faster on its inner orbit and **overtakes** Mars. It is similar to when a fast car overtakes a slower one on the motorway, and the slower one briefly seems to move backwards.

At the beginning of the 17th century, **Johannes Kepler** found that the planets move around the Sun not on circles but on **ellipses**. From 1610 **Galileo Galilei** used a telescope to observe moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus. This fitted the new model well. Because of it, Galileo came into conflict with the Church and was put on trial in 1633.

In 1838 **Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel** achieved an important proof: he measured the **parallax** of a star, a tiny apparent shift caused by the Earth's movement around the Sun. In 1851 **Léon Foucault** in Paris showed with a very long pendulum that the Earth rotates. Today we also know that the Sun is not the centre of the whole universe either, but one of billions of stars in our Milky Way.

begriffe.erklaerung: With the Earth at the centre.
With the Sun at the centre.
The apparent shift of an object when you look at it from two different places.
A shape like a stretched-out circle.

gewusst: Copernicus is said to have held a printed copy of his book in his hands only shortly before his death in 1543.
The pendulum with which Foucault demonstrated the Earth's rotation in the Panthéon in Paris in 1851 hung on a wire 67 metres long.
The idea of the Sun at the centre had already been proposed by Aristarchus around 1800 years before Copernicus.

teile.einleitung: Friedrich Miescher was a doctor and naturalist from Basel. In 1869 he discovered a substance in cell nuclei, which he called nuclein. Today we know that it was DNA, the building plan of all life.
wichtigste: Friedrich Miescher lived from 1844 to 1895 and came from Basel.
His uncle, the anatomist Wilhelm His, encouraged his path into research.
In 1869 he discovered nuclein in the laboratory of Felix Hoppe-Seyler in Tübingen.
He obtained the cell nuclei from white blood cells in the pus on bandages.
The nuclein contained a lot of phosphorus and so differed from proteins.
In 1889 Richard Altmann coined the term “nucleic acid”.
Later Miescher studied the salmon of the Rhine in Basel.

abschnitte.text: **Friedrich Miescher** was born in Basel in 1844 and came from a family of doctors and scholars. He studied medicine but, because of hearing problems, did not want to work as a doctor with patients. His uncle **Wilhelm His**, a well-known anatomist and embryologist, encouraged him to become a researcher. In 1872 Miescher became professor of physiology at the University of Basel.

In 1868 Miescher went to **Tübingen** to the laboratory of the chemist **Felix Hoppe-Seyler**, which was in an old castle kitchen. He wanted to find out what cells are made of. As material he used white blood cells from the pus on used bandages from a hospital. In 1869 he found an unknown substance in the cell nuclei, which he called **nuclein**, after the Latin word for kernel.

To get the cell nuclei clean, he dissolved the proteins with the digestive enzyme **pepsin**, which he obtained from pig stomachs. What was left were the nuclei, from which he extracted the nuclein. On examining it, he noticed that the substance contained a great deal of **phosphorus**. That was a clear sign that it was not an ordinary protein.

Back in Basel, Miescher studied the **salmon** that at the time swam up the Rhine. He found that during their long migration they hardly eat and live off their muscles. From the salmon he also obtained larger amounts of nuclein. He worked a great deal and died in Davos in 1895 of tuberculosis at the age of only 51.

Miescher did not yet guess what role his substance plays. In 1889 **Richard Altmann** called it **nucleic acid**. Only in 1944 did researchers show that DNA carries the genetic information, and in 1953 its double helix structure was discovered. In Basel the **Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research** keeps the discoverer's memory alive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Miescher's name for the substance from the cell nucleus, now called DNA
The giant molecule that stores the genetic information of all living things
The control centre of the cell, where the DNA is found
A digestive enzyme from the stomach that breaks down proteins
The study of how the body works

gewusst: Miescher's discovery was only published in 1871, because his boss Hoppe-Seyler wanted to check the results himself first.
The laboratory in Tübingen where DNA was discovered was in the former kitchen of Hohentübingen Castle.
Miescher never fully realised the importance of his find; only decades after his death did it become clear that he had discovered the substance of inheritance.

teile.einleitung: Yawning is a reflex in which you open your mouth wide, breathe in deeply and then slowly breathe out again. Almost all people and many animals yawn. Astonishingly, researchers still do not know exactly why we do it.
wichtigste: When yawning you open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply.
People yawn especially often when they are tired.
Yawning is catching; you often yawn when someone next to you yawns.
Even reading about yawning can make you yawn.
Many animals yawn too, and dogs even catch it from people.
Why we yawn is not yet fully explained.
Out of politeness you put your hand in front of your mouth when yawning.

abschnitte.text: When yawning you open your mouth very wide, your jaw drops and your lungs fill with a lot of air. Often you stretch your body too and your eyes water a little. A yawn usually lasts only a few seconds. Because the muscles in the throat move while you yawn, you often feel the pressure in your ears **equalise**.

Yawning is a **reflex** that can hardly be suppressed. People used to think the body wanted to take in more oxygen, but that could not be confirmed. A more recent idea says that yawning **cools the brain**, because cooler air and more blood flow through the head. Other researchers think that yawning wakes the body up, for example when changing between rest and activity.

People yawn especially often in the morning after waking up and in the evening before falling asleep. **Boredom** also often leads to yawning. Some athletes yawn just before the start because they are nervous. People yawn even before birth, as ultrasound pictures show.

If you see or hear someone yawn, you often have to yawn yourself, which is called **contagious yawning**. According to research, you catch it most easily from family and friends. That is why experts suspect it has something to do with empathy and closeness. Small children usually only start catching yawns after a few years of life.

Not only people yawn but also dogs, cats, monkeys, birds and even some fish. Dogs sometimes catch yawns from their humans. **Baboons** often yawn although they are not tired, to show their large canine teeth and warn others. Lions and hippos also show their teeth impressively when they yawn.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement the body makes by itself, without you wanting it.
Yawning that is set off because you see someone else yawn.
Matching the air pressure in the ear to the pressure outside.
The bones that hold the teeth and that open the mouth.

gewusst: You have probably yawned at least once while reading this article.
Chimpanzees also catch yawns from others of their own kind.
In great heat people yawn less often than on cooler days, which fits the idea of cooling the brain.

teile.einleitung: The Henle-Koch postulates are rules that can be used to test whether a particular pathogen really causes a disease. They go back to the doctor Jakob Henle and his student Robert Koch. In the 19th century these rules helped to find the pathogens behind many dangerous diseases.
wichtigste: A postulate is a requirement that must be met.
As early as 1840, Jakob Henle set out basic ideas about pathogens.
In the 1880s his student Robert Koch turned them into clear test rules.
The pathogen must be detectable in every case of the disease.
It must be possible to isolate it and grow it in pure culture.
The pure culture must cause the same disease in a healthy test animal.
With viruses and with healthy carriers, the rules reach their limits.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, many doctors still did not know what caused diseases. Some believed in bad air, the so-called miasmas. The **Henle-Koch postulates** give clear instructions on how to prove that a particular **microorganism** causes a disease. They became one of the foundations of modern bacteriology.

**Jakob Henle** was a German anatomist and doctor. As early as 1840 he wrote that tiny living pathogens could cause diseases, but he could not yet prove it. His student **Robert Koch** later discovered the pathogen that causes anthrax, in 1882 the tuberculosis pathogen and after that the cholera pathogen. Koch received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1905.

First, the pathogen must be detectable in every case of the disease. Second, it must be **isolated** from the sick body and grown in a **pure culture**, that is, completely without other germs. Third, the pure culture must cause the same disease in a healthy test animal. A fourth postulate is often added: that the pathogen can be isolated again from this animal.

Today we know that there are **healthy carriers** who carry a pathogen inside them without becoming ill. This contradicts the first postulate in its strict form. **Viruses** only multiply in living cells and cannot be grown on an ordinary culture medium. The leprosy pathogen does not grow on an artificial culture medium either, yet it is clear that it causes leprosy.

The postulates were a big step towards medicine based on **evidence**. Later, adapted rules were formulated for viruses and for individual genes of pathogens. But the basic idea has stayed the same: a connection must be tested carefully, not just assumed. This way of thinking still helps today when new diseases appear.

begriffe.erklaerung: A requirement or condition that must be met.
A culture in which only a single kind of microorganism grows.
A living thing or particle that can cause a disease, for example a bacterium or virus.
A substance containing nutrients on which bacteria are grown in the laboratory.

gewusst: To grow bacteria, Robert Koch's laboratory used agar, a substance made from algae that is still used today.
The flat glass dish for bacterial cultures is named after Julius Petri, one of Robert Koch's assistants.
The leprosy pathogen was discovered by the Norwegian Gerhard Armauer Hansen as early as 1873.

teile.einleitung: The cerebrum is the largest part of our brain. This is where thoughts, language, memories and conscious perception arise. When you read, do sums or make plans, it is mainly your cerebrum at work.
wichtigste: The cerebrum consists of two halves joined by the corpus callosum.
The surface is heavily folded so that more cerebral cortex fits into the skull.
Each half of the cerebrum has four lobes with different tasks.
The occipital lobe mainly processes what we see.
Broca's area is important for speaking, Wernicke's area for understanding language.
The white matter inside consists mainly of nerve fibres with a myelin sheath.
The left half of the brain mainly controls the right side of the body, and vice versa.

abschnitte.text: The cerebrum sits like a large cap over the other parts of the brain. It consists of a left and a right half, the **hemispheres**. They are connected by a thick bridge of nerves, the **corpus callosum**, with many millions of nerve fibres. In this way both halves can constantly exchange information.

On the outside is the **cerebral cortex**, a layer of grey matter only a few millimetres thick and full of nerve cells. The surface has many ridges and grooves, rather like a walnut. Spread out, the cortex would be about the size of a pillowcase. Thanks to the folds, it still fits into the skull.

The **frontal lobe** behind the forehead is important for planning, making decisions and controlling movements. The **parietal lobe** at the top processes touch sensations from the skin and helps with finding your way in space. The temporal lobe at the side contains the hearing centre and is important for memory. The occipital lobe right at the back processes what the eyes see.

There are special areas for language, usually in the left half of the brain. **Broca's area** in the frontal lobe helps to form words and speak. **Wernicke's area** in the temporal lobe is important for understanding language. They are named after the doctors Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke, who described them in the 19th century.

The grey matter contains the cell bodies of the nerve cells. Beneath it lies the **white matter**, made of nerve fibres that connect the areas like cables. Its pale colour comes from the **myelin sheath**, a fatty insulating layer. It makes sure that signals are passed on very quickly.

Most nerve pathways cross to the other side on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain mainly moves the right hand and the right leg. If part of one half stops working after a **stroke**, the other side of the body is often affected. But with training, the brain can relearn some tasks.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two halves of the cerebrum.
A broad bridge of nerves that connects the two halves of the brain.
The outer, folded layer of the cerebrum with many nerve cells.
A fatty sheath around nerve fibres that makes signals faster.

gewusst: An estimated 16 billion nerve cells work in the human cerebral cortex.
In adults the whole brain weighs only about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, but it uses around a fifth of the body's energy.
Dolphins and elephants also have a heavily folded cerebrum.

teile.einleitung: The habilitation is a special university qualification that you can obtain after a doctorate. Traditionally, anyone who passes it may teach independently at a university. For a long time it was the most important route to becoming a professor in German-speaking countries.
wichtigste: With the habilitation, you traditionally gain the right to teach at a university, the venia legendi.
The habilitation thesis is an extensive piece of research written after the doctorate.
In a cumulative habilitation, several published academic articles are submitted together.
People with a habilitation but no professorship often hold the title Privatdozent or Privatdozentin (PD).
In Germany, the addition “Dr. habil.” indicates a successful habilitation.
At the end, the newly qualified person often gives a formal inaugural lecture.
The habilitation is especially common in German-speaking countries and in parts of Central and Eastern Europe.
Increasingly, the tenure-track assistant professorship is replacing the habilitation as the route to a professorship.

abschnitte.text: The **habilitation** is the highest qualification a university can award. It follows the doctorate, for which you have already written a doctoral thesis. With the habilitation you show that you can represent a whole subject independently in research and teaching. Traditionally it gives you the **right to teach**, in Latin **venia legendi**, which means roughly “permission to read”. “Reading” used to be the word for giving a lecture.

First you usually write a **habilitation thesis**, a large piece of research that often takes several years. Instead of a book, you can also submit several published academic articles; this is called a **cumulative habilitation**. Experts from the faculty examine the work carefully and write reports on it. After that there is usually a scientific talk with a discussion and a trial lecture. As a formal conclusion, the new lecturer often gives a public **inaugural lecture**.

Someone who has a habilitation but no permanent professorship yet often holds the title **Privatdozent** or Privatdozentin, abbreviated PD. In Germany, the addition “Dr. habil.” shows that someone has passed the habilitation. In Switzerland, a university can later award experienced Privatdozenten the title of titular professor. France has a similar level, the “Habilitation à diriger des recherches”. The exact rules differ from country to country and from university to university.

The habilitation is especially common in German-speaking countries, that is, in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. It is also usual in parts of Central and Eastern Europe, such as Poland or the Czech Republic. In the USA, the United Kingdom and many other countries, on the other hand, it does not exist. In Switzerland its importance varies by university and subject; in **medicine**, for example, it still plays a big part. There it is often a requirement for senior posts at university hospitals.

The habilitation is sometimes criticised because it takes a long time and young researchers only become independent late. Many universities are therefore increasingly relying on the **tenure-track assistant professorship**. With this, you get your own temporary professorship early on. If your work is assessed positively after a few years, you get a permanent post. At ETH Zurich and EPFL this route is now the usual one.

begriffe.erklaerung: A course of study with your own large piece of research that leads to a doctor's title.
Latin for permission to teach independently at a university.
A person with a habilitation who teaches at a university but does not yet have a professorship.
A division of a university for particular subjects, for example the faculty of medicine.

gewusst: The term habilitation comes from the Latin word “habilis”, which means something like skilful or capable.
Many people are already around 40 years old when they complete their habilitation, because they do research for a long time beforehand.

teile.einleitung: Homo sapiens is the scientific name for us modern humans. Our species arose in Africa around 300,000 years ago and spread from there over the whole Earth. Today it is the only human species still alive.
wichtigste: Homo sapiens means “wise human” in Latin.
The oldest fossils found so far come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.
Today only a single human species lives on Earth.
Modern humans reached Europe around 45,000 years ago.
The early Homo sapiens of the Ice Age in Europe are often called Cro-Magnon people.
The Lion Man made of mammoth ivory is one of the oldest works of art.
Complex language and culture are especially distinctive.

abschnitte.text: **Homo sapiens** is the name researchers have given to our own species. It comes from the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century and means “wise human”. In the past, several human species lived at the same time, for example the **Neanderthals**. Today there is only one human species left, and all people on Earth belong to it.

The oldest fossils of Homo sapiens found so far were discovered at **Jebel Irhoud** in Morocco. They are about 300,000 years old. In **Blombos Cave** in South Africa, pieces of ochre around 75,000 years old with engraved patterns were found. They show that people were already making signs and decorations back then.

From Africa, Homo sapiens gradually spread out. Modern humans reached Europe around **45,000 years ago**, and Australia even earlier. They arrived in America more than 15,000 years ago. The early Ice Age people in Europe are often called **Cro-Magnon people**, after a site in France.

The **Lion Man** is a figure made of mammoth ivory, around 40,000 years old, which was found in a cave in southern Germany. It shows a being with a lion's head and a human body. Cave paintings, bone flutes and jewellery also come from the Ice Age. In Switzerland, a famous carving, the “Grazing Reindeer”, was found in the Kesslerloch near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen.

Homo sapiens has **complex language**, with which we can also talk about the past, the future and ideas. We pass on knowledge over many generations and build on it. This is how farming, cities, writing and technology came about. Today about 8.2 billion people live on Earth (as of 2025).

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of living things that are very similar in their important features.
A natural yellow or red pigment made from earth.
A long, cold period when large parts of the Earth were covered in ice.
An extinct human species that lived in Europe and Asia until about 40,000 years ago.

gewusst: All people alive today are genetically very similar to one another, more similar than some groups of chimpanzees are to each other.
The Lion Man was found in hundreds of fragments and was only pieced together again over many years.
The oldest known musical instruments are flutes made of bird bone and ivory that are around 40,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Hwang Woo-suk is a vet and researcher from South Korea who was once celebrated as a star of cloning research. At the end of 2005 it came out that he had faked important research results. His case is still regarded as one of the biggest frauds in science.
wichtigste: Hwang Woo-suk comes from South Korea and was a professor at Seoul National University.
In the journal “Science” he claimed to have obtained embryonic stem cells from cloned human embryos.
The fraud scandal was uncovered at the end of 2005.
His articles in “Science” were retracted.
He lost his professorship at the university.
The cloning of the dog Snuppy, on the other hand, was genuine.
The case showed that peer review does not always detect fraud.

abschnitte.text: Hwang Woo-suk is a South Korean vet and biologist. He worked as a professor at **Seoul National University**, the best-known university in the country. At first he did research on cloning animals such as cows. In the early 2000s he became a national hero in South Korea. He received a lot of money from the state and even appeared on postage stamps.

In 2004 and 2005 Hwang's team published two articles in the famous journal **“Science”**. In them it claimed to have obtained **embryonic stem cells** from cloned human embryos. Such cells can turn into many different types of cell. People hoped that one day they could be used to replace diseased tissue. The results were seen as a sensation worldwide.

In 2005 Hwang's team presented the dog **Snuppy**, an Afghan hound. He was the world's first cloned dog and was described in the journal “Nature”. The name combines SNU, the abbreviation for the university, with the English word puppy. Later investigations confirmed that Snuppy really was a genuine clone. So this achievement remained valid.

At the end of 2005, doubts arose about the stem cell articles. Among other things, it was noticed that in the articles **photos of the same cells had been used several times** and passed off as different samples. In early 2006 an investigation committee of the university found that the data had been faked. The journal “Science” retracted both articles. Hwang lost his professorship and was later also convicted in court.

The case showed that **peer review** does not always detect fraud. In peer review, experts check an article before it is published, but they usually do not see the raw data in the laboratory. Since then many journals have checked images more carefully. The scandal also made clear how important it is that other laboratories can repeat results. Only when a result has been confirmed several times is it considered secure.

begriffe.erklaerung: Producing a living thing that has exactly the same genetic material as another.
A cell that can still turn into different types of cell.
The checking of a scientific article by other experts before it is published.
When a journal officially declares an article invalid.

gewusst: A colleague from Hwang's own circle helped to bring the fraud to light.
The cloned dog Snuppy lived to about ten years old, as old as many ordinary dogs.

teile.einleitung: A glacier inventory is a detailed list of all the glaciers in an area. For each glacier it records how big it is, how high it lies and which direction it faces. By comparing inventories from different years, you can see how the glaciers are changing.
wichtigste: A glacier inventory lists all the glaciers in an area with features such as area and altitude.
The aspect tells you which compass direction a glacier faces.
According to the 2016 glacier inventory, Swiss glaciers covered around 960 square kilometres altogether.
Modern inventories are made mainly with satellite and aerial images.
Worldwide, the Randolph Glacier Inventory is used for climate models.
The World Glacier Monitoring Service is based at the University of Zurich.
Because large glaciers break up, the number in an inventory sometimes rises despite the shrinking.

abschnitte.text: A **glacier inventory** is like a catalogue of profiles for glaciers. Each glacier gets a number and an entry with important data. This includes its **area**, its length, and its highest and lowest points. The **aspect**, meaning the compass direction the glacier faces, is also recorded.

In the past, glaciers were measured laboriously on site or on maps. Today people mainly use **satellite images** and **aerial photographs**, on which the outlines are drawn on a computer. With elevation models you can also work out roughly how thick the ice is. It becomes difficult when **debris** or snow hides the edge of the ice, because then the boundary can hardly be seen.

Switzerland has been recording its glaciers in several inventories for decades. According to the **2016 glacier inventory**, there were around 1400 glaciers with an area of about 960 square kilometres. That is roughly the size of the canton of Schwyz. The data is looked after by the **GLAMOS** monitoring network, in which several universities take part.

For the whole Earth there is the **Randolph Glacier Inventory**, which contains the outlines of more than 200,000 glaciers. It is used for global climate models, for example to calculate sea level rise. The **GLIMS** project stands for Global Land Ice Measurements from Space and collects glacier outlines from space. The **World Glacier Monitoring Service** at the University of Zurich collects measurement data from glaciers all over the world.

You might think that the number of glaciers keeps getting smaller as they melt. But large glaciers can **break up** into several smaller parts. Each piece then counts as a separate glacier in the inventory. That is why people mainly compare the **total area** and the volume when they want to describe glacier retreat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A complete list of things with their most important details.
The compass direction that a slope or glacier faces.
Studying the Earth from a distance, for example with satellites or aircraft.
A layer of stones and rubble lying on top of the glacier ice.

gewusst: North-facing glaciers in the Alps usually last longer because they get less sun.
The vast majority of Swiss glaciers are smaller than one square kilometre.
A glacier that no longer moves does not really count as a glacier any more, but as dead ice.

teile.einleitung: Henri Nestlé was a pharmacist and entrepreneur who came to Switzerland from Germany. In Vevey on Lake Geneva he invented an infant cereal for babies in 1867. His small company grew into one of the largest food companies in the world.
wichtigste: Henri Nestlé was born in Frankfurt am Main in 1814 and was originally called Heinrich Nestle.
He trained as a pharmacist and moved to western Switzerland as a young man.
In Vevey in 1867 he developed an infant cereal made from milk, wheat flour and sugar.
The well-known nest logo goes back to his family coat of arms.
In 1905 the Nestlé company merged with the Anglo-Swiss Condensed Milk Company from Cham.
The Nestlé group still has its headquarters in Vevey today.
Henri Nestlé died in 1890 near Montreux.

abschnitte.text: Henri Nestlé was born on 10 August 1814 in **Frankfurt am Main**. In German his name was **Heinrich Nestle**. He trained as a pharmacist's assistant. Around 1839 he moved to French-speaking Switzerland and later settled in Vevey. There he adapted his name to the French language.

In Vevey, Nestlé tried many things: he made mineral water, lemonade, mustard and fertiliser, for example. He was curious and liked to try out new mixtures. At that time many babies died because they did not get enough good food. This hardship gave him an important idea.

In 1867 Nestlé developed an **infant cereal** for babies, in French “Farine lactée”. He mixed milk, wheat flour and sugar and dried it all into a powder. You only had to stir it with water. The product soon sold in many countries in Europe and beyond.

In the Swabian dialect, the name Nestle means something like “little nest”. That is why the family coat of arms showed a nest. Henri Nestlé turned it into a **logo** with a mother bird feeding her young in the nest. The company still uses a similar nest logo today.

In 1875 Henri Nestlé sold his company and retired. In 1905 the company merged with the **Anglo-Swiss Condensed Milk Company** from Cham in the canton of Zug. That company made condensed milk. Today the Nestlé group makes countless products, such as chocolate, coffee and pet food, and still has its headquarters in **Vevey**.

Henri Nestlé died on 7 July 1890 in Glion above Montreux. He had no children. In Vevey the food museum **Alimentarium** tells the history of food. In front of the museum, a giant fork stands in Lake Geneva and has become a popular photo spot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A specialist who makes and sells medicines.
A powder made from milk, flour and sugar as food for babies.
Milk from which part of the water has been removed so that it keeps longer.
A very large company with many firms and factories.
A picture symbol by which a company can be recognised.

gewusst: Henri Nestlé was not Swiss by birth at all, but an immigrant from Frankfurt.
Chocolate was not one of his inventions at the start; it only came later through mergers with other companies.
In Vevey, an eight-metre-tall fork rises out of Lake Geneva as a reminder of the subject of food.

teile.einleitung: The genetic code is the rule by which cells translate genetic information into proteins. Every three building blocks of the genetic material form a code word that stands for a particular amino acid. Almost all living things on Earth, from bacteria to humans, use the same assignment.
wichtigste: The genetic code lays down which group of three bases stands for which amino acid.
Such a group of three is called a codon; there are 64 different codons.
The code is degenerate, because most amino acids have several codons.
The code is comma-free: there are no separators between the codons.
The code is almost universal and applies to nearly all living things.
In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei cracked the first codon with poly-U RNA.
Nirenberg, Khorana and Holley received the Nobel Prize in 1968 for cracking the code.

abschnitte.text: Genetic information is stored in **DNA**, a long thread of four building blocks, the bases. They are called adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine and are abbreviated as A, T, G and C. In the cell a section is first rewritten into **RNA**, where uracil (U) occurs instead of thymine. Every three bases form a **codon**, rather as letters form a word.

The ribosomes in the cell read the RNA codon by codon. Small transport molecules, the **tRNA**, bring the matching amino acid when their anticodon fits the codon. In this way a chain of amino acids is formed that folds into a **protein**. The codon AUG usually means “start” and stands for the amino acid methionine. The codons UAA, UAG and UGA mean “stop”.

With four bases, 64 groups of three can be formed, but there are only 20 standard amino acids. That is why most amino acids have several codons, and the code is **degenerate**. It is also comma-free, so the codons follow one another without gaps. According to Francis Crick's **wobble hypothesis** of 1966, the third base of a codon may pair imprecisely with the anticodon. In this way a cell manages with fewer different tRNAs.

In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei put an artificial RNA made only of uracil into a test tube with cell components. A chain of the amino acid phenylalanine was formed, so UUU means phenylalanine. In the following years all 64 codons were cracked. Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert Holley received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine for this in 1968.

Because the code is **almost universal**, a bacterium can read a human gene and produce human insulin, for example. Genetic engineering makes use of this. But there are small exceptions. In human **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell, UGA does not mean “stop” but tryptophan. The universality is a strong sign that all living things have common ancestors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of three bases that stands for an amino acid or a stop signal.
A building block of proteins; living things mainly use 20 different ones.
A tiny protein factory in the cell that reads the RNA.
The counterpart to the codon on the tRNA, which docks onto it.

gewusst: The sequence of DNA building blocks in a single human cell would fill many thousands of books if printed out.
In the laboratory, researchers have given bacteria extra, artificial amino acids and so extended the code.
Heinrich Matthaei, who took part in the first code-cracking experiment, was a German biochemist.

teile.einleitung: Glaciers look like rigid masses of ice, but in reality they flow slowly down the valley, like an extremely stiff honey. This glacier flow arises through the own weight of the ice. In the process, crevasses, ice towers and other exciting forms come about.
wichtigste: Glaciers move through internal deformation of the ice and through sliding on the ground.
Glen's flow law describes how ice deforms under pressure; the exponent n is about 3.
If the shear stress doubles, the rate of deformation rises by a factor of 8.
Crevasses mostly reach only a few dozen metres deep, because the ice below them flows plastically.
In steep icefalls, ice towers arise that are called seracs.
Temperate glaciers can slide, because meltwater at the bed acts like a lubricant.
Below an icefall, light and dark bands form that are called ogives.

abschnitte.text: Ice seems hard and brittle when you strike it. Under great pressure and over a long time, however, it behaves like a very stiff mass and can deform **plastically**. A glacier therefore flows slowly downhill through its own weight. Most Alpine glaciers move a few dozen to a few hundred metres a year, and some glaciers in Greenland even several kilometres.

Glacier flow has two main causes. In **internal deformation**, tiny layers in the ice crystals glide past each other, so that the whole ice slowly deforms. In **sliding on the ground**, the glacier slides on its rock bed. That works in **temperate** glaciers, whose ice at the bed is exactly at melting point, because there meltwater arises that acts like a lubricant.

In the 1950s the British physicist John Glen described how fast ice deforms under a load. According to **Glen's flow law**, the deformation depends on the **shear stress** to the power of n, and for glacier ice n is about 3. That means that if the shear stress doubles, the ice deforms two times two times two, so eight times as fast. That is why thick ice flows especially quickly on steep slopes.

Where the glacier flows over an edge of the ground or is pulled apart, the brittle ice tears open at the surface, and **crevasses** arise. They are mostly only a few dozen metres deep, because further down the ice flows under the pressure and closes crevasses again. In steep **icefalls**, many crevasses cross each other and bizarre ice towers arise that are called **seracs**. They can collapse without warning and are very dangerous for mountaineers.

Below some icefalls you can see arched light and dark bands on the ice, the **ogives**. They arise because ice that flows through the icefall in summer gathers more dust than ice that flows through in winter. Some glaciers are so-called **surging glaciers**: after a long period of rest they suddenly flow many times faster for months. Such glaciers are found, for example, in Alaska, Svalbard and the Karakoram.

As early as the 1840s the natural scientist **Louis Agassiz** studied on the Unteraar Glacier in the Bernese Oberland how fast a glacier moves. For this he put stakes in a line across the ice and watched how they shifted. In this way it became clear that the middle flows faster than the edges, because there the friction at the valley side is missing. Today researchers measure the flow with GPS, satellites and drones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that tries to shift layers of a material against each other.
A glacier whose ice is roughly at melting point.
An ice tower that arises in a heavily broken-up icefall.
Arched light and dark bands on a glacier below an icefall.
A phase in which a glacier suddenly flows much faster than usual.

gewusst: Objects that fall onto a glacier sometimes reappear only after decades further down at the glacier tongue.
The Jakobshavn Glacier in Greenland is one of the fastest glaciers in the world and in places flows more than ten kilometres a year.
The word serac comes from French and originally meant a kind of curd cheese from the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The Gram stain is a method used to divide bacteria into two large groups under the microscope. After staining, some bacteria are violet and others red. That sounds simple, but it tells doctors a lot about how an infection can be treated.
wichtigste: The Danish researcher Hans Christian Gram developed the stain in 1884.
First the bacteria are stained with the dye crystal violet.
Lugol's iodine solution forms a poorly soluble complex with the crystal violet.
Gram-positive bacteria stay violet at the end, gram-negative ones turn red.
The difference lies in the thickness of the murein layer of the cell wall.
Gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli also have an outer membrane.
The stain is still one of the most important tests in the medical laboratory.

abschnitte.text: Bacteria are so small and transparent that you can hardly see them under the microscope. Dyes make them visible and allow them to be told apart. The **Gram stain** divides almost all bacteria into two groups: **gram-positive** and **gram-negative**. It takes only a few minutes and needs hardly any equipment.

First the violet dye **crystal violet** is put on the sample. Then Lugol's iodine solution is added, which forms a large, poorly soluble complex with the dye. Next the sample is rinsed with alcohol or acetone; this is the **decolourising** step. Finally it is stained again with a red dye such as safranin; this is called **counterstaining**.

The cell wall of bacteria contains a net-like material called **murein**. In gram-positive bacteria this layer is thick and holds on to the violet complex during decolourising. In gram-negative bacteria it is thin, but on the outside there is an **outer membrane** containing lipopolysaccharides. There the alcohol washes out the violet, and the red counterstain becomes visible.

Examples of gram-positive bacteria are staphylococci and streptococci, which can cause skin or throat infections. Gram-negative ones include the gut bacterium Escherichia coli and salmonella. Some bacteria do not fit the scheme. **Mycobacteria**, which include the germ that causes tuberculosis, have a waxy cell wall and stain poorly.

In 1884 Hans Christian Gram was working in a hospital in Berlin. He actually wanted to make bacteria in lung tissue easier to see. In doing so, he noticed that some bacteria kept the colour and others did not. Only later did people realise how useful this discovery is for **diagnosis**.

With the Gram stain, a laboratory can very quickly give a first clue as to what kind of bacteria is causing an illness. This helps in choosing the right **antibiotic**. Penicillin, for example, often works better against gram-positive bacteria. With serious infections every hour counts, which is why the quick test is so valuable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things made of just one cell that are found almost everywhere.
A net-like substance in the cell wall of bacteria that makes the cell stable.
A second stain that makes visible the bacteria that have lost the first colour.
A medicine that kills bacteria or slows down their growth.

gewusst: Hans Christian Gram published his method as a short note, without suspecting that it would become famous worldwide.
Gram-positive and gram-negative do not mean good and bad; they only describe the colour after the test.
For mycobacteria, the Ziehl-Neelsen stain is usually used instead of the Gram stain.

teile.einleitung: Gene flow is the exchange of gene variants between different populations of a species. It happens when animals migrate or when pollen and seeds of plants reach other areas. Gene flow makes sure that populations do not develop too far apart from each other.
wichtigste: Gene flow is the exchange of alleles between populations.
Strong gene flow reduces the genetic differences between populations.
In plants, gene flow often happens through pollen and seeds.
According to a rule of thumb, about one immigrant per generation is enough to prevent populations from drifting far apart.
Genetic difference is often measured with the fixation index FST.
Interrupted gene flow encourages the formation of new species.
In hybrid zones, such as that of the carrion crow and the hooded crow, mixed forms arise.

abschnitte.text: A species often consists of several **populations**, that is, groups living in different areas. When an animal moves from one group to another and has young there, it brings its gene variants with it. This exchange of **alleles** is called **gene flow**. It acts like a bridge that connects the populations genetically.

In animals, gene flow happens above all through **migration**, for example when young wolves look for a new territory. Plants cannot migrate, but their **pollen** is carried far by the wind or by insects. Seeds too are spread by birds, by water or by the wind. In this way a flower on an Alpine meadow can exchange genes with flowers on a far-off meadow.

How genetically different two populations are is often measured with the **fixation index FST**. A value near 0 means that they hardly differ, and a value near 1 that they are very different. A well-known rule of thumb says that about one immigrant per generation is enough to prevent populations from drifting far apart through **genetic drift**. So even a little exchange has a big effect.

High mountains, wide rivers, seas, but also motorways and built-up areas can interrupt gene flow. Separated populations then develop independently of each other. After a very long time, new species can arise from this, which is called **allopatric speciation**. In Switzerland, **wildlife bridges** are therefore built over motorways so that roe deer, red deer and other animals can reconnect their habitats.

When two distinguishable populations meet, a **hybrid zone** with mixed forms sometimes arises. A well-known example is the all-black **carrion crow** in the west of Europe and the grey and black **hooded crow** in the east and north. Where their ranges touch, there are crows with a mixed appearance. The zone is quite narrow, which shows that gene flow between the two forms is limited.

Gene flow brings new gene variants into a population and so increases its **genetic variety**. That is especially important for small, threatened populations. But very strong gene flow can also slow down local **adaptation**. If animals or pollen from quite different habitats keep arriving, alleles that are poorly suited to the place come in too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of living things of one species that live together in a particular area.
A version of a gene.
An area in which two different forms meet and mixed forms arise.
The formation of a new species from an existing one.
A bridge planted with vegetation on which animals can cross a road safely.

gewusst: The pollen of some trees can be carried by the wind over hundreds of kilometres.
There can also be gene flow between crop plants and their wild relatives.
The carrion crow and the hooded crow were long regarded as two species; today many experts see them as forms of the same species.

teile.einleitung: Shark skin is the special skin of sharks, which is covered with tiny teeth. If you stroke it from the tail towards the head, it feels as rough as sandpaper. Its structure helps sharks to swim and is a famous model for inventions.
wichtigste: Sharks are fish, more precisely cartilaginous fish.
The surface of shark skin consists of tiny skin teeth.
Stroked from tail to head, it feels as rough as sandpaper.
Fine grooves on the tiny teeth help the shark glide through the water more easily.
Swimsuits have been developed using shark skin as a model.
Ship paints based on this model are meant to stop mussels and algae from growing on hulls.
Aircraft are given films like shark skin to save fuel.

abschnitte.text: Sharks' skin is not covered with ordinary fish scales but with **skin teeth**, also called placoid scales. These tiny structures are built rather like our teeth, with a hard coating and dentine underneath. They lie close together and all point towards the tail. That is why the skin is smooth from front to back but as rough as **sandpaper** in the opposite direction.

Fine lengthwise grooves called **riblets** run along the skin teeth. They guide the water over the surface of the skin and reduce small swirls. As a result the shark has less resistance and glides through the water more easily and quietly. Sharks belong to the group of fish, but they have a skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone.

Taking nature as a model for technology is called **biomimetics**. Swimsuits with a special surface were developed using shark skin as a model. At the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing, swimmers in full-body suits set many world records. Because the suits gave such a big advantage, the most extreme models were banned in competition from 2010.

Aircraft can also learn from shark skin. Special **films** with fine grooves are stuck onto the fuselage and reduce air resistance a little. In this way the aircraft save fuel; the Swiss airline Swiss has also used such films. On ships, paints based on shark skin are meant to stop **mussels** and algae from attaching themselves, without using poisonous paints.

In earlier times people already used the dried skin of sharks and rays as an abrasive for wood. Under the name **shagreen** or galuchat, such skin was also used to cover sword handles and jewellery boxes. Today researchers are also studying the skin teeth in order to develop surfaces to which bacteria stick poorly. However, many shark species are endangered because they are overfished.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny, tooth-like scales on the skin of sharks.
A field that uses ideas from nature for technology.
Fine lengthwise grooves that reduce drag in a flow.
A fish with a skeleton made of flexible cartilage, for example sharks and rays.

gewusst: Sharks keep losing skin teeth and growing new ones, much like the teeth in their mouths.
The skin teeth do not grow bigger; instead, a growing shark simply gets more of them.
Shark skin used to be used to sand wood as finely as sandpaper.

teile.einleitung: A gene is a section of DNA that contains a particular piece of genetic information. Usually it is the building instructions for a protein that carries out a job in the body. Genes help to decide what colour our eyes are, how our body works and much more.
wichtigste: A gene is a section of DNA with a piece of genetic information.
Usually a gene contains the building instructions for a protein.
Humans have about 20,000 genes that contain building instructions for proteins.
Different versions of the same gene are called alleles.
Every three bases form a codon, which codes for one amino acid.
mRNA carries the copy of a gene out of the nucleus to the ribosomes.
The genetic code codes as standard for 20 different amino acids.

abschnitte.text: In almost every cell of our body there is **DNA**, a long, thread-like molecule in the shape of a twisted rope ladder. A **gene** is a particular section of this thread. You can picture DNA as a gigantic cookery book, with each gene a single recipe in it. Most genes are building instructions for **proteins**, which in the body serve as building materials, messengers or helpers in digestion, for example.

DNA is built from four building blocks, the **bases** adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine, A, T, G and C for short. Their order is the actual information, rather like the order of letters in a word. Every three bases in a row form a **codon**, which stands for a particular amino acid. There are 64 different codons, which as standard code for 20 different **amino acids**.

The DNA stays in the nucleus, well protected like a valuable original book. So a copy of a gene is made, the **mRNA**. It travels out of the nucleus into the cell plasma to the **ribosomes**, the protein factories of the cell. There, following the instructions codon by codon, the amino acids are joined into a long chain that then folds into a protein.

Many genes come in different versions, which are called **alleles**. For blood group, for example, there are the alleles A, B and 0. Every person has two copies of most genes, one from their father and one from their mother. But which features a person has depends not only on their genes but also on their **environment**, such as diet and way of life.

In 1865 the monk **Gregor Mendel** discovered in experiments with peas that features are inherited according to fixed rules. He spoke of “hereditary factors”. The word **gene** was introduced in 1909 by the Danish researcher Wilhelm Johannsen. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix structure of DNA, with X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin playing a decisive part.

If you understand genes, you can recognise and treat many diseases better. Some diseases arise because a gene has changed, and such a change is called a **mutation**. With gene tests, such changes can now be detected. Genes also play an important part in farming, in forensics and in research on evolution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in cells that stores genetic information.
One of several possible versions of a gene.
A group of three bases that stands for a particular amino acid.
A tiny part of the cell where proteins are put together.
A change in the genetic information.

gewusst: A water flea has more genes than a human.
Many human genes are very similar to those of a mouse.
Only a small part of human DNA consists of genes for proteins; the rest has other or still unknown jobs.

teile.einleitung: The Wright brothers were two American brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright. On 17 December 1903 they made the first controlled flight in a powered aircraft. With that, the age of aviation began.
wichtigste: In 1903 the Wright brothers built the first successful powered aircraft.
Wilbur lived from 1867 to 1912 and Orville from 1871 to 1948.
They came from Dayton in the US state of Ohio and ran a bicycle workshop.
The first flight took place near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina.
Their aircraft was called the Wright Flyer.
The first flight lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres.
Their most important idea was control around all three axes.

abschnitte.text: Wilbur Wright was born in 1867, and his brother Orville in 1871. They lived in **Dayton** in the state of Ohio in the USA. There they ran a **bicycle workshop** in which they repaired and built bicycles. With the money they earned they paid for their flying experiments.

The brothers read a great deal about the German flight pioneer **Otto Lilienthal**, who had flown gliders. From 1900 they tested their own gliders in the dunes of Kitty Hawk, where there is often a strong wind. They even built a small **wind tunnel** to test wing shapes. After that they built a light engine and their own propellers.

On 17 December 1903 Orville took off with the **Wright Flyer** near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina. The flight lasted 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres. On the same day the brothers took turns to fly three more times. Wilbur's longest flight lasted 59 seconds and covered about 260 metres.

Other inventors had concentrated above all on powerful engines. The Wrights realised that an aircraft must also be easy to **control**. They twisted the wing tips slightly to bank the aircraft into a turn. Together with the elevator and the rudder, they could steer it around all three **axes**, a principle that still applies today.

At first many people did not believe the brothers' reports. Only in 1908 did their public flights in France and the USA convince the world. After that, **aviation** developed at great speed. Only 66 years after the first powered flight, people landed on the Moon.

begriffe.erklaerung: An aircraft driven by an engine with a propeller or a jet.
An aircraft without an engine that sails through the air with the wind.
A tunnel in which air is made to flow, to test shapes for vehicles or aircraft.
A turning blade that pulls or pushes an aircraft or ship forward.

gewusst: The first powered flight was shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.
A piece of fabric from the Wright Flyer flew on Mars in 2021, on the small helicopter Ingenuity.
The brothers tossed a coin to decide who would fly the first attempt; Wilbur won, but his first attempt on 14 December failed.

teile.einleitung: A thunderstorm is a weather event with lightning and thunder, often accompanied by heavy rain, wind or hail. It arises in huge, towering clouds. Thunderstorms are impressive but also dangerous, so you should know how to protect yourself.
wichtigste: After a flash of lightning you hear the thunder.
You hear the thunder later, because light is faster than sound.
Sound covers about one kilometre in about 3 seconds.
If you count 6 seconds between lightning and thunder, the storm is about 2 kilometres away.
Inside a house you are safe during a thunderstorm.
A lightning conductor leads the lightning into the ground.
Anyone who notices a thunderstorm while swimming in a lake has to get out of the water at once.

abschnitte.text: Thunderstorms arise above all on hot summer days, when warm, moist air rises quickly. In the process a huge cloud forms, the **cumulonimbus**, which can grow more than ten kilometres high. Inside it, water drops, grains of ice and soft hail whirl about violently. In doing so they become electrically charged, rather like a balloon that you rub on your hair.

If the voltage is great enough, it discharges as **lightning**. The lightning heats the air in a flash to about 30,000 degrees, which is hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands explosively, and we hear that as **thunder**. Because light is much faster than sound, we see the lightning first and hear the thunder later.

Sound needs about **3 seconds** for one kilometre. So you count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by three. At 6 seconds the storm is about 2 kilometres away. If the gap is shorter than about 30 seconds, the storm is already dangerously close.

You are safest in a **house** or in a car with a closed metal roof. Out of doors you should not stand under lone trees and should keep away from summits and water. When swimming you have to get out of the water at once, because water conducts electricity. If you find no shelter, you crouch in a hollow with your feet together.

A **lightning conductor** is a metal rod on the roof that is joined to the earth by a wire. The lightning strikes there and is led harmlessly into the ground. It was invented by the American Benjamin Franklin in the 18th century. In Switzerland there are the most thunderstorms in summer, especially often in **Ticino** and in the pre-Alps, and MeteoSwiss warns of severe thunderstorms.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge, tower-like thunderstorm cloud.
A mighty electrical discharge in the air.
The bang when the air suddenly expands because of the lightning.
Grains of ice that fall from thunderstorm clouds.
A metal rod that leads lightning safely into the ground.

gewusst: On Earth there are about 40 to 50 flashes of lightning every second.
Contrary to an old saying, lightning does indeed strike the same place several times, for instance tall towers.
A car protects you during a thunderstorm not because of the rubber tyres but because of the metal shell.

teile.einleitung: A semiconductor is a material that conducts electricity better than an insulator such as glass, but worse than a metal such as copper. Its conductivity can be controlled precisely, and that is exactly what makes it so valuable. Without semiconductors there would be no computers, mobile phones, solar cells or LED lamps.
wichtigste: The most important semiconductor in microelectronics is silicon.
A pure semiconductor conducts better as the temperature rises.
In doping, tiny amounts of foreign atoms are mixed in, for example phosphorus for an n-type semiconductor.
In a p-type semiconductor, missing electrons act like positive charges; they are called holes.
Where a p-region and an n-region meet, a diode is created.
The Czochralski process is used to pull large single crystals of silicon from a melt.
Gallium nitride made efficient blue light-emitting diodes possible.
Silicon carbide is increasingly used in electric cars.

abschnitte.text: Materials can be grouped by how well they conduct electric current. **Conductors** such as copper conduct very well, **insulators** such as glass or rubber hardly at all. **Semiconductors** lie in between, and their conductivity can be changed greatly by heat, light or additives. Unlike metals, a pure semiconductor conducts better the warmer it is. The most important semiconductor is **silicon**, which is obtained from quartz sand.

abschnitte.titel: Doping: the trick with foreign atoms
abschnitte.text: Pure silicon conducts only weakly, so tiny amounts of foreign atoms are mixed into it. This process is called **doping**. If phosphorus is added, for example, extra free electrons are created and you get an **n-type semiconductor**. With boron, on the other hand, electrons are missing and a p-type semiconductor is created. The missing electrons behave like positive charges and are called holes.

Where a p-region and an n-region meet, a **diode** is created, which lets current through in only one direction. From three such layers you can build a **transistor**, a tiny electrical switch. The first transistor was built in 1947 at Bell Labs in the USA. Today a single computer chip holds billions of transistors that are smaller than many viruses. Solar cells and light-emitting diodes are also made of semiconductors.

Chips need extremely pure silicon with almost no foreign atoms. With the **Czochralski process**, a large single crystal is slowly pulled out of molten silicon. This crystal rod is cut into wafer-thin slices called **wafers**. On these, the tiny circuits are applied with light and chemicals in clean rooms. Making the most modern chips is so difficult that only a few companies in the world can do it.

Besides silicon there are other semiconductors with special properties. With **gallium nitride** it became possible to build efficient blue light-emitting diodes, for which Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014. Only with blue LEDs could bright white LED lamps be made. **Silicon carbide** can withstand high voltages and temperatures and is therefore increasingly used in electric cars and charging stations. In Switzerland, for example, ETH Zurich, EPFL and the Paul Scherrer Institute do research on semiconductors.

begriffe.erklaerung: How well a material passes on electric current.
Deliberately building foreign atoms into a semiconductor.
A tiny electrical switch or amplifier made of semiconductor material.
A thin slice of semiconductor material on which chips are made.
A component that lets current flow in only one direction.

gewusst: After oxygen, silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust; it is found in almost every grain of sand.
A clean room for making chips is much cleaner than an operating theatre, because even a speck of dust can ruin a chip.

teile.einleitung: The Higgs boson is a tiny elementary particle that was discovered in 2012 at CERN near Geneva. It helps to explain how other particles get their mass. The discovery is regarded as one of the greatest successes in physics of recent decades.
wichtigste: The Higgs boson is an elementary particle that explains how other particles get mass.
It was predicted in 1964 by Peter Higgs and other researchers.
On 4 July 2012 CERN announced its discovery.
It was found in the LHC particle accelerator near Geneva.
The particle belongs to the Higgs field, which fills the whole universe.
Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013.
The Higgs boson decays in a tiny fraction of a second.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of tiny building blocks, the **elementary particles**. Physics describes them in what is called the **Standard Model**. For a long time an important piece of the puzzle was missing from it, one that explains why particles have mass. This piece is the Higgs boson.

Physicists imagine that the whole universe is filled with an invisible **Higgs field**. Particles that interact strongly with this field are slowed down and get a lot of mass. Others, such as light, do not feel the field at all and stay massless. You can picture it like walking through honey: some get stuck more than others.

In 1964 several researchers published the idea of this field almost at the same time. They included the Briton **Peter Higgs** and the Belgians François Englert and Robert Brout. The particle was named after Higgs. The word boson recalls the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose.

For almost 50 years people searched for the particle in vain.
