Only the **Large Hadron Collider** at CERN, a ring about 27 kilometres round beneath the border between Switzerland and France, was powerful enough. There protons are made to collide at almost the speed of light. The two large detectors **ATLAS** and CMS found the particle, and on 4 July 2012 the discovery was announced.

With the Higgs boson, the Standard Model of particle physics was fully confirmed. In 2013 Peter Higgs and François Englert received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics. Thousands of researchers from all over the world work together at CERN. They continue to study the Higgs boson in order to solve open puzzles such as **dark matter**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that cannot be broken down into even smaller parts.
The European Organization for Nuclear Research near Geneva, the largest particle physics laboratory in the world.
A huge machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast and lets them collide.
The amount of matter in a body; it determines how heavy it is.

gewusst: The Higgs boson is sometimes called the God particle, but many physicists do not like this nickname.
Peter Higgs was present at CERN for the announcement in 2012 and wiped tears of emotion from his eyes.
A Higgs boson exists for only a tiny fraction of a second before it decays into other particles.

teile.einleitung: Wood is the hard material that the trunks, branches and roots of trees and shrubs are made of. It is one of the oldest materials used by humans and is needed for houses, furniture, paper and as fuel. Because it grows back and stores carbon, it is considered especially environmentally friendly.
wichtigste: Wood forms in the trunks of trees as they get thicker year after year.
The cell walls of wood consist mainly of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin.
Wood swells and shrinks because its cell walls take in and give off water.
Wood is anisotropic, which means its properties depend on the direction of the grain.
You can tell the age of a tree from its annual rings.
Wood used in building stores carbon that the tree took in from the air.
In Switzerland, about a third of the country is covered with forest.

abschnitte.text: Under the bark of a tree is a thin, living layer, the **cambium**. Every year it forms new wood towards the inside and new bark towards the outside. In spring, light, loose wood grows; in summer, darker, firmer wood. This creates the **annual rings**, from which you can tell the age of a tree. Wood carries water from the roots up to the leaves and gives the tree support.

Wood consists of tiny, elongated **cells** that lie side by side like little tubes. Their walls are built mainly of **cellulose**, hemicellulose and **lignin**. Cellulose forms fibres that are strong under tension, similar to the steel bars in concrete. Lignin glues these fibres together and makes the wood hard and resistant to pressure. Freshly felled wood contains a lot of water, which is why it is left to dry before use.

Wood is an **anisotropic** material: along the grain it is much stronger than across it. That is why a log can easily be split lengthwise with an axe, but hardly across. Because the cell walls take in and give off moisture, wood **swells** in damp air and **shrinks** in dry air. That is why wooden doors sometimes stick in autumn and open more easily again in winter. Relative to its weight, wood can carry a lot and is easy to work.

Every tree species has its own wood with its own colour, hardness and grain. Softwoods such as spruce, fir and larch are usually lighter and are used a lot in building. Hardwoods such as beech, oak and maple are often harder and are suitable for furniture, floors and tool handles. The very light balsa wood is used for model aeroplanes. In Switzerland, the **spruce** is the most common tree and supplies most of the timber for building.

Houses, roof structures, bridges, furniture, musical instruments and toys are made of wood. Wood fibres are used to make **paper** and cardboard. Wood is also used for heating as firewood and in the form of pellets or chips. In Switzerland, wooden buildings have a long tradition, for example the chalets in the Alps and the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne. Today even multi-storey flats and office buildings are built entirely of wood.

A growing tree takes in **carbon dioxide** from the air and stores the carbon in its wood. When wood is used in building, this carbon stays locked in the building for decades. In addition, making wooden beams needs much less energy than making steel or concrete. For wood to be truly sustainable, as much must grow back in the forest as is cut down. That is why Swiss forest law requires the area of forest to be preserved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ring in the wood that grew in one year.
A substance that glues the wood fibres together and makes wood hard.
A substance made of long fibres that gives plants their strength.
Having different properties in different directions.
The pattern of lines and colours on a wooden surface.

gewusst: Wood does burn, but thick wooden beams often last longer in a fire than steel girders, because a protective layer of charcoal forms on the outside.
The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is considered one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
Some kinds of wood, such as lignum vitae, are so heavy that they sink in water.

teile.einleitung: A herbarium is a collection of pressed and dried plants. Each plant lies on a sheet of paper and is precisely labelled. Herbaria help researchers to identify and compare plants, and you can also make one yourself.
wichtigste: The word herbarium comes from the Latin “herba”, which means herb or plant.
Plants are dried by pressing them between sheets of newspaper.
For each plant you write down its name, where it was found and the date.
Pressing takes about one to two weeks.
Some plants are protected and may not be picked.
Geneva has one of the largest herbaria in the world.
Scientific herbaria often contain millions of plant specimens.

abschnitte.text: A **herbarium** consists of many sheets of paper, each with one dried plant attached to it. Such a sheet is called a **specimen**. It comes with a label giving the name of the plant, where it was found, the date and the name of the person who collected it. Large herbaria are kept in museums, botanic gardens and universities.

Only collect plants that are common, and do not take more than you need. Lay the plant flat between sheets of **newspaper** and weigh it down with heavy books. Change the paper more often in the first few days so that nothing goes mouldy. After about one to two weeks the plant is dry and can be stuck onto stiff paper. You can find the name of an unknown plant with a **field guide** or an identification app.

In nature you may not pick every plant. Some species are **protected**, in Switzerland for example edelweiss and many orchids. In nature reserves, picking is usually completely forbidden. Anyone making a herbarium should therefore check beforehand which plants are allowed.

One of the largest herbaria in the world is in **Geneva**, at the city's Conservatory and Botanical Garden. It contains several million plant specimens from all continents. The University of Zurich and ETH Zurich also have a large collection together. Very famous is the herbarium of the Swedish researcher **Carl Linnaeus**, who gave many plants their scientific names in the 18th century.

Researchers compare specimens to identify species and to describe new ones. Old specimens show where a plant used to grow, so you can tell whether it has become rarer. It is even possible to study the **genetic material** of dried plants. Today many herbaria are photographed and digitised so that people all over the world can look at them on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sheet of paper with a dried plant and a label.
A frame with boards and straps used to press plants flat.
A book that helps you find out step by step what a plant is called.
The science of plants.

gewusst: The first herbaria were made in Italy in the 16th century.
Well-kept herbarium specimens can last for several hundred years.
A herbarium used to be called a “hortus siccus”, which is Latin for “dry garden”.

teile.einleitung: Herd immunity means that when enough people are immune to an infectious disease, the pathogen can hardly spread any more. This also protects people who are not immune themselves. It is also called community protection.
wichtigste: Herd immunity also protects people who are not immune themselves.
Babies and people who cannot be vaccinated benefit especially.
The more infectious a disease is, the more people need to be immune.
For measles, about 95 per cent of the population must be immune.
The basic reproduction number tells you how many people one sick person infects on average.
There is no herd immunity for tetanus, because it is not passed from person to person.
If the vaccination rate falls below the necessary threshold, outbreaks can happen again.

abschnitte.text: A pathogen such as a virus needs people it can infect. If many people are **immune**, it keeps meeting people with whom it gets no further. The chain of infection breaks, rather like a fire that can no longer find dry branches. This creates protection for the whole community: **herd immunity**.

Newborn babies are still too young for some vaccinations. People with a weakened **immune system**, for example during cancer treatment, may not be given some vaccines either. They depend on the people around them being protected. So anyone who gets vaccinated protects not only themselves.

The **basic reproduction number** R0 tells you how many people one sick person infects on average when nobody is immune. The required share of immune people can be calculated, in simple terms, as 1 minus 1 divided by R0. With R0 = 4, this gives 1 minus 0.25, which is 75 per cent. Measles is extremely infectious; one sick person can infect more than a dozen people, which is why about 95 per cent is needed.

You become immune either by getting over an illness or through a **vaccination**. Vaccination is the safer way, because you do not have to go through the illness. Thanks to worldwide vaccination, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. Polio has also disappeared in most countries.

Herd immunity only works for diseases that are passed from person to person. **Tetanus**, on the other hand, is caused by bacteria from soil and dirt that get into the body through wounds. That is why every person has to protect themselves. Community protection is also weaker when a pathogen changes quickly, as with flu.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) recommends in the Swiss vaccination schedule which vaccinations make sense at which age. Vaccinations are voluntary. One of the aims is to eliminate measles completely. If the vaccination rate in a region falls, **outbreaks** can happen there again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which the body is protected against a particular pathogen.
The average number of people one sick person infects when nobody is protected.
The share of people in a population who are vaccinated against a disease.
A tiny cause of disease such as a virus or a bacterium.

gewusst: The term herd immunity originally comes from veterinary medicine, where it was about whole herds of livestock.
Measles is one of the most infectious diseases of all; the virus can still float in the air of a room for a while.
Smallpox is so far the only human disease to have been eradicated worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Howard Carter was a British archaeologist who discovered the tomb of the Egyptian king Tutankhamun in 1922. It was almost untouched and full of treasures, including the famous golden death mask. This find is regarded as one of the most spectacular in archaeology.
wichtigste: Howard Carter came from Great Britain and was born in 1874.
As a young man in Egypt he first worked as a draughtsman.
His search for the tomb of Tutankhamun was funded by Lord Carnarvon.
In November 1922 he found the tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
Asked whether he could see anything, he is said to have replied: “Yes, wonderful things”.
Egyptologists list the tomb under the designation KV62.
Carter died in London in 1939.

abschnitte.text: **Howard Carter** was born on 9 May 1874 in London and grew up in a family of artists. At only 17 he travelled to Egypt, where he worked as a **draughtsman** copying wall paintings in ancient tombs. Over time he learned how to excavate and became an archaeologist himself. Later he worked as an inspector for the Egyptian Antiquities Service.

The wealthy British aristocrat **Lord Carnarvon** was very interested in Egypt and paid for Carter's excavations. From 1917 they searched the **Valley of the Kings** near Luxor for the tomb of the young king Tutankhamun. Year after year they found almost nothing, and Carnarvon was ready to give up. Carter persuaded him to fund one last season of digging.

On 4 November 1922, Carter's workers came across a step leading down into the rock. At the end of November, with Carnarvon present, Carter opened a sealed door and looked inside by candlelight. Asked whether he could see anything, he is said to have replied: **“Yes, wonderful things”**. In the tomb with the designation **KV62** lay furniture, chariots, jewellery, statues and finally the king's coffin with the golden death mask.

Carter's team needed around **ten years** to clear the tomb completely. Every object was photographed, drawn, described and carefully packed. Altogether more than 5000 objects were found. This careful documentation was exemplary for the time and is still very valuable for research today.

Lord Carnarvon died unexpectedly in Cairo in April 1923 of blood poisoning. Newspapers then spread the legend of the **curse of the pharaoh**, which was supposed to strike everyone who had disturbed the tomb. There is no scientific evidence for this. Carter himself lived for many more years and died in London on 2 March 1939.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who excavates and studies traces and objects from earlier times.
The science of ancient Egypt.
The title of the kings of ancient Egypt.
A valley near Luxor where many Egyptian kings were buried in rock tombs.

gewusst: The code KV62 means that it is the 62nd known tomb in the Valley of the Kings, in English “Kings' Valley”.
Tutankhamun's innermost coffin is made of solid gold and weighs more than 100 kilograms.
Tutankhamun was only a little-known king; he became famous only through Carter's find.

teile.einleitung: Gel electrophoresis is a method for separating tiny molecules such as DNA or proteins by size. To do this, they are pulled with an electric current through a gel that acts like a fine sieve. It is one of the most important tools in biology and medical laboratories.
wichtigste: In gel electrophoresis, molecules are pulled through a gel with an electric current.
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates pieces of DNA by their size.
DNA is negatively charged and therefore travels to the positive pole, the anode.
Short pieces of DNA get further in the same time than long ones.
Agarose is obtained from red algae.
A DNA ladder in its own lane serves as a size comparison.
Proteins are usually separated in gels of polyacrylamide.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of **gel** and **electrophoresis**, which means something like travelling in an electric field. You put a gel in a tray with a salty liquid, the buffer. At both ends of the tray there is a pole to which electricity is connected. Charged particles then travel through the gel to one of the poles.

DNA carries many negative charges and therefore travels to the **positive pole**, the **anode**. The gel is shot through with tiny pores like a dense forest. Short pieces of DNA slip through easily and get further in the same time than long pieces. In this way the pieces sort themselves by length and form so-called **bands** in the gel.

For DNA, **agarose** is usually used, a substance from red algae. You dissolve the powder in hot buffer and let it set in a mould into a wobbly block. For 150 millilitres of a 1.5 per cent gel you need, for example, 2.25 grams of agarose. The samples are mixed with a **loading buffer** containing glycerol, so that they are heavier and sink into the wells of the gel.

DNA is invisible in the gel, so it is stained with a special **dye**. This binds to the DNA and glows under **UV light**. In its own lane a **DNA ladder** runs alongside, containing pieces of known length. By comparing them you can estimate how long the pieces of DNA in the samples are.

**Proteins** can also be separated in this way, and for this gels of **polyacrylamide** are usually used. Beforehand, the proteins are treated with the substance SDS, which unfolds them and gives them an even negative charge. In this way proteins too are separated only by their size. This method is called **SDS-PAGE**.

With gel electrophoresis, researchers check whether an experiment with DNA has worked. In medicine it helps to detect inherited diseases or germs. The **genetic fingerprint**, with which the police examine traces, was also long based on this method. The Swedish chemist **Arne Tiselius** received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1948 for his work on electrophoresis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The genetic material in which the building plans of all living things are stored.
A substance from red algae that forms a firm gel as it cools.
The positive pole, towards which negatively charged particles travel.
A stripe in the gel in which molecules of the same size have gathered.
A salty liquid that conducts electricity and protects the sample.

gewusst: Agarose is related to agar, which is also known in the kitchen as a plant-based setting agent.
A single band can contain billions of pieces of DNA of the same length.
If the current runs too long, the smallest pieces of DNA simply travel out of the gel.

t3tg5fh.t: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research

teile.einleitung: The Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, or FMI for short, is a research institute in Basel. There, researchers from all over the world study how cells, genes and the brain work. It is named after Friedrich Miescher of Basel, who discovered DNA in 1869.
wichtigste: The FMI is in Basel.
It was founded around 1970.
It is closely linked with the pharmaceutical company Novartis.
It is named after the Basel researcher Friedrich Miescher.
In 1869 in Tübingen, Miescher discovered nuclein, which we now call DNA.
One important field of research at the FMI is epigenetics.
The cell biologist Susan Gasser led the institute from 2004 to 2019.

abschnitte.text: The **FMI** is an institute for **basic research** in biomedicine. Basic research means: first you want to understand how life works, even if you do not yet have a medicine in mind. Several hundred people from many countries work at the institute, and the working language is English. It also trains young researchers who write their doctoral theses here.

The institute was founded around **1970** by the Basel chemical and pharmaceutical company Ciba-Geigy. After the merger with Sandoz to form **Novartis** in 1996, it remained closely linked with that group. The FMI is also connected with the **University of Basel**, where many of its group leaders also teach. From 2004 to 2019 the well-known cell biologist **Susan Gasser** led the institute.

One focus is **epigenetics**: it studies how genes are switched on and off without the DNA sequence changing. Another focus is the **neurosciences**, that is, research into nerve cells and the brain. Other groups study how tissues grow and renew themselves. For this they use yeast cells, nematodes, fish, mice and modern microscopes, among other things.

abschnitte.titel: The man it is named after
abschnitte.text: **Friedrich Miescher** was born in Basel in 1844. In 1869 in **Tübingen** he discovered a substance rich in phosphorus in cell nuclei, nuclein. Today we know that it was DNA, the carrier of genetic information. Later he was a professor in Basel, so his name fits a Basel research institute well.

abschnitte.titel: Basel as a city of research
abschnitte.text: Basel is one of the most important cities for **life sciences** in Europe. Large pharmaceutical companies such as Novartis and Roche have their headquarters here. In addition there are the University of Basel, the Biozentrum and a department of ETH Zurich. Many people in the region work in research or in making medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Research that aims to understand how something works
Research into how genes are switched on and off without changing the DNA
Research on living things with the aim of understanding diseases better
Research on the nervous system and the brain

gewusst: Although the FMI belongs to Novartis, it publishes its research results freely for the whole of science.
Researchers from dozens of countries work at the FMI, which is why English is usually spoken in the laboratory.
The discovery made by the man the institute is named after was only properly understood more than 80 years later.

teile.einleitung: The Human Brain Project was a large European research project that aimed to understand the human brain better. It ran for about ten years, from 2013 to 2023, and in its early years was coordinated by EPFL in Lausanne. Hundreds of researchers from many countries worked together, mainly with computers and digital brain atlases.
wichtigste: The Human Brain Project was funded mainly by the European Union.
It ran for about ten years, from 2013 to 2023.
The neuroscientist Henry Markram is regarded as its initiator.
In its early phase, EPFL in Lausanne coordinated the project.
Originally a budget of around one billion euros was planned.
In 2014 an open letter from critical researchers sparked a big controversy.
A lasting result is the research infrastructure EBRAINS.

abschnitte.text: The **Human Brain Project**, HBP for short, was one of the largest research projects the **European Union** has ever funded. Its aim was to understand the human brain better with the help of computers. To do this, researchers from medicine, biology, computer science and physics worked together. The project started in 2013 and ended in 2023.

The neuroscientist **Henry Markram**, who did research at **EPFL** in Lausanne, is regarded as its initiator. There, back in 2005, he had started the Blue Brain Project, which rebuilt parts of a mouse brain on a computer. The HBP was meant to take this idea much further on a larger scale. In the early phase, the whole project was coordinated by EPFL.

The brain was to be studied mainly with **computer simulations** and **brain atlases**. A brain atlas is a very precise digital map of the brain, on which you can see where which cells are. Special computers that work in a similar way to nerve cells were also developed; they are called **neuromorphic** computers. The data were collected in such a way that researchers all over the world can use them.

At the start, the project was announced with big promises, such as rebuilding an entire human brain on a computer. In 2014 hundreds of researchers criticised the goals and the leadership of the project in an **open letter**. They felt that too much was being bet on simulations and too little on other research. After that the project was reorganised and the leadership spread more widely.

A lasting result is the research infrastructure **EBRAINS**. It offers researchers data, brain atlases, computing power and tools for brain research. The HBP also contributed to better methods in medicine, for example in planning operations for epilepsy. But many questions about the brain are still open today, because it is one of the most complicated things we know.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies the nervous system and the brain.
A reconstruction of a process on a computer in order to study it.
A precise digital map of the brain.
Built on the model of nerve cells.

gewusst: The human brain consists of around 86 billion nerve cells, which makes a complete simulation enormously difficult.
As part of the research, a brain was cut into thousands of wafer-thin slices to create a very detailed 3D atlas.
Neuromorphic computers from the project are located in Manchester and Heidelberg, among other places.

teile.einleitung: The Human Genome Project was a huge international research project that set out to read the complete blueprint of the human being. This blueprint is contained in the genetic material DNA in almost every one of our body cells. For the first time, researchers wrote down the entire sequence of letters of this genetic material.
wichtigste: The Human Genome Project officially started in 1990.
The public project cost around 3 billion US dollars.
A single set of human chromosomes contains around 3 billion base pairs.
According to current estimates, humans have around 20,000 genes that contain blueprints for proteins.
The company Celera Genomics under Craig Venter entered as a competitor and used fast shotgun sequencing.
From 1993 Francis Collins led the American genome research institute.
Only in 2022 did the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium present a truly gap-free sequence.

abschnitte.text: The **genome** is the entire genetic information of a living thing. It is stored in **DNA**, a long, twisted thread in the shape of a double helix. The information is written with only four building blocks, abbreviated with the letters A, C, G and T. Two building blocks together form a base pair. A single set of human chromosomes has around 3 billion of these base pairs.

The Human Genome Project officially began in **1990** in the USA. Soon research centres from Great Britain, Japan, France, Germany and China were working on it too. At first the famous DNA researcher James Watson led the American programme. From 1993 **Francis Collins** took over the leadership of the American genome research institute. Altogether the public project cost around 3 billion US dollars.

In 1998 the researcher Craig Venter announced that his company **Celera Genomics** would decode the genome faster. Celera relied on **shotgun sequencing**. In this method, the DNA is broken into a great many small pieces, which are read one by one and then put together by computers like a jigsaw puzzle. In 2000 both sides jointly announced a first draft. In 2003 the project was officially declared complete.

Many researchers had expected 80,000 to 100,000 genes. Today, however, it is estimated that there are only around **20,000 protein-coding genes**, that is, genes with a blueprint for proteins. That is not many more than in a small roundworm. Only a small part of the DNA consists of such genes; most of it has other tasks or is still poorly understood. It also turned out that the genetic material of all people is more than 99 per cent identical.

The sequence of 2003 was not quite complete. Difficult areas were missing, for example many repeating sections at the ends and in the middle of the chromosomes. The ends of the chromosomes are called **telomeres**. Only in 2022 did the **Telomere-to-Telomere** consortium publish a truly gap-free sequence. This was made possible by new machines that can read very long pieces of DNA in one go.

The Human Genome Project greatly changed medicine and biology. Today a person's genetic material can be read in a few days and for a fraction of the earlier cost. This helps doctors find the causes of some **hereditary diseases** faster. Some cancer medicines are also partly tailored to the genetic material. At the same time there are important questions about data protection, because genetic information is very personal data.

begriffe.erklaerung: The entire genetic information of a living thing.
Two matching building blocks of DNA, like the two halves of a rung on a ladder.
Reading the order of the building blocks of DNA.
A section of DNA that contains a blueprint, usually for a protein.
The end piece of a chromosome, similar to the plastic tip on a shoelace.

gewusst: If you printed the roughly 3 billion letters of one set of chromosomes in books, you would need hundreds of thick volumes.
Humans have roughly as many protein-coding genes as the tiny roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.
The data from the public project were put on the internet free of charge as they came in, so that all researchers could use them.

teile.einleitung: Helvetica is one of the best-known typefaces in the world and a genuine Swiss invention. It was created in 1957 in Münchenstein near Basel and today can be seen on signs, logos and posters all over the world. Its name simply means “Swiss” in Latin.
wichtigste: Helvetica was designed in 1957 by Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann.
It was created at the Haas type foundry in Münchenstein in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.
At first it was called “Neue Haas Grotesk”.
In 1960 it was given the name Helvetica, which means “Swiss” in Latin.
Helvetica is a sans-serif typeface, that is, a typeface without small feet on the letters.
Because it is clear and easy to read, it is used especially often for signs and logos.
It is regarded as a typical example of the Swiss graphic style.

abschnitte.text: In the 1950s, the **Haas type foundry** in Münchenstein wanted to offer a modern, plain typeface. The director **Eduard Hoffmann** gave the job to the graphic designer **Max Miedinger**. An older German typeface, Akzidenz-Grotesk, served as a model. In 1957 the new typeface came out under the name “Neue Haas Grotesk”.

The German partner company Stempel in Frankfurt wanted to sell the typeface abroad as well. For this, a catchier name was needed. In 1960 it was renamed **Helvetica**, after Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland. At that time Swiss graphic design was seen as especially modern, so the name was also a good selling point.

Helvetica is one of the **sans-serif typefaces**, which in German typography are also called Grotesk. Serifs are the small cross-strokes at the ends of letters, as seen in Times, for example. Helvetica has even strokes, clear shapes and horizontal ends, for example on the small “t” or the “e”. This makes it look calm, matter-of-fact and neutral.

Because it is so **easy to read**, Helvetica is often used for signs, signposts and **logos**. It is well known, for example, from signs on the New York subway and from the logos of large companies. Apple also used it for many years as the system font on iPhones. In 1983 a revised version called Helvetica Neue appeared.

Helvetica fits perfectly with the **Swiss Style**, a graphic style that arose in Zurich and Basel in the 1950s and 1960s. Typical features are clear grids, lots of white space and plain typefaces. This style was copied all over the world. In 2007 there was even a documentary film about this one typeface alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particular design for all the letters, numbers and symbols.
A small cross-stroke at the end of a stroke of a letter.
A company that used to cast metal letters for printing.
A technical term for a typeface without serifs.

gewusst: Helvetica was originally cast as hot-metal type, that is, as small metal letters for printing presses.
The well-known computer font Arial looks so similar to Helvetica that many people can hardly tell them apart.
Before working on Helvetica, Max Miedinger had worked as a typesetter and as a salesman for the type foundry.

teile.einleitung: Hildegard of Bingen was a nun from the Middle Ages who ran a convent as abbess. She wrote books about faith, nature and medicine and composed sacred music. Today she is regarded as one of the most important women of the Middle Ages and is a Doctor of the Church in the Catholic Church.
wichtigste: Hildegard of Bingen lived from 1098 to 1179 in what is now Germany.
She was a Benedictine nun and ran a convent as abbess.
Her book “Physica” describes plants, animals and stones and their healing effects.
Besides medicine and theology, she is known for her sacred music.
She reported having visions, which she wrote down in books such as “Scivias”.
In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church.
She founded the Rupertsberg convent near Bingen on the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: Hildegard was born in 1098 into a noble family in the area of today's Rhineland-Palatinate. As a child she was sent to the **Disibodenberg** monastery, where she was brought up by the nun Jutta. She became a **Benedictine**, meaning she lived by the rule of St Benedict, with prayer and work. After Jutta's death, the sisters chose her as their leader in 1136. Later she founded the Rupertsberg convent near Bingen and became **abbess** there.

Hildegard said that she had had **visions** since childhood, inner pictures that she understood as messages from God. When she was over 40 she began to write them down, and her most important work on them is called **Scivias**, which means “Know the Ways”. Because women at that time were hardly allowed to teach in public, she obtained permission from the Pope and the Church. She wrote in Latin and had her texts copied out by a monk. Her books were decorated with colourful pictures.

In her book **Physica**, Hildegard described hundreds of plants, animals, stones and metals. She explained how they could be used as remedies, for example fennel, spelt or herbs. Another work on illnesses and their treatment is called “Causae et curae”. Her knowledge came partly from old writings and partly from the folk medicine of her time. Many recipes of today's Hildegard medicine are popular, but their effects have mostly not been scientifically proven.

Hildegard composed many **sacred songs** for her sisters' church services. About 77 of these chants have survived, together with a musical play called “Ordo Virtutum”, in which virtues appear as characters. Her melodies are sung in unison, but often rise very high and range widely, which gives them a special sound. She is one of the first women composers whose names and works we know. Her music is still recorded and sung in concerts today.

For her time, Hildegard travelled unusually widely and preached in cities such as Cologne and Trier. She wrote letters to popes, to emperors such as Frederick Barbarossa and to many other people. After her death in 1179 she was venerated as a saint; her feast day is 17 September. In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI confirmed her **canonisation** and declared her a **Doctor of the Church**. Only a few people hold this title, among them only four women.

begriffe.erklaerung: The head of a convent of nuns.
A nun who lives according to the rule of St Benedict.
An inner picture or experience that someone understands as a message.
An honorary title of the Catholic Church for people whose teaching is especially important.

gewusst: Hildegard invented her own secret language with hundreds of new words and its own letters.
Hildegard recommended spelt as an especially healthy grain, which is why it is often linked with her today.
Hildegard was one of the few women in the Middle Ages who exchanged letters with popes and emperors.

teile.einleitung: The Green Revolution was a great change in farming from about 1950 into the 1970s. New, especially high-yielding cereal varieties, fertiliser and irrigation made harvests grow strongly in many poor countries. It saved millions of people from hunger, but it also brought new problems.
wichtigste: The American agricultural scientist Norman Borlaug is regarded as the father of the Green Revolution.
In Mexico, Borlaug bred semi-dwarf wheat varieties that do not bend over with heavy fertilising.
In 1970 Norman Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The rice variety IR8 was introduced in 1966 and became known as miracle rice.
The term Green Revolution was coined in 1968 by the American William Gaud.
The Indian state of Punjab is an example of successes and consequences such as falling groundwater levels.
The main criticisms are the loss of old varieties and the heavy use of chemicals.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, the population grew quickly in many countries, and there was often not enough to eat. Experts therefore developed new **high-yielding varieties** of wheat, rice and maize. Together with artificial fertiliser, pesticides and **irrigation**, they brought much bigger harvests. This development is called the Green Revolution.

From 1943 the **Rockefeller Foundation** funded a wheat programme in Mexico, in which Norman Borlaug worked from 1944. He cross-bred thousands of wheat varieties and searched for plants that were resistant to fungal diseases such as rust. Especially important were **semi-dwarf varieties** with short, strong stalks. They carry heavy ears without bending over when heavily fertilised.

At the International Rice Research Institute **IRRI** in the Philippines, a new rice variety was created. In 1966 it reached the fields as **IR8** and produced several times the old harvests. That is why it was called miracle rice. In 1966 the maize and wheat research centre CIMMYT was also founded in Mexico.

In the mid-1960s, severe famines threatened India and Pakistan. The countries imported large quantities of the new wheat seed from Mexico. Within a few years wheat harvests rose sharply, especially in the state of **Punjab**. In this way India went from being a grain-importing country to one that could largely feed itself.

The new varieties need a lot of water, fertiliser and **pesticides**. In Punjab the groundwater level is falling because so much water is pumped up for the fields. Many old varieties adapted to the region were lost; people speak of a loss of **variety diversity**. Small farmers who could not afford seed and fertiliser often benefited less.

Without the Green Revolution, many millions of people would have had less to eat. Today people are looking for ways to increase harvests while also protecting soils, water and diversity. Old varieties are stored in seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway. In Switzerland, too, organisations such as Pro Specie Rara preserve old crop plants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant variety that produces an especially large harvest on the same area.
Artificially supplying fields with water, for example with canals or pumps.
A substance used against pests, fungi or weeds in the field.
The large number of different varieties of a crop plant.

gewusst: Norman Borlaug was an agricultural scientist and still received the Nobel Peace Prize, because enough food is seen as a contribution to peace.
To make faster progress, Borlaug grew two generations of wheat a year in different places in Mexico.
The term Green Revolution was meant to express a contrast to violent revolutions.

teile.einleitung: A high-pressure area, or high for short, is a large zone in the Earth's atmosphere in which the air pressure is higher than in its surroundings. Highs usually bring calm, dry and sunny weather. In winter, however, they can also bring fog and icy cold.
wichtigste: In a high-pressure area, the air pressure is higher than in its surroundings.
The technical term for a high-pressure area is anticyclone.
In the northern hemisphere, the air turns clockwise around a high.
Highs usually bring fine, dry weather.
Without clouds the ground gives off a lot of heat, which is why nights in high-pressure weather are often cold.
In an inversion in winter, cold air lies at the bottom with warmer air above it.
The Russian high often brings very cold air to Central Europe in winter.

abschnitte.text: The air presses down on the Earth with its weight; this is called **air pressure**. It is measured in hectopascals and averages about 1013 hectopascals at sea level. In a **high-pressure area** the pressure is higher than all around, in a low-pressure area lower. The technical term for a high is **anticyclone**; on weather maps there is often a big H.

In a high, the air slowly sinks from above. As it does, it is compressed and warms up, so clouds dissolve. That is why highs usually bring **sunshine** and hardly any rain. Without a blanket of cloud, however, the ground radiates a lot of heat into space at night, which is why the nights are often cold.

At ground level the air flows out of the high towards areas of lower pressure, and this creates wind. Because the Earth is rotating, it does not flow straight but is deflected. In the northern hemisphere, the air therefore turns **clockwise** around the high. In the southern hemisphere it is exactly the other way round.

In winter, during high-pressure weather, cold air collects at ground level while warmer air lies above it. This reversed layering is called an **inversion**. In the Swiss Plateau a grey **blanket of high fog** often forms, which can stay for days. At the same time, on mountains such as the Rigi or the Napf, the sun shines above a sea of fog.

The **Azores High** usually lies over the Atlantic near the Azores and often brings Switzerland warm, sunny weather in summer. The **Russian high** over Eastern Europe sometimes sends icy air to Central Europe in winter. A strong high that stays in the same place for a long time is called a **blocking high**, because it steers lows around itself. Such situations can bring heatwaves and drought in summer.

When there is a high north of Switzerland, the **bise** often blows, a cold, dry wind from the north-east. It blows especially strongly on Lake Geneva, because the air is squeezed between the Jura and the Alps. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss watch highs and lows closely in order to forecast the weather. To do this, they measure air pressure at many stations with a **barometer**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing down on the Earth.
The technical term for a high-pressure area.
A weather situation in which cold air lies at the bottom and warmer air at the top.
An instrument for measuring air pressure.
The unit of measurement for air pressure.

gewusst: During high fog it can be grey and cold in Zurich while it is warm and sunny at 1500 metres above sea level.
In Central Europe, highs and lows are given first names so that it is easier to talk about them in the weather forecast.
The strongest highs on Earth form in winter over Siberia and Mongolia, where the air is especially cold and heavy.

teile.einleitung: The Galápagos Islands are a group of volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean that belong to Ecuador. Animals live here that exist nowhere else in the world, such as giant tortoises and marine iguanas. The naturalist Charles Darwin gained important ideas here for his theory of evolution.
wichtigste: The Galápagos Islands lie in the Pacific on the equator and belong to Ecuador.
Charles Darwin visited the islands in 1835.
The small Darwin's finches are named after him.
The marine iguana swims in the sea and eats algae.
The blue-footed booby has bright blue feet.
A penguin even lives on Galápagos, although you would expect one in colder regions.
Since 1978 the islands have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The Galápagos Islands lie about 1,000 kilometres west of the South American mainland, right on the **equator**. They belong to the country of **Ecuador**. All the islands were formed by **volcanoes**, and some volcanoes are still active today. The largest island is called Isabela.

On the remote islands, animals have developed that occur only here. The **giant tortoises**, which can live for more than a hundred years, are famous. The name Galápagos comes from an old Spanish word for tortoise. The **marine iguana** is the only lizard in the world that dives in the sea and eats algae.

The **blue-footed booby** stands out with its bright blue feet, which it likes to lift proudly into the air. The Galápagos penguin is the only penguin that lives so close to the equator. It survives here because cold ocean currents bring plenty of food. Sea lions, sharks and sea turtles are also common.

In 1835 the young naturalist **Charles Darwin** visited the islands on the ship HMS Beagle. He noticed that the animals differed slightly from island to island. Especially well known are **Darwin's finches**, whose beaks are shaped differently depending on their food. These observations helped him to develop his theory of evolution, which he published in 1859.

As early as 1959, most of the islands were declared a **national park**. In 1978 they were among the very first areas to be put on the list of **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**. Introduced animals such as goats and rats long threatened the native species. Today tourists may visit many places only with trained guides.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line that divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
Occurring only in one particular place in the world.
A large protected area in which nature comes first.

gewusst: The animals on Galápagos are hardly afraid of people, because for a long time they had no enemies.
The famous giant tortoise “Lonesome George” was the last animal of its subspecies and died in 2012.
Marine iguanas can simply sneeze out the surplus salt from the sea water.

teile.einleitung: Homo erectus was an early human species that appeared in Africa around two million years ago. It already walked upright like us and was one of the first human species to leave Africa and travel as far as Asia. Its species existed for over a million years, much longer than we modern humans have.
wichtigste: Homo erectus means “upright man”.
It arose in Africa around two million years ago.
According to current knowledge, it was one of the first human species to leave Africa.
In 1891 Eugène Dubois found bones of a Homo erectus on the island of Java.
In Dmanisi in Georgia, skulls of early humans around 1.8 million years old were found.
Peking Man from a cave near Beijing also belongs to Homo erectus.
A typical tool of its culture is the hand axe.

abschnitte.text: **Homo erectus** is an extinct species of the human genus. The name is Latin and means “upright man”. It had longer legs than earlier pre-humans, similar to ours today, and was a runner with great stamina. Its brain was bigger than that of earlier species, but smaller than ours. The species lived for more than a million years.

In 1891 the Dutch doctor **Eugène Dubois** discovered a skull cap and a thigh bone on the island of **Java** in Indonesia. At first he called the find “Pithecanthropus erectus”, meaning upright ape-man. In the 1920s and 1930s, many bones were found in a cave near Beijing; they became known as **Peking Man**. In 1984 the almost complete skeleton of a boy came to light in Kenya; he is famous as Turkana Boy.

abschnitte.titel: Out of Africa into the world
abschnitte.text: According to current knowledge, Homo erectus was one of the first human species to **leave Africa**. In **Dmanisi** in Georgia, skulls of early humans around 1.8 million years old have been found. Later, groups lived as far away as China and Indonesia. On their travels they had to adapt to very different landscapes and climates.

Typical of the culture of Homo erectus is the **hand axe**, a stone carefully shaped on both sides. It was used for cutting, scraping and chopping, almost like a Stone Age pocket knife. Such tools were made in almost the same way for a very long time. Some groups of Homo erectus probably also used **fire** already, as finds of burnt bones and charcoal suggest.

Homo erectus is very important for research because it stands between the early pre-humans and later humans such as the Neanderthals and **Homo sapiens**. Many experts suspect that later human species developed from it or from close relatives. How exactly the species are related to one another is still being studied. Every new find can change the picture.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species, for example the human genus.
A petrified or preserved remain of a living thing from earlier times.
A stone tool worked on both sides that fits well in the hand.
An early ancestor of humans that does not yet belong to the genus Homo.

gewusst: Turkana Boy was probably only about eight to twelve years old, but already about as tall as a teenager today.
Many of the original bones of Peking Man were lost in the Second World War and were never found again.
Homo erectus lived on Earth several times as long as Homo sapiens has existed so far.

teile.einleitung: In biology, homology means that body parts of different living things are similar because they come from a common ancestor. A human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper look completely different, but they have the same basic plan. Homologies are an important piece of evidence for evolution.
wichtigste: Homology means similarity due to common descent.
A classic example is the forelegs of horses, bats' wings and whales' flippers.
In 1952 Adolf Remane set out well-known criteria for recognising homologies.
The hammer and anvil in the ear of mammals are homologous to jawbones of reptiles.
Remains of the pelvic girdle in whales are a vestigial homologous organ.
The gene Pax6 controls eye development in fruit flies and mice.
Through divergence, homologous organs often look very different.

abschnitte.text: **Homology** comes from Greek and means roughly “agreement”. In biology, features are called homologous if they go back to a **common ancestor**. The best-known example is the forelimbs of mammals. A horse's leg, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a human arm all have an upper arm bone, two forearm bones and hand or foot bones.

In the course of evolution, homologous organs have often adapted to completely different tasks. This process is called **divergence**. That is why the bat flies with its arms, the whale swims and the horse runs. The counterpart to this is **analogy**: insect wings and bird wings are both used for flying, but have a completely different origin.

In 1952 the German zoologist **Adolf Remane** set out criteria for recognising homologies. One important one is the same position in the body plan. A special fine structure that matches is also a clue. Intermediate forms also help, for example in fossils, which show how a feature changed step by step.

The tiny ear bones, the **hammer and anvil** in the ear of mammals, are homologous to the articular and quadrate bones, which form the jaw joint in reptiles. Whales still have small remains of the **pelvic girdle**, even though they no longer have hind legs. Such leftovers are called vestigial organs. There are examples in humans too, such as the tailbone as the remnant of a tail.

**Genes** can also be homologous. The gene **Pax6** controls the development of the eyes in both fruit flies and mice, even though these eyes are built very differently. This is called deep homology. Homologous genes in different species that arose from a common gene when new species formed are called **orthologues**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Similarity due to the same task, but without a common origin.
The remnant of a body part that has lost its original task.
A section of the genetic material that controls a particular characteristic.

gewusst: The term homology was coined by the British researcher Richard Owen as early as 1843, even before Darwin published his theory of evolution.
The word homology also exists in chemistry and mathematics, but there it has other meanings.
A bat's wing consists mainly of greatly lengthened finger bones with a flying membrane stretched between them.

teile.einleitung: A plaster cast, or cast for short, is a firm bandage that holds a broken bone still. In this way the bone can grow back together in the right position. Many children wear a cast at some point, and friends like to decorate it with names and greetings.
wichtigste: You usually get a cast when a bone is broken.
The cast holds the bone still so that it grows back together properly.
A child with a broken arm usually wears the cast for a few weeks.
Many modern casts are made of plastic today.
With a leg in a cast you usually walk with crutches.
Under a cast that you wear for a long time it often itches.
The plaster cast was made known around 1850 by the Dutch military doctor Antonius Mathijsen.

abschnitte.text: When a bone breaks, the two broken pieces have to lie exactly against each other and must not move. Only then does the bone grow back together in the right shape. A **plaster cast** encloses the injured part of the body like a hard shell. Usually the joints above and below the break are kept still too. Beforehand the doctor takes an **X-ray** in order to see the break exactly.

First a soft stocking and some padding wool go onto the skin. Then damp bandages soaked with plaster or plastic are wound around them. After a short time they become hard. Classic plaster consists of **calcium sulphate**, a mineral that hardens with water. Sometimes you first get only a **splint**, because the injured place can swell up.

Today many casts are made of **plastic**, often reinforced with glass fibres. They are lighter, harden faster and come in many colours. Classic plaster, on the other hand, can be shaped especially well. Neither kind should be made wet, unless the doctor expressly allows it.

In children, bones heal faster than in adults. A broken arm in a child usually needs a few weeks until it is stable again. After that the cast is removed with a special saw that only cuts hard materials and does not injure the skin. Afterwards the muscles are often a little weaker, and the arm or leg has to be trained again, sometimes with **physiotherapy**.

Anyone with a leg in a cast walks with **crutches** and takes the weight off the leg. The injured part of the body should often be raised, so that it swells up less. If it itches under the cast, you must not push pointed objects in, because you could injure yourself. If fingers or toes become cold, blue, numb or very painful, you have to go to the doctor at once.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm bandage of plaster or plastic that keeps a part of the body still.
When a bone breaks wholly or partly, also called a fracture.
A picture that shows the inside of the body, especially the bones, with invisible rays.
Walking supports with which you can take the weight off an injured leg.

gewusst: Plaster is also used for walls, figures and moulds, for instance at the dentist.
After healing, a bone is often especially stable at the place where it broke.
The saw for removing the cast does not cut but vibrates quickly to and fro, which is why it is harmless to the skin.

teile.einleitung: Glass is a hard, mostly transparent material that is made from melted sand. We meet it every day in windows, bottles, spectacles and screens. Although glass is solid, its particles are disordered as in a frozen liquid.
wichtigste: The main ingredient of ordinary glass is quartz sand.
Glass is melted from its raw materials at about 1500 degrees Celsius.
Soda lowers the melting temperature of the sand.
Glass is amorphous, so its particles are disordered.
Obsidian is a natural glass from volcanoes.
Window glass is made as float glass, with the melt floating on liquid tin.
Fibre optic cables carry information with light.

abschnitte.text: Glass is a solid whose particles are not arranged in a regular lattice. This structure is called **amorphous**, that is, without a fixed form. That is why glass is transparent and does not break along straight surfaces like a crystal. It conducts no electricity, does not rust and hardly reacts with most substances.

Ordinary glass consists above all of **quartz sand**, with **soda** and lime added. The soda lowers the melting temperature, and the lime makes the glass more durable. The mixture is melted in big furnaces at about 1500 degrees Celsius. Today a lot of **waste glass** is added as well, which saves raw materials and energy.

abschnitte.titel: From the window to the windscreen
abschnitte.text: Window glass is made as **float glass**, a method that was developed in England in the 1950s. The hot molten glass flows onto a bath of liquid **tin** and spreads out on it quite flat and smooth. The windscreen of a car is made of **laminated safety glass**. Between two panes of glass lies a tear-resistant plastic film that holds the splinters in place.

Glass is found in nature too. When lava cools very quickly, the shiny black volcanic rock **obsidian** arises. Stone Age people made razor-sharp blades and arrowheads from it. When lightning strikes sand, a tube of glass can form as well.

People have been making glass for several thousand years, at first above all beads and small vessels. Around the beginning of our era the **blowpipe** was invented in the eastern Mediterranean. With this long tube, glassblowers blow up liquid glass like a balloon into bottles and vases. Later splendid coloured **church windows** came about, and today glass is a mass product.

In **fibre optic cables**, light is led through wafer-thin threads of glass and so carries huge amounts of data for the internet. Glass is also found in spectacles, camera lenses, solar cells and mobile phone screens. In Switzerland, waste glass is collected sorted by colour, namely white, brown and green. In this way the glass can be melted down and used again and again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Without a regular order of the particles.
Fine sand that consists above all of the mineral quartz.
Flat window glass that is made on liquid tin.
A natural, mostly black glass from volcanoes.

gewusst: Glass can be melted down and reused an endless number of times without losing quality.
The light in a fibre optic cable is reflected back from the inner wall again and again and so can also travel round bends.
That old church windows are thicker at the bottom is not because glass flows but because of the way they were made at the time.

teile.einleitung: A glacial lake is a lake that was created by a glacier. Some lie right next to or on top of the ice, others fill basins that glaciers scooped out long ago. Many glacial lakes shine turquoise, but some can also become dangerous.
wichtigste: Many glacial lakes shine turquoise because fine rock flour scatters sunlight.
An ice-dammed lake is a lake that a glacier holds back like a dam.
Moraine-dammed lakes form behind a ridge of glacial debris.
If the dam of a glacial lake breaks, a sudden flood wave can result.
Because the glaciers are melting, many new lakes are forming in the Alps today.
Lake Trift in the Bernese Oberland only formed when the Trift Glacier retreated.
Large lakes in the Swiss Plateau, such as Lake Zurich, were scooped out by Ice Age glaciers.

abschnitte.text: A **glacial lake** is any lake whose formation has something to do with a glacier. This includes small pools on the ice just as much as huge lakes in the lowlands. Experts classify the lakes by what holds the water back: ice, debris or rock. Many glacial lakes get their water directly from meltwater. That is why they are usually very cold and fuller in summer than in winter.

An **ice-dammed lake** forms when a glacier blocks off a side valley like a dam wall. A **moraine-dammed lake** lies behind a ridge of stones and debris that the glacier pushed up in the past. Rock basin lakes fill hollows that the ice has ground out of the rock. On the glacier itself there are small meltwater lakes, which often last only one summer. A well-known example of a former ice-dammed lake is Lake Märjelen beside the Great Aletsch Glacier.

Meltwater brings tiny grains of ground-up rock with it, known as **rock flour**. These particles float in the water and scatter sunlight. Mainly blue and green light is reflected, so the lake looks turquoise or milky green. Depending on the amount of flour and the position of the sun, the colour changes over the course of the day and the year. Lake Oeschinen near Kandersteg is a famous example of this glowing colour.

If the dam of ice or debris suddenly breaks, a glacial lake can empty in a short time. This creates a **flood wave** that sweeps rubble along and can damage bridges, roads and houses. On the Plaine Morte Glacier, the Lac des Faverges forms every summer and drains almost every year through channels in the ice towards Lenk. The municipality of Lenk has therefore built protective structures and monitors the lake closely. At other dangerous glacial lakes, too, experts measure the water level and have set up warning systems.

abschnitte.titel: New and old lakes in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Because the glaciers are melting, **new lakes** keep forming in the Alps where there used to be ice. Lake Trift in the Bernese Oberland formed only in the last few decades, when the Trift Glacier retreated. Today a well-known suspension bridge, the Trift Bridge, crosses the gorge there. Much older are the large lakes of the Swiss Plateau, such as Lake Zurich, Lake Geneva or Lake Constance. Their basins were scooped out by the mighty glaciers of the **Ice Ages**, which reached into the lowlands around 20,000 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ridge of stones, sand and debris that a glacier has pushed up or left behind.
A lake that a glacier holds back like a natural dam.
A long, cold period when glaciers covered much larger areas than today.
The sudden draining of a lake when its dam gives way.

gewusst: Researchers estimate that more than a thousand new small lakes have formed in the Swiss Alps since 1850 where glaciers used to be.
New glacial lakes can also be put to use, for example as water reservoirs for hydroelectric power stations.

teile.einleitung: In artificial intelligence, a hallucination is an answer that sounds convincing but is wrong or made up. Chatbots based on large language models in particular make such mistakes. Because they sound just as confident as when they give correct answers, hallucinations are treacherous.
wichtigste: An AI hallucination is a convincing-sounding but false statement.
Language models produce likely sequences of words, but have no built-in fact-checking.
In scientific texts, invented references are especially common.
Hallucinations are often worded just as confidently as correct answers.
The technique retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is meant to reduce hallucinations by using suitable documents.
In 2023 a lawyer in New York submitted court judgements that a chatbot had invented.
Important information should be checked in reliable sources.

abschnitte.text: For humans, a **hallucination** means seeing or hearing something that is not really there. In artificial intelligence, the word is used for invented or false information from a program. A chatbot might, for example, name a book that does not exist or give a wrong date. The program is not lying on purpose; it simply does not notice the mistake. Some experts therefore suggest the word **confabulation** from psychology, which describes unconscious inventing.

A **language model** learns from huge amounts of text which words are likely to follow one another. So it produces text that sounds plausible, but it does not automatically check whether it is true. If the model is missing a piece of information, it fills the gap with something that fits well. Errors in the training data or outdated knowledge can also lead to wrong answers. Hallucinations are especially common with rare topics, exact figures and **references to sources**.

In 2023 a lawyer in **New York** hit the headlines. In court he had cited earlier judgements that a chatbot had completely made up. The court noticed that these cases did not exist and imposed a fine. In scientific texts, chatbots often invent references with real-sounding titles and authors' names. False details also sometimes turn up in biographies of people.

Developers are trying in various ways to reduce hallucinations. In **retrieval-augmented generation**, RAG for short, the system first searches for suitable documents and gives them to the model as a basis. Other programs can search the internet and give their sources. Models are also trained to admit more readily when they do not know something. So far, however, hallucinations cannot be prevented completely.

If you use a chatbot, you should always check important information in **reliable sources**. These include school books, encyclopedias, official websites or experts. Be especially careful with health, law, money and with homework that needs references. A good question is always: where does this information come from, and can I check it? That way you use the strengths of AI and protect yourself from its mistakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer program you can have a conversation with in normal language.
An AI program that has learned to understand and write texts.
Unconsciously inventing memories or information, without meaning to lie.
Where a piece of information comes from, for example a book or a website.

gewusst: In 2023 the English word “hallucinate” was chosen as Word of the Year by the Cambridge Dictionary because of its new AI meaning.
A chatbot can answer the same question correctly once and wrongly another time, because chance also plays a part in choosing the text.

teile.einleitung: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves slowly downhill. It arises where more snow falls over many years than can melt in the summer. In Switzerland there are about 1400 glaciers, most of them in the Alps.
wichtigste: A glacier arises from a lot of snow that is pressed into ice over the years.
Out of old, grainy snow, called firn, glacier ice later forms.
A glacier flows slowly but steadily downhill.
The front, lower part is called the glacier tongue.
Glaciers store large amounts of fresh water.
Most of the glaciers of Switzerland lie in the Alps; there are about 1400 of them.
Most of the ice on Earth lies on the continent of Antarctica.

abschnitte.text: If more snow falls in the mountains in winter than melts in summer, some of it stays each year. The snow is pressed together by the weight of the new layers and becomes grainy; it is then called **firn**. After many years dense, bluish **glacier ice** forms out of it. Once the mass of ice is thick enough, it begins to **flow** under its own weight.

In the upper part, the **accumulation area**, more snow gathers than melts. In the lower part, the **ablation area**, more ice melts than is added. The front, lower part is called the **glacier tongue**. From its gate a milky meltwater often streams out that contains fine rock dust.

A glacier behaves like an account with income and spending. If a lot of snow falls in winter and little melts in summer, then it **grows**. If, on the other hand, it is warm for a long time, it loses ice and becomes shorter and thinner. Since the 19th century most Alpine glaciers have shrunk a great deal, above all because of **global warming**.

Glaciers and ice sheets store the greatest part of the **fresh water** of the Earth. Most of the ice lies on **Antarctica**, and a large part on Greenland too. In Switzerland, glaciers supply meltwater in summer for rivers such as the Rhone, the Rhine and the Inn. This water is also used in reservoirs for producing electricity.

The biggest glacier of the Alps is the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais; it is over 20 kilometres long. Also well known are the Rhone Glacier at the Furka Pass, the Gorner Glacier near Zermatt and the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine. Glaciers have shaped the landscape of Switzerland, for example broad valleys and many lakes. In the last **ice age** the glaciers reached as far as the Central Plateau.

begriffe.erklaerung: Old, grainy snow that has lasted through at least one summer.
The front, lower part of a glacier.
The upper part of a glacier, in which snow gathers.
A ridge of stones and rubble that a glacier pushes ahead of it or deposits at its edge.

gewusst: Glacier ice often looks blue, because the dense ice swallows red light and lets blue light through.
Lake Geneva, Lake Zurich and many other Swiss lakes lie in basins that glaciers gouged out in the ice age.
Huge blocks of rock in the middle of the Central Plateau, so-called erratic boulders, were once carried there by glaciers from the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A genetically modified organism, or GMO for short, is a living thing whose genetic material has been deliberately changed in the laboratory. In this way plants can be protected against pests, for example, or bacteria can be used to make medicines. Hardly any topic is discussed as intensely in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In a GMO the genetic material has been changed in a way that does not occur under natural conditions through crossing or recombination.
The Flavr Savr tomato came onto the market in the USA in 1994 as the first genetically modified food.
Soya is the genetically modified crop plant with the largest growing area worldwide.
In Switzerland the Gene Technology Act of 2003 governs the handling of GMOs.
In Switzerland, food has to be labelled from a share of 0.9 per cent of approved GMO material.
In 2015 a faster-growing salmon was approved in the USA as the first genetically modified animal for food.
Genetic engineering in farming and plant breeding is called green genetic engineering.

abschnitte.text: A **genetically modified organism** can be a plant, an animal, a fungus or a bacterium. Swiss law says that a GMO is an organism whose genetic material has been changed in a way that does not occur under natural conditions through crossing or **recombination**. Often a gene from a quite different species is built in, which is called **transgenesis**. If only genes from the same species or a species it can be crossed with are brought in, this is called **cisgenesis**.

In 1994 the **Flavr Savr tomato** came onto the market in the USA as the first genetically modified food; it was meant to stay fresh longer. Today it is above all **soya**, maize, cotton and rape that are grown in genetically modified form, especially in North and South America. Soya has the largest growing area of these. Many of these plants are insensitive to certain weedkillers or themselves make a substance that keeps harmful insects away, like so-called **Bt maize**.

Experts divide genetic engineering up by colours. **Green genetic engineering** concerns farming and plant breeding. **Red genetic engineering** serves medicine; since the 1980s, genetically modified bacteria have been producing human insulin for people with diabetes. White genetic engineering uses modified micro-organisms in industry, for example for enzymes in washing powder.

In Switzerland the **Gene Technology Act** of 2003 governs the handling of GMOs in animals, plants and other organisms. In 2005 the voters accepted a popular initiative that temporarily forbade the growing of genetically modified plants in farming. This **moratorium** has been extended several times since then. Food that contains more than 0.9 per cent of approved genetically modified material has to be labelled.

In 2015 the USA approved a genetically modified **salmon** as the first such animal for human food. It carries a growth gene from another kind of salmon and therefore reaches market size faster. In research, genetically modified mice or fish are used to understand diseases better. Some even glow, because they carry a gene for a fluorescent protein from a jellyfish.

Supporters see GMOs as a way to produce more food with fewer plant protection products or to make plants more resistant to drought. One example is **Golden Rice**, which contains more of the precursors of vitamin A. Critics fear that modified genes could spread out of control or that farmers could become dependent on big seed companies. New methods such as the gene scissors **CRISPR** have given the discussion fresh fuel in recent years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The short form for a genetically modified organism.
The building in of a gene from another species into the genetic material of a living thing.
The building in of genes from the same species or a species it can be crossed with.
A temporary ban or postponement.
A modern method with which genetic material can be changed very precisely, also called gene scissors.

gewusst: Almost all the insulin that people with diabetes inject today is made with genetically modified micro-organisms.
In Switzerland, genetically modified plants are researched in field trials, for example disease-resistant potatoes.
Many enzymes used in cheesemaking or in washing powder also come from genetically modified micro-organisms.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Rohrer was a Swiss physicist who invented the scanning tunnelling microscope together with the German Gerd Binnig. With this instrument, people were able to make individual atoms on a surface visible for the first time. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
wichtigste: Heinrich Rohrer was born in Buchs in the canton of St Gallen in 1933 and died in 2013.
He studied physics at ETH Zurich.
From 1963 he did research at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich.
In 1981 he and Gerd Binnig made the first measurements with the scanning tunnelling microscope.
In 1986 Rohrer and Binnig received one half of the Nobel Prize in Physics; the other half went to Ernst Ruska.
With the scanning tunnelling microscope you can not only see individual atoms but also move them.
His invention is regarded as one of the starting points of nanotechnology.

abschnitte.text: **Heinrich Rohrer** was born on 6 June 1933 in Buchs SG. He studied physics at **ETH Zurich** and wrote his doctoral thesis there. After that he did research in the USA for a few years. In 1963 he started at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich, where he spent most of his working life. He died in 2013 in Wollerau in the canton of Schwyz.

At the end of the 1970s, Rohrer began working on a new microscope together with the young German physicist **Gerd Binnig**. In 1981 the first measurements with the **scanning tunnelling microscope** succeeded. In 1983 they used it to image the famous 7x7 reconstruction of the silicon surface, a pattern of atoms that researchers had long puzzled over. The scientific world was thrilled, because nobody had ever seen anything like it directly.

An extremely fine metal tip is brought to within about a millionth of a millimetre of the sample. Although tip and sample do not touch, a tiny current flows, known as the **tunnelling current**. This current changes very strongly if the distance changes even a tiny bit. The tip is moved line by line over the surface with **piezoelectric actuators**, and a computer puts together a picture of the atoms. For this, the sample must conduct electricity.

In 1986 Rohrer and Binnig received half of the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. The other half went to Ernst Ruska, who had developed the electron microscope back in the 1930s. An invention is rarely honoured with the Nobel Prize so quickly; here only five years passed. Rohrer later worked hard to support research in Switzerland and Europe.

The scanning tunnelling microscope works in a vacuum, in air and even in liquids. Researchers can use it to **move individual atoms deliberately** and so build tiny structures. Other instruments grew out of the idea, such as the **atomic force microscope**, which can also scan samples that do not conduct electricity. Today these microscopes are important tools of nanotechnology, for example in the development of computer chips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle that all substances are made of.
An effect of quantum physics: particles get through a gap that they should not actually be able to cross.
A component that stretches or contracts by a tiny amount when an electrical voltage is applied.
Technology with things that are only a few millionths of a millimetre in size.

gewusst: In 1989 IBM researchers used a scanning tunnelling microscope to write the company's name with just 35 individual atoms.
At best, the tip of the microscope is so fine that only a single atom sits right at the front.
Rohrer did research almost his entire working life in Rüschlikon, just a few kilometres from Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Hermann Rorschach was a Swiss psychiatrist who invented one of the best-known psychological tests in the world. In the Rorschach test, people look at inkblots and say what they see in them. Rorschach lived to be only 37, but his test is still discussed today.
wichtigste: Hermann Rorschach was born in Zurich in 1884 and grew up in Schaffhausen.
At school his nickname was “Klecks”, which means blot.
He studied medicine and became a psychiatrist, a doctor for mental illnesses.
Finally he worked at the Krombach psychiatric clinic in Herisau.
In 1921 he presented his test in the book “Psychodiagnostics”.
The Rorschach test consists of ten cards with inkblot pictures.
Rorschach died in 1922 at the age of 37.

abschnitte.text: **Hermann Rorschach** was born on 8 November 1884 in Zurich. His father was a painter and art teacher, and the family soon moved to **Schaffhausen**. Hermann also loved drawing and was good at it. His classmates called him **“Klecks”**, meaning blot, perhaps because he was so interested in blot pictures.

Rorschach studied medicine, among other places in Zurich, where the famous psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler taught. After that he worked in several psychiatric clinics, for example in Münsterlingen on Lake Constance and in Bern. From 1915 he was a senior doctor at the **Krombach clinic in Herisau** in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. There he developed his famous test further.

For his test, Rorschach folded paper with blots of ink on it, creating **symmetrical** pictures. He chose ten of these pictures: some are black and grey, others have red or many bright colours. The person being tested says what they see in each card, for example a butterfly or two figures. Experts pay attention to what someone sees and which parts of the picture they use for it. A test like this is called a **projective test**.

In 1921 Rorschach published his main work, **“Psychodiagnostics”**. In it he presented his form interpretation test, as he himself called it. At first only a few experts found the book interesting. Just a year later, on 2 April 1922, Rorschach died in Herisau of peritonitis, an inflammation in the abdomen.

After his death the test became known in many countries, especially in the USA. Later, experts developed precise rules for scoring it. Critics, however, doubt the **reliability** and validity of the test, that is, whether it really measures what it is supposed to measure. Today the Rorschach test is very well known above all in popular culture, and many people recognise its inkblot pictures straight away.

begriffe.erklaerung: A doctor who treats people with mental illnesses.
A test in which you interpret something ambiguous and in doing so reveal something about yourself.
When both halves of a picture look like mirror images of each other.
An old game in which you make pictures from inkblots and interpret them.

gewusst: Even before Rorschach there was a popular game called klecksography, in which people looked for figures in inkblots.
The ten original cards are still used today in almost exactly the form in which Rorschach chose them.
Many experts say the inkblots have no single right answer, and that is exactly what the test is about.

teile.einleitung: Golden rice is a genetically modified variety of rice whose grains contain beta-carotene and therefore look golden yellow. It was developed to fight vitamin A deficiency in poor countries. One of its two inventors, Ingo Potrykus, did research at ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: Golden rice makes beta-carotene in the grain, which ordinary rice does not make there.
