The body turns beta-carotene into vitamin A.
Golden rice is meant to fight vitamin A deficiency, which can make children in particular ill and blind.
It was developed by Ingo Potrykus of ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer from Freiburg im Breisgau.
In the first golden rice, one gene for making carotene came from the daffodil.
In “Golden Rice 2”, a gene from maize replaced the daffodil gene, so it contains much more beta-carotene.
In 2016, more than a hundred Nobel Prize winners supported golden rice in an open letter.

abschnitte.text: Rice is the most important staple food for billions of people. Ordinary white rice, however, contains no **beta-carotene**, the yellow-orange pigment that is also found in carrots. The rice plant does make beta-carotene in its green leaves, but not in the grain. In golden rice, extra genes were added so that the grain also produces beta-carotene. That is why the grains are golden yellow.

The body needs **vitamin A** for good eyesight and a strong immune system. People who eat almost nothing but rice often do not get enough of it. Vitamin A deficiency can lead to blindness, especially in children, and makes people more prone to illness. Many millions of children worldwide are affected, especially in Asia and Africa.

Ingo Potrykus of **ETH Zurich** and Peter Beyer of the University of Freiburg im Breisgau worked on the project in the 1990s. In 2000 they presented the first golden rice. One gene came from the **daffodil**, another from a bacterium. Later **Golden Rice 2** was developed, in which a gene from maize replaces the daffodil gene, so that it contains much more beta-carotene.

There have been heated debates about golden rice for years. Supporters say it could protect many children from illness and blindness. Environmental organisations such as Greenpeace criticise it because they reject genetically modified plants on principle and prefer other solutions such as a more varied diet. In 2016 more than a hundred **Nobel Prize winners** published an open letter supporting plant genetic engineering and golden rice.

The inventors gave away the rights in such a way that small farmers in poor countries may use the rice free of charge. In 2021 the **Philippines** became the first country to allow it to be grown for farming. Later a court there temporarily stopped the growing again. So the question of whether and how golden rice should be used has still not been finally settled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A yellow-orange plant pigment from which the body makes vitamin A.
A vital substance for the eyes, the skin and the body's defences.
Methods used to change the genetic material of living things in a targeted way.
A section of genetic information containing building instructions, for example for a pigment.

gewusst: In 2000 Ingo Potrykus appeared on the cover of the American magazine “Time”.
The golden colour of the rice comes from the same substance that makes carrots orange.
The name “golden rice” refers to the colour and not to the price.

teile.einleitung: Grasshoppers and crickets are insects with long, strong hind legs that let them jump a long way. In summer, many of them make the typical meadow music with their chirping. Around 100 species live in Switzerland, from the large great green bush-cricket to the field cricket.
wichtigste: Grasshoppers usually move by jumping.
In everyday language they are also called hoppers.
Many grasshoppers are green or brown and well camouflaged in the grass.
In Switzerland, many grasshoppers live in meadows.
The great green bush-cricket and the field cricket are well-known Swiss species.
Bush-crickets have their ears on their front legs.
Young grasshoppers already look like small adults, just without fully formed wings.

abschnitte.text: Like all insects, grasshoppers have six legs, and the back pair is built into powerful **jumping legs**. Many species are **green or brown** and therefore well camouflaged in the grass. There are two large groups: **long-horned** species such as bush-crickets and crickets with very long antennae, and **short-horned** species such as the true grasshoppers. Worldwide there are more than 25,000 species.

In many species it is mainly the males that make sounds to communicate with others of their kind. Grasshoppers rub a hind leg against their wings to do this, while bush-crickets and crickets rub their wings together. This way of making sounds is called **stridulation**. Bush-crickets have their ears on their **front legs**, whereas grasshoppers have them on the sides of the abdomen. Each species has its own song, by which experts can recognise it.

Many grasshoppers live in **meadows**, at the edges of woods and on dry, sunny slopes. Grasshoppers mainly eat grasses and other plants. The **great green bush-cricket**, on the other hand, also hunts small insects. Grasshoppers themselves are important food for birds, lizards and spiders.

The females usually lay their eggs in the ground or in plants. A **nymph** hatches from the egg; it already looks like a small grasshopper, just without fully formed wings. It moults several times and grows bigger each time until it is an adult. A development like this without a pupa is called **incomplete metamorphosis**. The field cricket spends the winter as a nymph in its burrow and chirps in front of it in early summer.

Around 100 species of grasshopper and cricket live in Switzerland. Well known are the great green bush-cricket in meadows and gardens, the field cricket and the dark bush-cricket. Many species have become rarer because meadows are mown more often and fertilised more heavily. If part of a meadow is left standing, grasshoppers find food and hiding places again. By the way, since 2017 certain crickets and grasshoppers may be sold as food in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with six legs and a body made of three parts.
Making sounds by rubbing body parts against each other.
A young animal that still has to develop into an adult.
Shedding the old skin that has become too small.

gewusst: A grasshopper can jump many times its own body length.
In Africa and Asia, desert locusts sometimes form huge swarms of billions of animals that eat whole fields bare.
You can roughly tell the temperature from the chirping of some crickets, because they chirp faster when it is warm.

teile.einleitung: The moratorium on genetic engineering is a ban in Switzerland on using genetically modified plants and animals in farming. It goes back to a popular initiative that the voters accepted in 2005. The moratorium has been extended several times since then, and the question of new breeding methods is still being discussed.
wichtigste: A moratorium is a ban or a postponement for a limited time.
In 2005 the Swiss voters accepted the initiative “for food from farming free of genetic engineering”.
The share of yes votes was about 56 per cent.
Originally the moratorium applied for five years.
It forbids the growing of genetically modified plants and the keeping of genetically modified animals in farming.
Open-field trials for research purposes are allowed with a permit, for example on the Protected Site of Agroscope in Zurich.
The National Research Programme NRP 59 studied the benefits and risks of genetically modified plants.

abschnitte.text: Genetically modified organisms, or **GMOs** for short, are living things whose genetic material has been deliberately changed in the laboratory. In some countries such as the USA or Brazil, genetically modified maize and soya are widely grown. In Switzerland, farmers may not grow such plants. This ban is called a **moratorium**, because it is limited in time and has to be decided anew again and again.

In November 2005 Switzerland voted on the **initiative for farming free of genetic engineering**. About 56 per cent of those voting said yes, and all the cantons agreed as well. In this way the moratorium was written into the Federal Constitution. At first it applied for five years.

After the five years ran out, Parliament extended the moratorium several times, each time by a few years. Many people in Switzerland want food without genetic engineering. Others think that research shows no particular dangers and that Switzerland is missing out on opportunities. Today there is especially lively discussion about new methods such as the **gene scissors** CRISPR/Cas, with which plants can be changed very precisely.

The moratorium does not forbid research. **Open-field trials** with genetically modified plants are allowed with a permit from the federal authorities. Since 2014 there has been a secured trial site for this at Agroscope in Zurich Reckenholz, the **Protected Site**. There, for example, potatoes have been tested that are meant to resist late blight.

During the moratorium the federal authorities had the benefits and risks of releasing genetically modified plants studied in the National Research Programme **NRP 59**. Trials were carried out with wheat and many studies were evaluated. The researchers found no particular health or environmental risks in the plants they studied. For Swiss farming, however, they saw only a small economic benefit at the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ban or postponement of an activity for a limited time.
A genetically modified organism, that is, a living thing with genetic material changed in the laboratory.
The right of the people to demand a vote on a change to the constitution with enough signatures.
A trial with plants outdoors in a field instead of in the laboratory or greenhouse.

gewusst: The initiative for farming free of genetic engineering was accepted in all the cantons in 2005.
On the Protected Site, fences and monitoring protect the trial fields from destruction.
Animal feed and food with genetically modified ingredients may only be sold in Switzerland with a permit and a label.

teile.einleitung: Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer and one of the most inventive researchers of the 20th century. He was the first to recognise signs of the mysterious dark matter and coined the term supernova. Many of his ideas were only confirmed decades later.
wichtigste: Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer with roots in the canton of Glarus.
He did research for decades at Caltech in California.
In 1933 he coined the term dark matter for invisible mass in space.
He noticed that galaxies in a cluster of galaxies were moving far too fast.
Together with Walter Baade he coined the term supernova.
In 1934 Zwicky and Baade predicted neutron stars.
Zwicky discovered more than a hundred supernovae.

abschnitte.text: Fritz Zwicky was born in 1898 in Varna in Bulgaria, and his father came from **Glarus**. As a child he came to Switzerland and later studied physics at **ETH Zurich**. In 1925 he went to the USA to the California Institute of Technology, **Caltech** for short, in Pasadena. He remained a Swiss citizen all his life and died in Pasadena in 1974.

In 1933 Zwicky studied the **Coma cluster of galaxies**, a huge group of galaxies. He found that the galaxies were moving far too fast. With the visible mass alone, the cluster should have flown apart. From this he concluded that there must be a great deal of invisible mass, and he called it **dark matter**.

Together with the German astronomer Walter Baade, Zwicky coined the term **supernova** for enormous explosions of stars. In 1934 the two predicted that extremely dense remains of stars would be left behind, the **neutron stars**. The first neutron star was not discovered until 1967. Zwicky systematically searched the sky at the Palomar Observatory and found more than a hundred supernovae.

Zwicky developed a way of thinking, the **morphological method**, for systematically finding all the solutions to a problem. He also worked on rocket propulsion and predicted that galaxies can act like huge lenses and bend the light of objects behind them. Today this is called gravitational lensing. He was regarded as a difficult man who often quarrelled with colleagues.

For a long time many astronomers did not take Zwicky's ideas seriously. Today **dark matter** is one of the greatest puzzles in physics, and researchers all over the world are looking for it. An asteroid and a crater on the Moon are named after Zwicky. He is buried in Mollis in the canton of Glarus, where a foundation also keeps his memory alive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible mass in space that can only be detected by its gravity.
The enormous explosion of a star.
An extremely dense remnant of a star after a supernova.
A huge group of galaxies held together by gravity.

gewusst: A teaspoon of material from a neutron star would weigh many millions of tonnes on Earth.
Zwicky was known for his stubbornness and often argued fiercely with other astronomers.
According to current knowledge there is about five times more dark matter in space than ordinary matter.

teile.einleitung: Genetic drift is a process of evolution in which the frequency of gene variants in a population changes purely by chance. Some variants become more common, others disappear altogether, without being better or worse. This chance effect is especially strong in small populations.
wichtigste: Genetic drift means random changes in allele frequencies in a population.
In small populations, genetic drift acts especially strongly.
The founder effect arises when a few individuals found a new population.
Because of heavy hunting in the 19th century, the northern elephant seal now has very little genetic variety.
In 1968 Motoo Kimura put forward the neutral theory of molecular evolution.
The effective population size describes the size of an ideal population with equally strong drift.
Cheetahs often accept skin grafts from unrelated members of their own species, because their genetic variety is so small.

abschnitte.text: Genes often come in different versions, the **alleles**. How common an allele is in a population is called the **allele frequency**. In genetic drift these frequencies change not because one version is more useful but simply by **chance**. That distinguishes genetic drift from natural selection, in which better adapted versions are favoured.

Imagine a jar with 50 red and 50 blue marbles. You pull out ten marbles blind and use them to fill a new jar with the same proportions. By chance you may have pulled out seven red and only three blue, so that red is now much more common. If you repeat this over many **generations**, one colour eventually disappears completely and the other is **fixed**.

If a population shrinks sharply, it is called a **bottleneck effect**. In the 19th century the northern elephant seal was hunted for its oil down to just a few dozen animals. Today there are very many again, but their genetic variety is very small. In the **founder effect**, only a few animals settle a new area, such as an island, and their gene pool differs by chance from that of the original population.

The **cheetahs** too probably went through a severe bottleneck about 10,000 years ago. They are so similar genetically that they often accept skin grafts from unrelated members of their own species. In Switzerland the **Alpine ibex** was wiped out in the 19th century. All the Swiss ibex of today descend from a few animals from the Gran Paradiso area in Italy and therefore have rather little genetic variety.

A new allele that neither helps nor harms rarely becomes established. In a population of 50 individuals, each with two copies of every gene, there are 100 gene copies. The chance that a single new allele finally becomes established throughout is therefore only 1 in 100, that is **1 per cent**. Because in nature not all animals have the same number of offspring, experts work with the **effective population size**, which is often much smaller than the actual number.

In 1968 the Japanese researcher **Motoo Kimura** put forward the neutral theory of molecular evolution. It says that many changes in genetic material become established not through selection but through genetic drift. Genetic drift is important for **species protection**: small populations quickly lose genetic variety and are then less able to adapt to new diseases or changes in climate. That is why people try to connect isolated remaining groups of rare animals with one another.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share that a particular gene variant has of all the variants of that gene in a population.
A group of living things of the same species that live in the same area.
The loss of genetic variety when a population shrinks sharply.
A random difference in genetic material when a few animals found a new population.
The state in which only a single version of a gene is left in the population.

gewusst: The northern elephant seal is one of the animal species with the least genetic variety of all.
Genetic drift acts in every population but is hardly noticeable in large populations.
The English term is “genetic drift”, like a boat drifting without a rudder.

teile.einleitung: Graphene is a material made of just a single layer of carbon atoms. This makes it as thin as anything can possibly be, and yet it is extremely tear-resistant. Because it conducts electricity and heat very well, it is seen as a wonder material of the future.
wichtigste: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
Graphite, the material in pencil leads, consists of many stacked layers of graphene.
Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated graphene with sticky tape in 2004.
For their experiments they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.
A single layer of graphene absorbs only around 2 per cent of visible light.
If you imagine rolling a layer of graphene into a cylinder, you get a carbon nanotube.
Large sheets of graphene are made by chemical vapour deposition on copper foil.

abschnitte.text: In graphene, every **carbon atom** is joined to three neighbours. This creates a pattern of hexagons that looks like a honeycomb or a chain-link fence. The atoms have what is called **sp2 hybridisation**, which means their bonds lie flat in one plane. One layer is only about a third of a billionth of a metre thick.

The **graphite** in a pencil lead consists of countless layers of graphene lying loosely on top of each other. When you write, layers slide off and stay on the paper. So a pencil line can contain tiny pieces made of only a few layers. For a long time, however, experts believed that a single layer on its own could not be stable at all.

In 2004 Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester showed the opposite. Using **sticky tape**, they peeled layers off a piece of graphite again and again until only a single one was left. This simple method is also called the Scotch tape method. In 2010 the two received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for it.

Relative to its thickness, graphene is much more tear-resistant than steel. It conducts electricity and heat excellently and is almost **transparent**. At the same time it is flexible and lets practically no gases through. It has one weakness: pure graphene lacks a **band gap**, so electric current in it cannot simply be switched on and off as in a computer chip.

For large areas, **chemical vapour deposition** is used, in which carbon from a gas settles on hot copper foil. Researchers are testing graphene for flexible screens, sensitive sensors, better batteries and light, strong composite materials. It is already found today in some sports equipment and coatings. Many applications, however, are still being developed.

Carbon can form many shapes, for example diamond, graphite and graphene. If you imagine rolling graphene into a little tube, you get a **carbon nanotube**. If you fold it into a ball, it resembles the fullerenes, which look like a football. All these substances are made only of carbon, and yet they are completely different.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element that diamond, graphite and coal are also made of.
A soft, grey material made of many layers of graphene, for example in pencils.
A property of a material that determines whether the flow of current in it can be controlled well.
A tiny tube made of carbon, much thinner than a hair.

gewusst: Before the Nobel Prize, Andre Geim had already received an Ig Nobel Prize for making a frog levitate with magnets.
A layer of graphene is about a hundred thousand times thinner than a human hair.
Despite its thinness, a single layer of graphene can be seen with the naked eye on a suitable background, because it absorbs some light.

teile.einleitung: Peer pressure, or group pressure, is the pressure a group puts on an individual to make them fit in. You feel it in your school class, in a sports club or among friends. Psychologists have long studied why we sometimes do or say something just because the others do it too.
wichtigste: When someone adapts their opinion or behaviour to a group, this is called conformity.
Group pressure among people of the same age is called peer pressure.
In 1951 Solomon Asch published a famous experiment in which the lengths of lines were compared.
In around a third of the critical rounds, the test subjects went along with the wrong group opinion.
If one other person also gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply.
Groupthink is the name for bad decisions by a group that is mainly seeking agreement.
In the bystander effect, people help less often when many others are watching.

abschnitte.text: Humans are **social beings** and want to belong to a group. That is why we often adapt without noticing, for example in clothing, language or taste in music. When a group expects you to join in and you feel pushed into it, this is called **group pressure**. Among people of the same age it is known as **peer pressure**. Group pressure can be loud and open, for example through laughing at someone, or very quiet, just through looks.

The American psychologist **Solomon Asch** published a famous experiment in 1951. The test subjects had to say which of three lines was the same length as a comparison line, which was actually very easy. However, the other people in the room were in on it and deliberately all gave the same wrong answer. In around a third of these critical rounds, the real test subject joined the wrong majority. On their own, without a group, almost nobody made a mistake.

Asch changed his experiment in various ways. If just one other person said the right answer, going along with the majority dropped sharply. So even one **ally** makes it much easier to stand by your own opinion. The size of the group also played a part, although the pressure hardly increased beyond three to four people. Going along with the group, known as **conformity**, was also lower when the answers could be written down secretly.

Whole groups can also make bad decisions because they want to agree. In 1972 the psychologist Irving Janis called this **groupthink**: critical voices stay silent, and nobody checks the plans carefully. Another well-known phenomenon is the **bystander effect**. In an emergency, people help less often when many others are watching, because everyone thinks someone else will help. If you know this, you can act deliberately, for example by asking one particular person directly for help.

Group pressure is not always bad; it can also lead people to play fair or follow rules. It becomes difficult when you are supposed to do something that you yourself think is wrong or that is dangerous. Then it helps to pause for a moment and ask yourself what you really want. A clear, calm **no** is allowed, and real friends accept it. Often you can also find someone in the group who thinks the same, and together it is easier to stand firm.

begriffe.erklaerung: Adapting your own opinion or behaviour to a group.
Group pressure among people of the same age.
When a group makes bad decisions because it is so focused on agreeing.
People help less often in an emergency when many others are present.

gewusst: In the Asch experiment, around a quarter of the test subjects stuck to their own, correct answer in all the critical rounds.
Even yawning is contagious, a sign of how strongly we unconsciously adapt to others.

teile.einleitung: Gene therapy is a treatment method in which genetic material is brought into cells in order to cure or ease a disease. So it tackles the cause of hereditary diseases directly instead of only treating the complaints. For some years there have been the first approved gene therapies, including ones from Swiss companies.
wichtigste: In gene therapy, genetic material is brought into cells in order to treat a disease.
Viruses made harmless often serve as “gene ferries”.
In ex vivo gene therapy, cells are taken out, changed in the laboratory and given back.
The first recognised gene therapy took place in the USA in 1990 in a case of a severe inborn immune defect.
Zolgensma from Novartis works against the hereditary disease spinal muscular atrophy.
Kymriah from Novartis was approved in the USA in 2017 as the first CAR T cell therapy.
In 2023 Casgevy became the first approved therapy that is based on CRISPR.

abschnitte.text: Many diseases arise because a **gene** is faulty and the body therefore cannot make an important protein properly. In **gene therapy**, a working copy of the gene is brought into the cells, or the faulty gene is repaired. The cells can then make the missing protein themselves again. In the best case a single treatment is enough for many years.

To bring a gene into a cell you need a means of transport, a so-called **gene ferry** or vector. Often **viruses** are used for this, because by their nature they can smuggle genetic material into cells. Beforehand they are changed so that they can no longer cause a disease. Adeno-associated viruses or lentiviruses are often used.

In **ex vivo gene therapy**, cells are taken out of the body, for example blood stem cells. They are genetically changed in the laboratory and then given back. In **in vivo gene therapy**, the gene ferry is injected directly into the body, for instance into the bloodstream. Which way is better depends on the disease.

In 1990 the first recognised gene therapy was carried out in the USA on a girl with a severe inborn **immune defect** caused by a lack of ADA. In the following years there were setbacks as well. In early studies with retroviruses, the virus became built in next to a cancer gene in some children and caused **leukaemia**. After that the gene ferries were made considerably safer.

The Basel company **Novartis** is one of the pioneers of gene therapy. Its therapy **Zolgensma** works against spinal muscular atrophy, a hereditary disease in which the muscles of babies grow ever weaker. It is given only once and is one of the most expensive medicines in the world. With **Kymriah**, the first CAR T cell therapy was approved in the USA in 2017, in which the defence cells of patients are changed so that they attack blood cancer cells.

The gene scissors **CRISPR** were developed by Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 2020. With them, genes can be changed very precisely. In 2023 **Casgevy** became the first approved therapy that is based on CRISPR. It is used against the hereditary blood diseases sickle cell anaemia and beta thalassaemia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A means of transport that brings a gene into a cell, often a virus made harmless.
Latin for “outside the living”, that is, in the laboratory outside the body.
Latin for “in the living”, that is, directly in the body.
A disease that arises through a change in the genetic material and can be passed on.
Defence cells changed in the laboratory that recognise and attack cancer cells in a targeted way.

gewusst: At its approval in the USA, Zolgensma cost about 2 million dollars for a single treatment.
The viruses that serve as gene ferries are changed so that they can no longer multiply in the body.
Hundreds of gene therapies are being tested in studies worldwide today, among other things against hereditary blindness.

teile.einleitung: A hot-air balloon is an aircraft that flies because the hot air inside its envelope is lighter than the cooler air outside. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers in France sent the first people up in one. Today hot-air balloons float over the countryside mainly on excursions and at festivals.
wichtigste: A hot-air balloon rises because warm air is lighter than cold air.
The Montgolfier brothers built the first hot-air balloon in which people flew.
In 1783 people flew in a hot-air balloon for the first time.
Before that, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel flew along as the first passengers.
Today the air in the balloon is heated with a gas burner.
The passengers stand in a basket under the envelope.
The wind decides the direction of flight, which is why balloons like to go up early in the morning.

abschnitte.text: Hot air expands and is therefore lighter than cold air. If you fill a large envelope with hot air, it creates **lift**, which carries the balloon upwards. A **gas burner** above the basket heats the air with a large flame, usually using propane gas. If the pilot wants to rise, he heats more. If he wants to sink, he lets the air cool down or opens a flap at the top.

A hot-air balloon consists of the **envelope**, the burner and the **basket**. The envelope is made of light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon and can be as tall as a house of several storeys. The basket is usually made of woven willow, because this is light and flexible and cushions bumps on landing. The passengers and the gas cylinders stand in it.

You cannot steer a hot-air balloon like an aeroplane. The **wind** decides the direction. The pilot can only change the height and so look for layers of air in which the wind blows in a different direction. That is why, in German, balloonists prefer to say that they “drive” rather than “fly”. Early in the morning the air is usually calm and steady, so many trips start then.

The French brothers **Joseph-Michel and Étienne Montgolfier** were paper manufacturers. In September 1783 at Versailles, in front of the king, they sent up a balloon carrying a sheep, a duck and a cockerel; all the animals landed safely. On 21 November 1783 in Paris, people went up for the first time: Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes. After their inventors, hot-air balloons are also called **montgolfières**.

In Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud, a well-known international balloon festival takes place every January. From there, in 1999, Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones set off in the balloon **Breitling Orbiter 3** and became the first to fly non-stop around the Earth in a balloon. That balloon, however, was a combination of a gas balloon and a hot-air balloon. On calm days you can also often see colourful balloons over the Swiss Plateau.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes a body upwards in air or water.
The balloon's large fabric bag, which is filled with hot air.
Another name for a hot-air balloon, after the Montgolfier brothers.
A device that heats the air in the balloon with a gas flame.

gewusst: At the first demonstration in June 1783, the Montgolfiers' unmanned balloon rose above the little town of Annonay.
At first the Montgolfiers believed that a special kind of smoke, not the warm air, carried their balloon.
After their first trip, balloonists often celebrate with a “balloon christening”.

teile.einleitung: The major histocompatibility complex, MHC for short, is a group of genes that are very important for the immune system. They build recognition molecules with which body cells show what is going on inside them. In humans this system is called the HLA system, and it plays a big part in organ transplants.
wichtigste: In humans, the major histocompatibility complex is called the HLA system.
In humans the HLA genes lie on chromosome 6.
MHC class I molecules are found on almost all body cells that have a nucleus.
MHC class II molecules are carried by antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells.
After a transplant, foreign HLA molecules trigger a rejection reaction.
In 1996 the Swiss Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty received the Nobel Prize for discovering MHC restriction.
The MHC is one of the most genetically varied regions in humans.

abschnitte.text: The **major histocompatibility complex** is a section of the genetic material with many genes for the immune system. The long word means roughly “most important group for tissue compatibility”. It is abbreviated **MHC**, after its English name. In humans it is called the **HLA system**, where HLA stands for “human leukocyte antigens”. The HLA genes lie on chromosome 6.

The MHC molecules sit on the surface of cells and work like little shop windows. In them the cells display short pieces of protein called **antigens**. **Class I molecules** are found on almost all body cells with a nucleus and show fragments from inside the cell. If a cell is infected by a virus, it shows pieces of the virus, and defence cells can recognise and destroy it. **Class II molecules** are carried mainly by antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, which have taken up pathogens.

The MHC was first discovered in mice, when researchers were investigating why transplanted tissue is rejected. In the 1950s the Frenchman Jean Dausset found the first HLA features in humans. In 1980 Baruj Benacerraf, Jean Dausset and George Snell received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine for this. The Swiss immunologist **Rolf Zinkernagel** from Riehen near Basel showed, together with Peter Doherty, that defence cells only recognise viruses together with the body's own MHC. For this so-called MHC restriction, the two received the Nobel Prize in 1996.

If a person receives an organ from someone else, their immune system recognises the foreign HLA molecules as foreign. It attacks the organ, which is called a **rejection reaction**. That is why the HLA features of donor and recipient are tested before a transplant; this is called **HLA typing**. A good match is especially important for blood stem cells, for example in leukaemia. Worldwide there are registers with millions of voluntary stem cell donors, including in Switzerland.

Many HLA genes exist in thousands of different versions. That is why the MHC is one of the most genetically **varied** regions in humans. This variety is an advantage for the population as a whole, because it means as many different pathogens as possible can be recognised. So hardly any new virus can hit all people equally hard. Certain HLA versions are also linked to a higher risk of some diseases, for example HLA-B27 with the joint disease ankylosing spondylitis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body's defence system against pathogens.
A substance or piece of protein that is recognised by the immune system.
The transfer of an organ or tissue from one person to another.
A defence cell that recognises infected cells by their MHC molecules.

gewusst: Because there are so many HLA versions, two unrelated people only rarely have exactly the same HLA features.
Rolf Zinkernagel made his Nobel Prize discovery in the 1970s in Australia, where he did research on mice with Peter Doherty.

teile.einleitung: The incandescent lamp, often called a light bulb, makes light with a glowing wire. From 1879 Thomas Edison made it practical for everyday use, and it fundamentally changed people's lives. Today it is being replaced almost everywhere by more economical LED lamps.
wichtigste: In an incandescent lamp, electric current makes a thin wire glow.
From 1879 Thomas Edison made the light bulb practical for everyday use.
Other inventors such as Joseph Swan also worked on the incandescent lamp.
Modern incandescent bulbs have a wire made of tungsten.
Only a small part of the energy becomes light; the rest becomes heat.
Because of their high electricity consumption, incandescent bulbs were gradually banned in Europe and Switzerland from 2009.
Today it is mostly LED lamps that shine, and they use much less electricity.

abschnitte.text: Inside a glass bulb is a very thin wire, the **filament**. When current flows through it, it becomes more than 2000 degrees hot and glows brightly. So that it does not burn up, there is no normal air inside the bulb. It is either a vacuum or filled with a gas such as **argon**, which contains no oxygen.

Even before 1879, several researchers built glowing wires. In England, **Joseph Swan** presented an incandescent lamp. In the USA, **Thomas Edison** developed a lamp in 1879 with a filament made of carbonised material that burned for a long time. Edison also built electricity networks and power stations so that lamps could shine in many homes.

The first filaments were made of carbon and broke quickly. At the beginning of the 20th century, **tungsten** became the standard. This metal has the highest melting point of all metals, about 3422 degrees. That is why the wire can withstand the great heat well.

An incandescent bulb is really more of a heater than a lamp. Only about 5 per cent of the energy becomes visible light. Most of the rest is lost as **heat**, which is why a light bulb gets very hot. An **LED lamp** gives the same amount of light using only a small part of the electricity.

From 2009 Switzerland gradually banned inefficient incandescent bulbs, much like the European Union. The most powerful bulbs were affected first, later the weaker ones too. Today classic light bulbs are found almost only as special-purpose lamps. Energy-saving lamps and above all **LEDs** have replaced them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin wire in an incandescent bulb that is made to glow by electric current.
A metal that only melts at a very high temperature.
Light-emitting diode, a small electronic component that shines brightly using little electricity.
The fitting into which you screw a bulb so that it gets electricity.

gewusst: In a fire station in Livermore, California, a light bulb has been burning almost without a break since 1901.
The screw thread of most bulbs is called E27; the E stands for Edison.
Edison and his team tested thousands of materials, including bamboo, before they found a good filament.

teile.einleitung: The sense of balance makes sure that we can stand, walk and find our way without falling over. Its most important organ sits well hidden in the inner ear. Together with the eyes and the sensors in muscles and joints, it tells the brain how our body lies in space.
wichtigste: The organ of balance sits in the inner ear.
In each ear there are three semicircular canals.
After turning round quickly you feel dizzy, because the fluid in the inner ear keeps moving.
The eyes help with balance too, which is why standing on one leg with closed eyes is harder.
Reading in a moving car can lead to travel sickness.
Balancing on a slackline trains your sense of balance.
When cats fall they mostly turn so that they land on their paws.

abschnitte.titel: The organ in the inner ear
abschnitte.text: The **organ of balance** lies deep in the skull bone in the **inner ear**, right next to the cochlea. It consists of three **semicircular canals** and two small sacs. All of them are filled with fluid and lined with fine sense cells that carry little hairs. The whole organ is only about the size of a pea.

The three semicircular canals stand roughly at right angles to each other, like the corner of a box. In this way they pick up **turning movements** in all directions, such as nodding, shaking the head or tilting it. When the head turns, the fluid lags behind briefly and bends the sensory hairs. In the sacs lie tiny crystals, the **ear stones**, which press on the hairs through gravity and so show where up and down are.

The brain does not rely on the inner ear alone. The **eyes** also report whether we are standing still or moving. Sensors in muscles, tendons and joints tell us how our arms and legs are lying, and this sense is called **proprioception**. That is why it is much harder to stand on one leg with your eyes closed.

Anyone who turns in circles quickly for a long time and then stands still becomes **dizzy**. The fluid in the semicircular canals goes on moving for a while, and the brain thinks you are still turning. When reading in a moving car, the eyes report standing still but the inner ear reports movement. These contradictory reports can lead to nausea, that is, to **travel sickness**.

Balance can be trained well, for example by balancing on a **slackline**, by cycling, skiing or doing gymnastics. Children practise it quite naturally when climbing and romping about. Animals have a sense of balance too. When a **cat** falls, it turns with a lightning-fast movement so that it mostly lands on its paws.

begriffe.erklaerung: The innermost part of the ear, with the cochlea and the organ of balance.
Three curved little tubes filled with fluid that measure turning movements.
Tiny crystals in the inner ear that make gravity noticeable.
The sense with which we feel the position of our body parts, even with closed eyes.
The feeling that everything is turning or swaying.

gewusst: Astronauts often feel sick in weightlessness, because the ear stones no longer pull downwards.
Figure skaters and ballet dancers train themselves to feel less dizzy after turns.
You can also become seasick on land by looking at a swaying screen.

teile.einleitung: GLAMOS is the Swiss glacier measuring network and stands for Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. With it, experts observe every year how the glaciers of Switzerland are changing. The measurements show clearly how strongly the glaciers are shrinking because of climate change.
wichtigste: GLAMOS stands for Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
ETH Zurich leads GLAMOS together with universities such as Fribourg and Zurich.
The changes in length of Swiss glaciers have been measured regularly since about 1880.
The mass balance shows whether a glacier has gained or lost ice in a year.
With long poles in the ice, experts measure how much ice melts away in the summer.
In spring they dig snow pits in order to measure the depth and the density of the snow.
Aerial photographs and elevation models help to record whole glaciers.

abschnitte.text: **GLAMOS** is the short form for Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. It is the official measuring network that keeps watch on the Swiss glaciers over the long term. It is led by **ETH Zurich** together with the universities of Fribourg and Zurich. It is financed among others by the Federal Office for the Environment, by MeteoSwiss and by the Swiss Academy of Sciences.

Since about 1880 the **change in length** has been measured regularly on many Swiss glaciers. In this, people determine how far the **glacier tongue**, that is, the lower end of the glacier, has moved forwards or backwards. Today measurements are made on about a hundred glaciers. Almost all of them have been retreating year after year for decades, some by dozens of metres.

The **mass balance** states whether a glacier has gained or lost ice in a year. In winter mass is added through snowfall, in summer mass is lost through melting. If the loss is greater than the gain, the balance is negative and the glacier becomes smaller. The measurement series on the Claridenfirn and the Silvretta glacier are among the longest in the world and reach back to the 1910s.

In spring, experts dig **snow pits** into the glacier and measure the depth and the density of the snow. From this they work out how much water is held in the winter snow. They also drill long poles, so-called **ablation stakes**, into the ice. In autumn they can see on the pole how many metres of ice have melted away during the summer.

Because not every glacier can be surveyed on foot, GLAMOS also uses **aerial photographs** and digital **elevation models**. If you compare elevation models from different years, you see how much the ice surface has sunk. Radar measurements also help to determine the thickness of the ice. In this way it is possible to estimate how much ice is still held in all the Swiss glaciers together.

The data from GLAMOS show that the Swiss glaciers have been shrinking strongly for decades. The hot summers of 2022 and 2023 in particular brought record losses; in these two years the glaciers together lost about a tenth of their volume. Smaller glaciers have already disappeared completely. The measurements are important for **climate protection**, the water supply and safety in the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A comparison between the ice that a glacier gains and loses in a year.
The lower end of a glacier.
A pole in the ice on which you can read off how much ice has melted.
A digital map that gives the height of the surface for every point.

gewusst: For their measurements the researchers often climb onto glaciers at over 3000 metres in all weathers.
Switzerland has about 1400 glaciers, many of them very small.
GLAMOS data flow into worldwide glacier statistics that are collected in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: A generic medicine is a medicine that contains the same active ingredient as a well-known original product and works in the same way. It may only be sold once the patent protection of the original has expired. Because generics are usually cheaper, they help to save health costs.
wichtigste: A generic medicine contains the same active ingredient in the same amount as the original product.
Generics may only come onto the market after the patent protection has expired.
For approval, the maker has above all to prove bioequivalence with the original.
The additional ingredients, colour, shape and name of the tablet may differ from the original.
Generics are cheaper because the expensive research on the active ingredient is not needed.
Copies of medicines made by biotechnology are called biosimilars.
In Switzerland, since 2024 you usually pay 40 per cent of the cost yourself if you choose the more expensive original without a medical reason.

abschnitte.text: When a company invents a new active ingredient, it can protect it with a **patent**. A patent usually lasts up to 20 years from the application. During that time only this company may make and sell the medicine. After that, other companies may make copies, which are called **generics**.

A generic medicine must work in the body in the same way as the original. This is checked with studies on **bioequivalence**: the active ingredient must reach the blood equally fast and in the same amount. There are differences in the **additional ingredients**, that is, substances such as fillers or colourings. That is why a tablet can have a different colour or shape although it works in the same way.

Developing a new medicine often takes many years and costs a great deal of money. A maker of generics does not have to research the active ingredient afresh and does not have to carry out large clinical studies on how well it works. That is why it can offer the medicine more cheaply. For health insurers and the insured, that means lower costs.

In Switzerland the authority **Swissmedic** checks whether a medicine is approved. Pharmacists may replace an original with a cheaper generic, unless the doctor expressly asks for the original. Anyone who chooses the more expensive original without a medical reason has, since 2024, usually paid 40 per cent of the cost themselves instead of the usual 10 per cent. This is meant to bring health costs down.

Some modern medicines are made with the help of living cells, for example insulin or antibodies. Such active ingredients are very large and complicated. A copy can never be made exactly the same, only very similar. That is why these copies are called **biosimilars** and are checked especially thoroughly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient as the original.
The first medicine with a new active ingredient, developed by the company that invented it.
A protection right giving sole ownership of an invention for a certain time.
Proof that an active ingredient reaches the blood as fast and as strongly as in the original.
A copy of a medicine made by biotechnology.

gewusst: Generics often carry the name of the active ingredient, for example ibuprofen or paracetamol, plus the name of the company that makes them.
Some of the world's large makers of generics have sites in Switzerland, such as Sandoz with its headquarters in Basel.
A medicine with the same active ingredient can be sold under quite different names depending on the country.

teile.einleitung: A fairy ring is a circle of mushrooms growing in a meadow or on a lawn. In German it is called a “witches' ring”, because people used to think witches had danced there at night. In reality, an invisible network of fungus in the soil is behind it, spreading outwards year after year.
wichtigste: A fairy ring consists of mushrooms growing in a circle or an arc.
The fungal network in the soil grows evenly outwards from the centre.
That is why a fairy ring gets bigger from year to year.
The grass along the ring is often darker green than next to it.
Large fairy rings can be several hundred years old.
The fairy ring champignon often forms fairy rings on lawns.
People used to believe that witches or elves had danced there.

abschnitte.text: A **fairy ring** is a circle of mushrooms that all spring up from the ground at the same time. Sometimes it is a complete circle, sometimes only an arc. The rings can be small or have a diameter of many metres. They are especially easy to find on **meadows and lawns**, but also in woods.

The actual fungus lives invisibly in the soil as a fine network of threads called **mycelium**. What we see as a mushroom is only its **fruiting body**. The mycelium grows evenly outwards in all directions from one spot. In the centre the nutrients are soon used up and the network dies there. At the outer edge it keeps growing, and that is where the mushrooms appear, which is why a ring forms.

At a fairy ring the grass often looks **darker green** than next to it. This is because the fungus breaks down dead plant material in the soil and releases nitrogen, which acts like fertiliser. Sometimes, though, there is also a strip of withered or brown grass. There the dense mycelium has grown through the soil so thickly that hardly any water reaches the roots. So you can sometimes recognise a fairy ring even without mushrooms.

In the past people could not explain the circles. In many regions it was believed that **witches** had danced there at night, which is where the German name comes from. In England people told stories of elves, and the rings are still called “fairy rings” there today. Some people believed it brought bad luck to step into such a ring.

A well-known ring-former is the **fairy ring champignon**, a small, light brown edible mushroom that often grows on lawns. The trooping funnel and various field mushrooms also form fairy rings. Because a ring grows a little further every year, you can roughly estimate its age from its size. Large fairy rings can be **several hundred years** old. Important: you should only eat mushrooms if an expert has identified them reliably, for example at a mushroom inspection.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fine, underground network of threads of a fungus.
The visible part of a fungus with its stem and cap.
A nutrient that plants need in order to grow.
A place where experts check collected mushrooms free of charge.

gewusst: A fairy ring is actually a single fungus, because all the mushrooms in the circle belong to the same network.
In Switzerland, many municipalities have official mushroom inspection points where you can have collected mushrooms checked.
Some fairy rings are so large that they can only be seen completely from the air.

teile.einleitung: Horizon Europe is the European Union's large research programme for the years 2021 to 2027. With around 95 billion euros, it funds research and innovation, from basic research to new products. Switzerland takes part too, but its participation has had an eventful history.
wichtigste: Horizon Europe is the EU's research and innovation programme from 2021 to 2027.
Its budget is around 95 billion euros.
The programme is divided into three pillars.
The European Research Council (ERC) awards sought-after grants to individual researchers.
The European Innovation Council (EIC) supports start-ups and SMEs with groundbreaking ideas.
In Switzerland, the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI) is responsible.
Under the agreement signed in 2025, Switzerland is associated retroactively from 1 January 2025.

abschnitte.text: Horizon Europe is the EU's ninth **framework programme** for research and innovation. It followed the Horizon 2020 programme and runs from 2021 to 2027. With around 95 billion euros, it is one of the largest research programmes in the world. Universities, research institutes and companies from many countries can apply for money.

The first pillar is called **Excellent Science** and funds basic research, for example through the European Research Council. The second pillar supports research on global challenges such as health, climate, energy and digitalisation, often in large joint projects. The third pillar, **Innovative Europe**, is meant to bring new ideas to market faster. In addition there is a cross-cutting part intended to strengthen participation across Europe.

The **European Research Council** (ERC) awards prestigious grants to individual researchers, based only on the quality of their idea. The **European Innovation Council** (EIC) helps start-ups and SMEs with money and advice. The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions fund the training and mobility of researchers, for example in doctoral networks. They are named after the famous physicist and chemist Marie Curie.

New in Horizon Europe are five **missions**, programmes with clear goals up to about 2030. They deal with cancer, adapting to climate change, healthy oceans and waters, climate-neutral cities and healthy soils. Research, politics and the public are meant to work together on them. In this way, research is meant to contribute directly to solving big problems.

Switzerland was closely involved in earlier EU research programmes. After the Federal Council broke off negotiations on a framework agreement with the EU in 2021, it was treated in Horizon Europe only as a **non-associated third country**. During this time the Swiss government funded Swiss researchers itself. With an agreement signed in 2025, Switzerland became **associated** again, retroactively from 1 January 2025.

In Switzerland, **SERI** in Bern is responsible for participation in Horizon Europe. The **Euresearch** network advises researchers and companies on how to write an application. Competition for the funding is fierce, and only some of the applications are approved. Swiss universities such as ETH Zurich and EPFL have traditionally been among the most successful participants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A funding programme lasting several years with a fixed budget and rules.
A treaty with which a non-EU country takes part in a programme almost like an EU country.
Funding money for a particular research project.
Small and medium-sized enterprises, that is, companies with few employees.

gewusst: A single ERC grant can bring a researcher several million euros for her project.
Countries outside Europe, such as New Zealand or Canada, have also become associated with Horizon Europe.
The missions were inspired by the Moon landing programmes, in which one clear goal brought many forces together.

teile.einleitung: IBM Research Zurich is a famous research laboratory of the computer company IBM in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. Inventions were made here that make it possible to see individual atoms. In the 1980s, two Nobel Prizes in Physics went to researchers from this laboratory.
wichtigste: IBM founded its research laboratory in the Zurich area in 1956.
Today the laboratory is in the municipality of Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich.
Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer invented the scanning tunnelling microscope here and received the Nobel Prize in 1986.
Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for high-temperature superconductivity in ceramics.
In 1986 Gerd Binnig developed the atomic force microscope with Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber.
In 2009 a picture of the chemical structure of a single molecule was achieved here for the first time.
The Token Ring networking method was also developed largely in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: **IBM** is a large American company for computers and information technology. In 1956 it founded its first research laboratory outside the USA in the Zurich area. Later the laboratory moved to **Rüschlikon** on Lake Zurich. Researchers from many countries work here on physics, computer science and materials science.

In the early 1980s, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer developed the **scanning tunnelling microscope**. An extremely fine metal tip moves very close over a surface. Between the tip and the surface flows a tiny **tunnelling current**, which changes strongly with the distance. This creates a picture in which individual atoms can be seen, and for this the two received the Nobel Prize in 1986.

Only a year later came the next Nobel Prize. In 1986 Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller discovered that certain **ceramics** conduct electricity without any resistance at comparatively high temperatures. This phenomenon is called **superconductivity**. Their discovery set off a wave of new research worldwide.

In 1986 Gerd Binnig, together with Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber, developed the **atomic force microscope**. It scans surfaces with a fine tip and also works on materials that do not conduct electricity. In 2009 researchers in Rüschlikon used it to obtain the first picture showing the chemical structure of a single **molecule**. You could see the rings of carbon atoms in it.

Research on computer networks was also done in the laboratory. The **Token Ring** method, in which a data packet is passed from computer to computer like a relay baton, was developed largely here. Today the researchers work on quantum computers, artificial intelligence and data security, among other things. Many ideas find their way into IBM products.

In 2011 IBM and **ETH Zurich** jointly opened the Binnig and Rohrer Nanotechnology Center in Rüschlikon. It is a clean room centre in which tiny structures are built and studied. It has rooms that are especially well shielded against vibrations and interference. It is named after the laboratory's two Nobel Prize winners.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument that scans surfaces so precisely that you can see individual atoms.
A tiny current that can flow across an extremely small gap.
The property of some substances of conducting electricity with no resistance at all at low temperatures.
Technology with structures that are only millionths of a millimetre in size.

gewusst: In 1989, IBM researchers in the USA wrote the three letters IBM with 35 individual atoms, using a technique based on the invention from Rüschlikon.
IBM Research Zurich won two Nobel Prizes in Physics in two consecutive years.
The scanning tunnelling microscope can not only show atoms but also move them.

teile.einleitung: The Hippocratic Oath is a promise made by doctors that is more than 2000 years old. It is named after the Greek doctor Hippocrates and describes how a good doctor should behave. Many of its ideas, such as medical confidentiality, still apply in medicine today.
wichtigste: The Hippocratic Oath is linked to the profession of doctors.
It is named after Hippocrates, who lived around 400 BC.
Hippocrates was born on the Greek island of Kos and is regarded as the father of medicine.
In the original oath, the doctor first swears by the god Apollo.
The oath already contains the duty of confidentiality about everything you learn from the sick.
The Declaration of Geneva of the World Medical Association continues the oath in modern form.

abschnitte.text: **Hippocrates** lived from about 460 to 370 BC and came from the island of **Kos** in the Aegean. He founded a famous school of medicine there. What was new was that he looked for natural causes of illness instead of seeing it as a punishment from the gods. That is why he is often called the father of medicine.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the oath come from?
abschnitte.text: The oath belongs to a large collection of medical writings, the **Hippocratic Corpus**. Whether Hippocrates wrote it himself is uncertain. Many researchers suspect that it comes from his students or from later doctors. It is nevertheless one of the oldest documents on medical **ethics**.

The oath begins with a vow by the gods Apollo, Asclepius, Hygieia and Panacea. The doctor promises to help the sick to the best of his ability and not to harm them. He also promises never to give anyone a deadly poison, even if asked to. In addition, he promises to keep silent about everything he learns in his work; this is **medical confidentiality**.

After crimes committed by doctors in the Second World War, the **World Medical Association** created the **Declaration of Geneva** in 1948. It takes over the basic ideas of the old oath in modern language. It states, for example, that the health and well-being of patients come first. The declaration has been revised several times, most recently in 2017.

In Switzerland, doctors today do not take an official oath. Their duties, however, are set out in laws and in the code of conduct of the doctors' association **FMH**. Professional secrecy is even protected in the Criminal Code. Anyone who breaks it can be punished.

The Hippocratic Oath has become a symbol of responsible medical conduct. People say, for example, that a doctor is bound by the oath if she always helps. At some universities, graduates still recite a pledge at the graduation ceremony. The symbol of medicine is the **rod of Asclepius**, a staff with a snake that goes back to the god of healing Asclepius.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solemn promise, often made in front of witnesses or by something sacred.
Thinking about what right and good action is.
The duty not to pass on the secrets of patients.
A staff with a snake, the symbol of medicine and doctors.

gewusst: The famous phrase “first, do no harm” does not actually appear in the Hippocratic Oath; it was formulated much later.
On the island of Kos, people still point out an old plane tree under which Hippocrates is said to have taught.
The oath also required the doctor to honour his teacher like his own parents.

teile.einleitung: The heart is a powerful muscle that pumps blood around our body. It beats without a break for a whole lifetime, day and night. In doing so, it supplies every cell with oxygen and nutrients.
wichtigste: The heart is the organ that pumps blood around our body.
It is a hollow muscle and about the size of its owner's fist.
The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.
In adults at rest it beats about 60 to 80 times a minute.
The right half of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, the left half to the whole body.
Heart valves make sure that the blood flows in only one direction.
Exercise and a healthy diet keep the heart fit.

abschnitte.text: The heart lies in the chest, slightly to the left of the middle, between the two lungs. In adults it weighs about 300 grams. A dividing wall separates it into a right half and a left half. Each half has an **atrium** and a **ventricle**, with the **heart valves** between them.

The right half of the heart pumps blood that is low in oxygen into the lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen; this is the **pulmonary circulation**. The left half pumps the oxygen-rich blood through the main artery into the whole body; this is the **systemic circulation**. Through the veins, the blood comes back to the heart.

The heart beats by itself, driven by its own pacemaker, the **sinus node**. In adults at rest it beats about 60 to 80 times a minute, in children faster. During sport the **pulse** can rise to more than 150 beats. You can feel the heartbeat at your wrist or your neck.

Cardiovascular diseases are among the most common causes of death in Switzerland. Smoking, being overweight and little exercise harm the heart. Regular sport, vegetables and fruit keep it healthy. In a **cardiac arrest**, immediate chest compressions help, and a **defibrillator** can bring the heart back into the right rhythm.

In 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town transplanted a human heart for the first time. In 1969 Switzerland's first **heart transplant** succeeded in Zurich. Many people today live with a **pacemaker**, which sets the rhythm for the heart. In an emergency in Switzerland, you call 144.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two large chambers in the heart that pump the blood out powerfully.
A valve in the heart that lets blood through in only one direction.
The heartbeat you can feel in your blood vessels, counted per minute.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart into the body.

gewusst: In one day the heart pumps about 7000 litres of blood, which would fill a small bathtub more than 40 times.
In a long life a heart beats about three billion times.
The heart of a blue whale can weigh about 180 kilograms, as much as two to three adult people.

teile.einleitung: Patience is the ability to wait calmly and not to give up straight away when something takes longer. You need it when queuing at a kiosk, when learning an instrument or when waiting for the holidays. Patience can be practised, and it helps in many situations in life.
wichtigste: You need patience when you have to wait a long time.
The opposite of patient is impatient.
If you keep yourself busy while waiting, the time passes more quickly.
In the marshmallow test, children had to wait in order to get more sweets.
The saying “good things take time” fits patience.
The snail is a symbol of slowness.
An apple tree grown from a pip only bears apples after several years.

abschnitte.text: **Patience** means staying calm even when you have to wait or when something does not work straight away. Someone who is patient does not give up at once and is not easily upset. The opposite is **impatient**: you get fidgety, annoyed or want everything immediately. You do not simply have patience; you can train it like a muscle.

Around 1970 the psychologist **Walter Mischel** carried out a famous experiment at Stanford University in the USA. Children were given a sweet, for example a marshmallow, and were allowed to eat it at once. But anyone who waited a while until the researcher came back got a **second sweet**. Some children covered their eyes, sang songs or played in order to bear the wait.

Many children queue at a kiosk, and being patient means waiting until it is your turn. When learning an **instrument** or a sport you often need many weeks of practice before it goes well. Friendships and animals need patience too, for example when teaching a dog a trick. If you are patient with others, you listen to them and let them finish speaking.

While waiting it helps to **keep busy**, for example by reading a book or playing a game. Calm, deep **breathing** can help when you get impatient. Big goals can be divided into small steps, and then you see progress sooner. It also helps to remember what the waiting is worth it for.

In nature, many things take **time**. An apple tree that grows from a pip only bears fruit after several years. The **snail** is a symbol of slowness, and the tortoise too stands for calm and endurance. The saying “good things take time” means that good things often need time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to wait calmly and keep going
When you do not like waiting and want everything at once
The strength to keep going for a long time
A short, well-known sentence with a piece of wisdom about life

gewusst: In the marshmallow test many children managed only a few minutes before they ate the sweet.
With puzzles such as the Rubik's cube you can practise patience and concentration in a playful way.
The English word patience comes from a Latin word meaning “to bear” or “to endure”.

teile.einleitung: The tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea level, which is called low tide and high tide. They are caused above all by the pull of the Moon. On some coasts the beach lies dry for kilometres at low tide.
wichtigste: At high tide the water rises, at low tide it draws back.
The tides are caused above all by the Moon, with the Sun helping.
In one day there is high tide about twice and low tide about twice.
From high tide to low tide takes about 6 hours.
At full moon and new moon the tides are especially strong.
On the North Sea the sea floor lies dry at low tide as mud flats.
In lakes such as Lake Geneva you hardly notice low and high tide.

abschnitte.text: The **tides** are the regular movements of the sea. When the water rises, people speak of the **flood** or incoming tide, and the highest level is called high water. When it falls, people speak of the **ebb**, and the lowest level is called low water. Such a change from high tide to low tide takes about 6 hours.

abschnitte.titel: The part played by the Moon
abschnitte.text: The Moon pulls on the water of the Earth with its **gravity**. On the side that faces the Moon, a mountain of water arises. On the opposite side of the Earth a tidal bulge forms as well, because the Earth and the Moon turn around a common centre of mass. The Earth turns underneath these two bulges, and that is why there is high tide about twice a day.

The Sun also influences the tides, but only about half as strongly as the Moon. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth stand in a line at full moon or new moon, their forces reinforce each other and an especially high **spring tide** arises. At half moon the Sun and the Moon pull in different directions, and then there is a weak **neap tide**. Because the Moon stands in the same place a little later each day, high and low water shift by about 50 minutes every day.

How strong the tides are depends on the shape of the coast and of the sea floor. In the **Bay of Fundy** in Canada the difference between high and low water is up to about 16 metres, more than anywhere else. In the Mediterranean, low and high tide are mostly only weak, because it is almost entirely surrounded by land. In lakes such as Lake Geneva the tides are so small that you hardly notice them.

On the North Sea coast from the Netherlands through Germany to Denmark lies the **Wadden Sea**. At low tide the sea floor, the mud flats, falls dry here, and you can walk on it with guides. In the mud live worms, mussels, snails and crabs that feed many migrating birds. The Wadden Sea is part of the UNESCO World Natural Heritage.

The movement of the water can be used to generate electricity. At the mouth of the Rance in France stands one of the first big **tidal power stations** in the world, which was opened in 1966. There the water flows through turbines in a dam at high and low tide. Because there are only a few suitable coasts, tidal power stations are still rare today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the tides, that is, ebb and flood together.
An especially strong tide at full moon or new moon.
A weak tide at half moon.
The sea floor that lies dry at low tide.
The force with which bodies such as the Moon and the Earth attract each other.

gewusst: Not only the sea but also the solid ground rises and falls by a few decimetres through the tides, without our noticing it.
The tides very slowly brake the turning of the Earth, which is why the days grow longer over millions of years.
The abbey island of Mont-Saint-Michel in France is surrounded by water at high tide and can be reached on foot across the sand at low tide.

teile.einleitung: Cave paintings are pictures that people in the Stone Age painted on the walls of caves. Many of them are more than 30,000 years old. They mainly show animals and are among the oldest works of art made by humans.
wichtigste: Cave paintings come from the Palaeolithic.
Most of the pictures show animals such as horses, bison, deer and mammoths.
The painters used earth pigments and charcoal.
Light came from torches and fat lamps.
Handprints are also often found on the walls.
Famous painted caves are Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain.
The oldest cave pictures in Europe are over 30,000 years old.

abschnitte.text: Cave painting is the name for pictures that people of the **Palaeolithic** painted on rock walls in caves. Most of the well-known painted caves are in southern France and northern Spain. They were painted by people of the species Homo sapiens, who at that time lived as hunter-gatherers. The pictures are often deep inside the caves, where it is completely dark.

Most often the pictures show **animals**: horses, bison, aurochs, deer, ibex and mammoths. People, on the other hand, are rarely seen. There are also dots, lines and other signs whose meaning we do not know. **Handprints** are also very well known: people placed a hand on the wall and blew paint around it, or pressed the painted hand against the rock.

The painters used **earth pigments** such as red and yellow ochre, as well as black charcoal. They ground up the pigments and probably mixed them with water or fat. They painted with their fingers, with brushes made of animal hair or by spraying with their mouths. Light came from **torches** and small stone lamps in which animal fat burned. Sometimes the artists used bulges in the rock so that the animals look almost three-dimensional.

The cave of **Lascaux** in France was discovered in September 1940 by some teenagers who had followed a dog. Its pictures are around 17,000 years old. The cave of **Altamira** in Spain is famous for its coloured bison. The Chauvet Cave in France was discovered in 1994, and its oldest pictures are over 30,000 years old.

Many visitors brought moisture and germs into the caves, and the pictures began to suffer. That is why Lascaux was closed to the public in 1963. Today you can visit exact **replicas**, for example Lascaux IV. Lascaux and Altamira are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

In Switzerland there are no known painted caves like those in France. But in the **Kesslerloch** near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen, a piece of antler was found with an engraved drawing of a reindeer. It comes from the late Palaeolithic. Finds like this show that people created art here too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very long period of human history in which people lived as hunter-gatherers and used stone tools.
A natural earth pigment that can be yellow, red or brown.
An exact copy of an original.
A list of especially valuable places in the world that are to be protected.

gewusst: Because caves are cool and evenly damp, the colours there have survived for many thousands of years.
When the pictures of Altamira became known in the 19th century, many experts at first did not believe that Stone Age people could paint so beautifully.
On the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, animal pictures were found that are even more than 40,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: A large language model is an artificial intelligence computer program that understands texts and can write them itself. It learns from huge amounts of text which word is likely to come next. Well-known chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini are based on such models.
wichtigste: A large language model is pre-trained to predict the next token of a text.
A token is a unit of text, often a word or part of a word.
A higher temperature makes the answers more varied and more random.
In instruction tuning, the model is trained further with examples of tasks and good answers.
The scaling laws state that performance rises predictably with parameters, data and computing power.
In 2025 ETH Zurich, EPFL and CSCS released the open language model Apertus.
Without extra tools, a model only knows the state of its training data.

abschnitte.text: A **language model** is a program that calculates how likely certain sequences of words are. It is called “large” because it consists of billions of numbers, the so-called **parameters**, and has been trained with huge amounts of text. Technically it is an artificial neural network, loosely inspired by the structure of the brain. Most of today's models use the **transformer** architecture, which Google researchers presented in 2017. Language models became known to everyone when ChatGPT appeared in November 2022.

A text is first broken into small pieces called **tokens**. A token can be a whole word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. During **pre-training**, the model reads enormous quantities of text from books, websites and program code. In doing so it practises the same task again and again: predicting the next token. If it is wrong, its parameters are changed a tiny bit, and so over time it gets better and better.

After pre-training, the model can continue texts, but it does not yet follow instructions well. That is why, in **instruction tuning**, it is trained further with examples of tasks and good answers. Often people also rate different answers so that the model becomes more helpful and safer. When writing, the model chooses word by word, and the **temperature** determines how random the choice is. In few-shot prompting, you show the model a few examples in the prompt, and it adopts the pattern without being retrained.

Researchers have observed that language models become predictably better when they are made bigger. These **scaling laws** describe how performance rises with the number of parameters, the amount of data and the computing power. That is why models are trained in huge data centres with thousands of special graphics chips. Training a large model needs a great deal of electricity and costs a lot of money. An example from Switzerland is **Apertus**, which ETH Zurich, EPFL and the CSCS supercomputing centre in Lugano released in 2025 as an open model.

Language models can summarise texts, translate, answer questions and help with programming. But they do not have real knowledge of the world like a human; instead they reproduce what is likely according to their data. Sometimes they invent convincing-sounding but false statements, which is called **hallucination**. Without extra tools such as a web search, they only know the state of their training data. That is why you should always check important information in reliable sources.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small unit of text that a language model calculates with, often a word or part of a word.
The many numbers inside a model that are adjusted during training.
The input or question that you give to a language model.
The learning process in which a model gets better and better from examples.

gewusst: During training, a large language model has often read more text than a person could read in many thousands of lifetimes.
The Swiss model Apertus was trained with texts in over a thousand languages, including Swiss German and Romansh.

teile.einleitung: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is a basic law of quantum physics, the physics of the very smallest particles. Put simply, it says that you cannot measure the position and momentum of a particle exactly at the same time. The German physicist Werner Heisenberg formulated it in 1927.
wichtigste: The uncertainty principle is a basic principle of quantum mechanics.
It states that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be determined exactly at the same time.
The more precisely you know the position, the less precisely you know the momentum, and vice versa.
Momentum depends on the mass and speed of a particle.
