Werner Heisenberg formulated the principle in 1927.
The uncertainty is not due to poor measuring instruments, but to nature itself.
In everyday life you notice nothing of it, because it only matters for tiny particles.

abschnitte.text: To describe a particle such as an **electron**, you want to know where it is and how it is moving. Its motion is described by its **momentum**, that is, mass times speed. The uncertainty principle says that knowing both exactly at the same time is impossible. If one becomes sharper, the other becomes fuzzier.

Imagine you want to find a ball in the dark by throwing other balls at it. If you hit it, you know roughly where it was, but you have given it a knock and changed its motion. With tiny particles it is similar, only even more fundamental. Experts stress that the uncertainty is part of the nature of **quantum particles** even without any measurement.

Werner Heisenberg lived from 1901 to 1976 and was a German physicist. At only 25, he formulated the uncertainty principle in 1927. He was one of the founders of **quantum mechanics**. For his work he received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for the year 1932.

The formula contains a very small constant of nature, **Planck's constant**. The uncertainty in position multiplied by the uncertainty in momentum is always at least as large as a tiny fixed value. Because this value is so small, the uncertainty plays no part for a bicycle or a football. For electrons in an atom, on the other hand, it is crucial.

The uncertainty principle explains why electrons do not fall into the atomic nucleus and why atoms stay stable. It greatly changed the way physics sees the world. Before, people thought that with enough knowledge you could calculate everything in advance exactly. Today we know that in the world of the smallest particles, **chance** plays an important part.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of physics that describes the world of the very smallest particles.
A quantity made from mass and speed that describes how much impetus a body has.
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of an atom.
A very small constant of nature that appears everywhere in quantum physics.

gewusst: Heisenberg had the basic idea of quantum mechanics in 1925 on the island of Heligoland, where he was recovering from hay fever.
There are similar uncertainty relations for other pairs of quantities too, for example for energy and time.
Albert Einstein did not agree with chance in quantum physics and is said to have remarked that God does not play dice.

teile.einleitung: Freeze-drying is a process for gently removing water from food, medicines and other substances. The goods are first frozen, and then the ice evaporates in a vacuum without melting first. The result is light, keeps for a long time and holds its shape and flavour.
wichtigste: In freeze-drying, frozen water evaporates in a vacuum.
The direct change from solid to gas is called sublimation.
A vacuum is needed, because ice only sublimates quickly at very low pressure.
Shape, aroma and nutrients are better preserved than in drying with heat.
Instant coffee is often freeze-dried.
Freeze-dried meals are very light and therefore popular with mountaineers.
The technical term for freeze-drying is lyophilisation.

abschnitte.text: Freeze-drying is an especially gentle way of **drying** something. Instead of evaporating the water with heat, it is first frozen and the ice is then made to disappear at very low pressure. The technical term for it is **lyophilisation**. Because hardly any heat is needed, sensitive substances such as vitamins, flavours or proteins are hardly damaged.

First the product is deep-frozen, often to minus 40 degrees or colder. Then it goes into a chamber from which a pump sucks the air out, so that a **vacuum** is created. Now a little heat is very carefully supplied, and the ice turns directly into water vapour without becoming liquid. This process is called **sublimation**. The vapour settles again as ice on an ice-cold surface, the condenser.

Many people know **instant coffee**, which is often freeze-dried and dissolves at once in hot water. You find freeze-dried strawberries or raspberries in muesli, and they are crunchy and light. Because they are full of tiny **pores**, they take water up again very quickly. Mountaineers, hikers and astronauts take freeze-dried meals with them, which you only have to pour hot water over.

Freeze-drying is also very important in **medicine**. Many vaccines, antibiotics and other medicines are stored as a dry powder and only dissolved shortly before use. In this way they keep for much longer. In the Second World War, freeze-dried **blood plasma** was brought to the front to treat the wounded.

The peoples of the **Andes** in South America were using the principle hundreds of years ago. They let potatoes freeze in the frost at night and dry in the thin, dry mountain air during the day. This produced **chuño**, a kind of dried potato that keeps for years. At altitude the air pressure is lower, which makes it easier for the ice to sublimate.

Freeze-dried products are very light, because most of the water is missing, and sealed airtight they often keep for many years. Shape, colour, **aroma** and nutrients are largely preserved. The disadvantage is that the process needs a lot of energy and takes a long time, sometimes several days. That is why freeze-dried foods are usually more expensive than those dried with hot air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direct change of a substance from solid to gas, without becoming liquid.
A space from which almost all the air has been pumped out, so that the pressure there is very low.
The technical term for freeze-drying.
A very cold surface in the machine on which the water vapour settles again as ice.

gewusst: Washing that freezes outside on the line in winter also becomes dry, because the ice slowly sublimates.
Museums use freeze-drying to save wet books and documents after water damage.
Freeze-dried foods can sometimes keep for 20 years or longer if they are packed airtight.

teile.einleitung: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms that form a hollow ball or egg. The best known, C60, looks like a classic football. Their discovery in 1985 was a sensation and was rewarded with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996.
wichtigste: Fullerenes are hollow molecules made of pure carbon.
The best-known fullerene, C60, consists of 60 carbon atoms.
C60 has the shape of a classic football.
Every closed fullerene contains exactly 12 pentagons.
They are named after the architect Buckminster Fuller.
Kroto, Curl and Smalley received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996 for their discovery.
Fullerenes also form naturally, for example in the soot of flames.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is known as graphite in pencils and as diamond. Fullerenes are another form, in which carbon atoms are joined into **hollow cages**. The most famous is **C60**, in which 60 atoms form a ball. It is about one nanometre across, so roughly a hundred thousand times smaller than the thickness of a hair.

The surface of a fullerene consists of pentagons and hexagons, just like an old **football** made of leather patches. C60 has 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. Mathematically it can be shown that every closed fullerene needs exactly **12 pentagons**, however large it is. The number of hexagons, on the other hand, can change; in the longer **C70** there are more, which is why it looks like a rugby ball.

The shape reminded the discoverers of the **geodesic domes** of the American architect **Richard Buckminster Fuller**. His best-known dome stands in Montreal and was built for the world exhibition in 1967. So they called C60 “buckminsterfullerene”. In English the molecules are also jokingly called “buckyballs”.

In 1985 **Harold Kroto**, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley and their team fired a laser at graphite. In the vapours produced they found strikingly many molecules with exactly 60 carbon atoms. In 1990 researchers in Heidelberg and the USA succeeded for the first time in making larger amounts. In 1996 Kroto, Curl and Smalley received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it.

Fullerenes form in small amounts in the **soot** of flames, for example from candles. They have also been found in a rare rock from Russia, shungite. A single atom can be shut inside the cavity of a fullerene, and then it is called an **endohedral fullerene**. Fullerenes are being studied for solar cells, lubricants and medicine and are related to carbon nanotubes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle made of several firmly joined atoms
A chemical element that diamond, graphite and soot are made of, for example
A millionth of a millimetre
A fullerene with an atom trapped inside it
A dome made of many triangles or polygons, as designed by Buckminster Fuller

gewusst: A C60 molecule compares to a football roughly as a football compares to the Earth.
Researchers have even detected fullerenes in space, in clouds of gas around dying stars.
The discoverers first built a model of C60 with paper, scissors and sticky tape.

teile.einleitung: Glacial milk is the cloudy, whitish grey meltwater that flows out of a glacier. It looks almost like watered-down milk, but it is ice cold and full of tiny grains of rock. These grains are also the reason why many mountain lakes shine such a beautiful turquoise.
wichtigste: Glacial milk gets its name because the meltwater looks cloudy and whitish.
The cloudiness comes from rock flour, which is rock ground down very finely.
Rock flour is made when the glacier grinds over the bedrock.
On warm summer days the most glacial milk flows, especially in the afternoon.
The stream that comes out of the glacier is called a glacial stream.
In lakes, the fine grains slowly sink to the bottom and the water becomes clearer.
The Rhone carries glacial milk from Valais into Lake Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Glacial milk is the **meltwater** of a glacier, loaded with the finest particles. It has a milky grey, sometimes greenish colour. You cannot see the bottom of the stream, even if it is only knee-deep. The water is almost zero degrees, because it comes straight from the melting ice. If you put your hand in, it becomes painfully cold after a few seconds.

A glacier is a huge river of ice that slowly moves down the valley. Stuck in the ice are stones that scrape over the bedrock like **sandpaper**. In this way rock is ground into the finest **rock flour**, whose grains are often smaller than a thousandth of a millimetre. The meltwater under the glacier picks up this flour and carries it out of the glacier mouth. In this way a glacier can carry away thousands of tonnes of rock every year.

abschnitte.titel: In the rhythm of the day and year
abschnitte.text: How much glacial milk flows depends very much on the weather. On hot summer days a lot of ice melts, and the **glacial stream** swells until late afternoon or evening. At night and early in the morning it carries much less water. In winter the stream is often almost dry, because hardly anything melts. Hikers should therefore cross glacial streams in the morning if possible, because in the afternoon they can be dangerously fast-flowing.

When glacial milk flows into a lake, the lake often shines **turquoise** or milky blue. The floating grains scatter sunlight and reflect mainly blue and green light. Well-known examples are Lake Oeschinen near Kandersteg or lakes at the foot of glaciers in Valais. In the lake the particles slowly sink and form fine layers on the bottom called **lake clay**. Researchers can read from these layers how much a glacier melted in the past.

The **Rhone** rises at the Rhone Glacier in Upper Valais and carries its cloudy water all the way into Lake Geneva. There the rock flour settles, so the Rhone leaves the lake in Geneva clear again. Shortly after Geneva, the Arve joins the Rhone, bringing glacier water from the Mont Blanc area. At the confluence you can therefore see clear and cloudy water flowing side by side. Glacial milk also matters for hydroelectric power stations, because its sand and mud settle in the reservoirs and have to be removed from time to time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rock that the glacier has ground so finely that it looks like flour.
The opening at the lower end of a glacier from which the glacial stream flows out.
A stream formed from the meltwater of a glacier.
Material such as sand or mud that settles on the bottom of a body of water.

gewusst: The finest grains of glacial milk are so light that they can float in a lake for months before reaching the bottom.
Over many centuries the Rhone is slowly filling the eastern end of Lake Geneva with its mud, and it has already built a whole delta.

teile.einleitung: Georges de Mestral was a Swiss engineer who invented the hook and loop fastener. The idea came to him after a walk with his dog, when burrs got caught in its fur. His invention is found today on shoes, jackets and even in spacecraft.
wichtigste: Georges de Mestral was a Swiss engineer from the canton of Vaud.
He lived from 1907 to 1990.
After a walk with his dog he invented the hook and loop fastener.
The model for it were the fruits of the burdock with their tiny hooks.
The fastener consists of a hook side and a loop side.
He had his invention protected under the name Velcro.
He is a well-known example of bionics, that is, learning from nature.

abschnitte.text: Georges de Mestral was born in **Lausanne** in 1907. He studied at the technical university in Lausanne and became an engineer. He was a keen tinkerer and hunter. He died in 1990 in the canton of Vaud.

Around 1941 de Mestral went for a walk in the mountains with his dog. Afterwards many **burrs** were hanging in his clothes and in the dog's fur. Curious, he looked at them under the **microscope**. He saw that the burrs have tiny hooks that catch in loops of cloth and fur.

A hook and loop fastener has two bands. On one of them sit many small, hard **hooks**, on the other soft **loops**. If you press the two together, thousands of hooks catch in the loops. If you pull hard, they come apart again with the typical ripping sound.

It took many years before de Mestral found the right material. Only with the plastic **nylon** did durable hooks succeed. At the beginning of the 1950s he applied for a patent. He made the name **Velcro** out of the French words velours for velvet and crochet for hook.

Hook and loop fasteners are found today on children's shoes, bags, jackets and blood pressure cuffs. Spaceflight uses them too, so that objects do not float away in weightlessness. De Mestral is regarded as a prime example of **bionics**. In this, researchers look at how nature solves a problem and copy it in technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant whose fruits catch in fur and clothes with small hooks.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.
A protection right that secures the rights to an invention for an inventor for a certain time.
A tear-resistant plastic from which threads and fabrics are made.

gewusst: Velcro is so well known that in English the word is often used for any hook and loop fastener.
The burdock is related to the sunflower and the dandelion; all of them belong to the daisy family.
Georges de Mestral was admitted to the American National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1999.

teile.einleitung: The Galápagos giant tortoise is one of the largest tortoises in the world and lives only on the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific. It can weigh more than 200 kilograms and live for more than 100 years. The island group is even named after it.
wichtigste: Galápagos giant tortoises live only on the Galápagos Islands.
They can weigh more than 200 kilograms.
They live for more than 100 years.
They eat only plants.
When in danger they pull back into their shell.
In the past, sailors took them on board as a living supply of meat.
Lonesome George was the last giant tortoise from the island of Pinta.

abschnitte.text: The shell of a fully grown Galápagos giant tortoise can be more than a metre long. The animals can weigh more than **200 kilograms**, as much as three adult people. On damp islands they have a round **dome-shaped shell**, and on dry islands a **saddle-shaped shell** that is raised at the front. With this saddle shell they can stretch their necks far upwards to reach higher plants.

The **Galápagos Islands** lie about 1,000 kilometres west of Ecuador in the Pacific Ocean. On different islands, different forms have developed, which experts today often regard as separate species. The tortoises live in the dry lowlands and in the damper highlands. They like lying in muddy puddles to cool down and protect themselves from insects.

Giant tortoises eat only **plants**: grasses, leaves, fruit and even prickly **prickly pears**, a kind of cactus. They can go a long time without food and water, because they store reserves in their bodies. They move very slowly and spend a lot of time resting. When in danger they pull their head and legs back into their **shell** with a hiss.

In the past, sailors, whalers and pirates took thousands of tortoises on board. Because the animals survive for months without food, they served as a **living supply of meat**. Later, introduced animals such as rats, goats and pigs ate their eggs and their food. Several island forms therefore died out, for example the one from the island of **Pinta**, whose last representative Lonesome George died in 2012.

The naturalist **Charles Darwin** visited the islands in 1835 on the ship Beagle. He noticed that animals on different islands look different, which gave him ideas for his **theory of evolution**. Today the islands are a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In breeding stations, young tortoises are raised and released into the wild again, and their numbers have risen since then.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard covering of bone and horn that protects a tortoise's body
A shell raised at the front so that the neck can reach far upwards
A cactus with flat, prickly segments
Bringing animals raised in human care back into nature

gewusst: The old Spanish word “galápago” means something like tortoise, which is why the islands are called Galápagos.
Giant tortoises can survive up to a year without food and water.
Lonesome George became a symbol of species protection, and his preserved body is now on display on the Galápagos Islands.

teile.einleitung: The brainstem is the lowest part of the brain and connects it to the spinal cord. It controls vital processes such as breathing and heartbeat, without us having to think about them. Without the brainstem we could not live.
wichtigste: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata.
At the bottom it is connected to the spinal cord.
It controls vital functions such as breathing and heartbeat.
Protective reflexes such as coughing and swallowing are controlled in the brainstem.
Most of the twelve cranial nerves arise from the brainstem.
The reticular formation in the brainstem is important for wakefulness and attention.
The brainstem is regarded as the oldest part of the brain.

abschnitte.text: The **brainstem** sits on the underside of the brain, roughly where the head meets the neck. It is about as thick as a thumb. It consists of three parts: the **midbrain**, the **pons** and the medulla oblongata, which at the bottom merges into the spinal cord. Behind it lies the cerebellum, which, however, is not counted as part of the brainstem.

In the medulla oblongata there are centres that control **breathing**, **heartbeat** and blood pressure. They work automatically day and night, even while we sleep. The brainstem is also like a switching point: all signals between the brain and the body pass through it. If you want to move your hand, for example, the command goes from the cerebrum through the brainstem into the spinal cord.

Many **protective reflexes** are controlled in the brainstem, for example coughing, swallowing, sneezing and blinking. These reflexes happen in a flash, without us having to think. If a doctor shines a light into your eye, the **pupil** becomes smaller. This is how she checks whether a reflex via the brainstem is working.

We have twelve pairs of **cranial nerves**, and most of them arise from the brainstem. They control, for example, eye movements, the facial muscles, hearing and taste. The brainstem also contains a network of nerve cells, the **reticular formation**. It makes sure that we are awake and alert, and it plays a part in switching between sleeping and waking.

abschnitte.titel: The oldest part of the brain
abschnitte.text: The brainstem is regarded as the **oldest part** of the brain, because even very early vertebrates had similar structures. Fish, frogs, lizards and birds also have a brainstem. Over the course of evolution, larger areas such as the cerebrum were added in mammals. But the basic functions of life are still controlled by the brainstem today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fast, automatic reaction of the body to a stimulus.
A bundle of nerves inside the spine that connects the brain and the body.
Nerves that come directly from the brain and mainly supply the head and neck.
The lowest part of the brainstem, which merges into the spinal cord.

gewusst: The cerebellum sits directly behind the brainstem and is connected to it by thick bundles of nerves.
The nerve pathways cross over in the brainstem, which is why the left half of the brain controls the right side of the body.
The brainstem is only a few centimetres long, but it controls things without which we could not live for a single minute.

teile.einleitung: The Great Aletsch Glacier in the canton of Valais is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps. Its river of ice is a good 20 kilometres long and more than 900 metres thick at Konkordiaplatz. Since 2001 the area has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps and lies in the canton of Valais.
Today it is a good 20 kilometres long.
At Konkordiaplatz several large firn streams flow together, and the ice there is more than 900 metres thick.
Its meltwater forms the mountain stream Massa, which flows into the Rhone.
Since 2001 the area has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.
Because of global warming, the glacier is melting and steadily getting shorter.
From the Eggishorn and the Jungfraujoch there are famous views of the ice.

abschnitte.text: The glacier lies on the south side of the Bernese Alps in the **canton of Valais**. It begins below peaks such as the Jungfrau and the Mönch, close to the **Jungfraujoch** with its railway station “Top of Europe”. From there the ice flows south towards the Rhone Valley. At a good 20 kilometres long, it is the longest glacier in the Alps. It contains more ice than any other glacier in the Alps.

At **Konkordiaplatz** several large streams of ice flow together, including the Great Aletsch Firn, the Jungfrau Firn and the Ewigschneefäld. Here the glacier is at its thickest, more than 900 metres. That is about three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. **Firn** is old, compacted snow that slowly turns into glacier ice. From here the ice flows down the valley as a broad band.

At the lower end of the glacier, the meltwater emerges as the mountain stream **Massa**. The Massa flows through a deep gorge and joins the Rhone near Naters and Bitsch. At the edge of the glacier lies **Lake Märjelen**, an ice-margin lake. In the past it often burst suddenly and caused floods in the valley. Today it is much smaller than it used to be because of glacier retreat.

At the edge of the glacier grows the **Aletsch Forest** with ancient Swiss stone pines, some of them several hundred years old. It is one of the oldest nature reserves in Switzerland. Chamois, marmots and many mountain birds live in the area. The nature conservation organisation **Pro Natura** runs a centre in the historic Villa Cassel on the Riederfurka that provides information about the glacier and the forest.

Since the end of the Little Ice Age around 1850, the Great Aletsch Glacier has become several kilometres shorter. At the same time it has become much thinner. **Global warming** is speeding up this retreat. Researchers expect that by the end of this century only a small remnant could be left if the Earth keeps warming so strongly. The glacier is therefore an important object of observation for climate research.

The region around Riederalp, Bettmeralp and Fiesch is called the **Aletsch Arena** and can be reached car-free by cable car. From the **Eggishorn** you look down on the long, curving river of ice with its dark stripes. These stripes are **medial moraines** made of rock debris, which form where the firn streams flow together. On guided tours you can even walk on the glacier. You should never do this alone, because crevasses are dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large mass of ice that moves slowly down the valley.
Old, compacted snow that gradually turns into glacier ice.
A ridge or stripe of stones and debris that a glacier carries along or deposits.
Places that are especially valuable for all humankind because of their nature or culture.
A lake at the edge of a glacier that is dammed up by the ice.

gewusst: The ice at Konkordiaplatz takes many decades to reach the end of the glacier.
In 2001 the UNESCO World Heritage Site Jungfrau-Aletsch was the first natural World Heritage Site in the Alpine region.
As a young man, the British politician Winston Churchill spent holidays at the Villa Cassel on the Riederfurka.

teile.einleitung: A boiled egg is a hen's egg cooked in hot water in its shell. Exciting chemistry happens inside: liquid, transparent egg white becomes firm and white. Depending on the cooking time, the egg is soft, medium or hard boiled.
wichtigste: When cooking, the egg white becomes firm and white.
A soft-boiled egg still has a runny yolk.
You boil a hard-boiled egg for about 10 minutes.
Boiled eggs are put in cold water so that they do not go on cooking.
A boiled egg can never become raw and runny again.
A hard-boiled egg spins fast and smoothly on the table like a top.
Boiled and coloured eggs are part of Easter in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What happens when you boil it?
abschnitte.text: Egg white consists largely of water and many long protein particles, the **proteins**. The heat makes these particles unfold and tangle with one another. This is called **denaturation** or setting. In the process the egg white becomes firm and opaque white, and this process cannot be reversed.

How firm an egg becomes depends on the **cooking time**. After about 4 to 5 minutes the egg white is firm but the yolk is still **runny**, so the egg is soft. After about 6 to 7 minutes the yolk is creamy, so medium boiled. A hard-boiled egg needs about 10 minutes, and then the yolk is completely firm too.

After boiling you put the eggs in cold water, which is called **cooling them down**. In this way they do not go on cooking in their own heat. If an egg boils too long, the yolk sometimes gets a greenish edge, which is harmless. Large eggs and eggs straight from the fridge need a little longer.

You can find out whether an egg is boiled or raw without cracking it. You spin it on the table like a **top**. A hard-boiled egg is firm inside and spins fast and smoothly. A raw egg wobbles and soon stops, because the liquid inside slows the spin.

abschnitte.titel: Eggs in the mountains and at Easter
abschnitte.text: High in the mountains, water boils below 100 degrees, because the **air pressure** is lower there. So eggs in the mountains take a little longer to become firm. In Switzerland, boiled eggs are coloured brightly and hidden at Easter. In **egg tapping**, two people knock their eggs against each other, and whoever's egg stays whole wins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of the body.
When protein particles change shape through heat and become firm.
Putting something hot quickly into cold water.
The yellow part in the middle of the egg.

gewusst: A boiled egg is sometimes hard to peel if it is very fresh.
The egg white sets at a little over 60 degrees, and the yolk only at a slightly higher temperature.
In German the word “Eiweiss” means both the white of an egg and the proteins in food.

teile.einleitung: Gregor Mendel was a monk and naturalist who discovered the basic rules of heredity. To do so, he cross-bred pea plants in the garden of his monastery for years. Today he is regarded as the father of genetics.
wichtigste: Gregor Mendel lived from 1822 to 1884.
He was an Augustinian monk in the monastery in Brünn, today's Brno in the Czech Republic.
He discovered the rules of heredity by cross-breeding pea plants for years.
He published his results in 1866, but hardly anyone paid attention.
His rules were only rediscovered around 1900.
Mendel's laws explain how traits are passed on from parents to offspring.
Mendel is regarded as the founder of genetics.

abschnitte.text: Johann Mendel was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf in Silesia, which today lies in the Czech Republic. His parents were farmers. In 1843 he entered the **Augustinian monastery** in Brünn and was given the religious name Gregor. He studied natural sciences in Vienna and later worked as a teacher.

Between 1856 and 1863 Mendel grew thousands of **pea plants** in the monastery garden. Peas were well suited because they have clear traits, such as yellow or green seeds and round or wrinkled peas. Mendel deliberately **cross-bred** different plants and counted exactly what the offspring looked like. He analysed his results with mathematics, which was new in biology at the time.

Mendel found out that traits are inherited in units that we now call **genes**. Some traits are **dominant** and win out, others are **recessive** and can skip a generation. In the second generation, the traits appeared in a ratio of about 3 to 1. From this came the law of uniformity, the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment.

Mendel presented his work in 1865 and published it in 1866. Scientists at the time did not understand its importance. From 1868 Mendel was abbot of his monastery and hardly had any time left for research. Only in 1900 did three researchers, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, rediscover his rules.

Mendel's laws form the basis of **genetics**, the science of heredity. They can be used to explain why children look like their parents. Breeders use them to obtain plants and animals with particular characteristics. Medicine also needs this knowledge to understand hereditary diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: The passing on of traits from parents to their offspring.
A section of the genetic material that influences a particular characteristic.
A trait that wins out over another one.
A trait that only shows if it is inherited from both parents.
Breeding two plants or animals with different traits with each other.

gewusst: Mendel failed his teacher's examination twice, but carried on doing research anyway.
The word gene did not even exist in Mendel's lifetime; it was only introduced in 1909.
Besides peas, Mendel also studied bees and the weather.

teile.einleitung: Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher who lived around AD 400 in Alexandria in Egypt. She is regarded as one of the first known women in the history of mathematics. Many students came to her to learn from her.
wichtigste: Hypatia lived in Alexandria, a large city of the ancient world in Egypt.
Her father was the mathematician Theon of Alexandria.
She taught mathematics, astronomy and the philosophy of Neoplatonism.
Her student Synesius wrote her letters that still survive today.
Hypatia is said to have explained to him how to build an astrolabe.
Almost all of her own works have been lost.
A crater on the Moon bears her name.

abschnitte.text: Hypatia was probably born around AD 355; the exact year is uncertain. She lived in **Alexandria**, a port city in Egypt that at that time belonged to the Roman Empire. Alexandria was a famous centre of science. Hypatia spoke and wrote Greek, the language of scholars at that time.

Her father, **Theon of Alexandria**, was a mathematician and astronomer. He edited works by the famous mathematician Euclid and the astronomer Ptolemy. Hypatia worked with him and probably helped with these texts. Later she is said to have written her own explanations, called **commentaries**, on difficult mathematics books.

Hypatia taught philosophy, above all **Neoplatonism**, a school of thought that goes back to the Greek thinker Plato. Students from different regions and religions came to her. She was respected throughout the city and also advised important men in government. For a woman in the ancient world, this was very unusual.

Her student **Synesius of Cyrene**, who later became a bishop, wrote her letters that still survive today. From them we know that she explained to him how to build an **astrolabe**. With this instrument you could work out the position of the stars and tell the time. Hypatia's own writings, by contrast, have almost all been lost.

In the year 415, Hypatia was caught up in a fierce power struggle between leaders of the city and was killed by an angry mob. Her death shocked many people. Later she became a role model for women in science. A **lunar crater** and an asteroid are named after her, and in 2009 the film “Agora” told her story.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about big questions such as truth, knowledge and how to live well.
A school of philosophy in late antiquity that builds on the teachings of Plato.
An old measuring instrument used to work out the position of stars and the time.
The time of the ancient Greeks and Romans, up to about AD 500.

gewusst: Almost everything we know about Hypatia comes from texts by other people, not from her herself.
In his letters, Synesius respectfully called Hypatia his mother, sister and teacher.
An asteroid with the number 238 also bears the name Hypatia.

teile.einleitung: Hero of Alexandria was a Greek mathematician and engineer who lived in Egypt in the 1st century AD. He invented astonishing machines that worked with air, water and steam. To this day, pupils calculate with formulas that bear his name.
wichtigste: Hero lived in the 1st century AD in the port city of Alexandria in Egypt.
Heron's formula is used to calculate the area of a triangle from its three sides.
Heron's method approximates the square root of a number step by step.
He described an early coin-operated machine that dispensed holy water.
His work “Pneumatica” describes devices that work with air and water pressure.
The aeolipile turned thanks to escaping steam.
Very little is known about his life; what is known is mainly his writings.

abschnitte.text: **Hero** lived in **Alexandria**, a large city at the mouth of the Nile that belonged to the Roman Empire at the time. The city was a centre of science with a famous library. Hero wrote books about mathematics, surveying and machines. Hardly anything is known about his life itself.

With **Heron's formula** you can work out the area of a triangle if you only know the lengths of its three sides. First you calculate half the perimeter, s. Then you multiply s by the three differences s minus a, s minus b and s minus c, and take the square root of the result. For a triangle with sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, s is 6 and the area is 6 cm². The formula appears in his work “Metrica”.

Hero also described a method for approximating the **square root** of a number more and more precisely. You take an estimate, divide the number by this estimate and take the average of the two. The result is the new, better estimate. For the square root of 10, the estimate 3 becomes about 3.17 after just one step, which is very close to the correct value.

In the **“Pneumatica”**, Hero describes devices that work with air and water pressure. They include a **coin-operated machine** that dispensed holy water when a coin was put in. With a fire on an altar he made temple doors open as if by magic, because the heated air pushed water out and so drove a mechanism. **Hero's fountain** gushes only by air pressure, without any pump at all.

Especially famous is the **aeolipile**, also called Hero's engine: a ball with two bent tubes. When water inside it is heated, steam streams out of the tubes and the ball spins. This makes the aeolipile one of the first known steam engines. It was not used for work at the time, though; it served more as a toy and as something to marvel at.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who plans and invents machines and buildings.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives a particular number; for example, 3 is the square root of 9.
The technology that works with air pressure.
The length of the edge of a shape; for a triangle, the sum of all three sides.

gewusst: Hero's coin-operated machine is around 1900 years older than modern drinks machines.
Hero also built a small theatre with figures that moved by themselves with the help of strings and weights.
The method for calculating square roots was probably already known to the Babylonians, but Hero wrote it down precisely.

teile.einleitung: Hedy Lamarr was an Austrian-American film actress and inventor. In Hollywood she became world-famous as a film star, and at the same time she developed frequency hopping together with the composer George Antheil. Similar ideas are found today in technologies such as Bluetooth.
wichtigste: Hedy Lamarr was born in Vienna in 1914 as Hedwig Kiesler and died in Florida in 2000.
She first became world-famous as a film actress in Hollywood.
Together with the composer George Antheil, she invented frequency hopping.
The invention was meant to make the radio control of torpedoes safe from jamming in the Second World War.
Her patent provided for 88 frequencies, as many as a piano has keys.
Technologies such as Bluetooth build on similar ideas.
Her birthday, 9 November, is Inventors' Day in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Hedy Lamarr was born on 9 November 1914 in **Vienna**; her real name was Hedwig Kiesler. As a young woman she was already acting in films in Austria and Germany. In 1937 she went to the USA and in **Hollywood** was given the stage name Hedy Lamarr. She appeared in many films, such as “Algiers” from 1938 and “Samson and Delilah” from 1949, and was considered one of the greatest stars of her time.

Besides acting, Hedy Lamarr was very interested in technology and tinkered with inventions in her spare time. During the **Second World War** she wanted to help the USA and its allies. Radio-controlled torpedoes could easily be jammed at the time if the enemy knew the radio frequency. Together with the composer **George Antheil**, she developed a solution and received a patent in 1942.

The idea was to keep changing the radio frequency according to a secret pattern. Transmitter and receiver jump from frequency to frequency at the same time, so that an enemy can hardly disrupt the connection. This is called **frequency hopping**. Antheil was familiar with player pianos, which are controlled by punched paper rolls. That is why the patent provided for 88 frequencies, exactly like the 88 keys of a piano.

The US Navy did not use the invention in the Second World War. Only later were similar methods used in military technology and then in civilian radio technology. Today **Bluetooth**, for example, uses frequency hopping, and related ideas also play a part in Wi-Fi and mobile networks. Hedy Lamarr received recognition only late; in 1997 she and Antheil were given an award for their pioneering work.

Hedy Lamarr died on 19 January 2000 in Florida. Her birthday, 9 November, is celebrated in Germany, Austria and Switzerland as **Inventors' Day**. Today she is seen as a role model showing that women achieve great things in technology and invention. In 2014 she was inducted into the American **National Inventors Hall of Fame**, a hall of fame for inventors.

begriffe.erklaerung: Here: a particular radio channel on which a transmitter sends out signals.
A radio technique in which the frequency keeps changing according to a pattern, so that it is hard to jam.
A legal right for an invention that secures it to the inventor for a certain time.
An underwater missile that propels itself through the water.

gewusst: The idea of the 88 frequencies came from the paper rolls of player pianos.
Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil never earned any money from their patent.
There is a documentary film about her life called “Bombshell”.

teile.einleitung: Homo naledi is an extinct human species whose bones were found in a cave in South Africa. It had a very small brain, but was still alive around 300,000 years ago. This means it existed at the same time as the first modern humans in Africa.
wichtigste: The fossils of Homo naledi come from the Rising Star Cave in South Africa.
The research was led by the palaeoanthropologist Lee Berger.
The word naledi means star in the Sesotho language.
The fossils are around 236,000 to 335,000 years old.
At about 450 to 600 cm³, the brain was very small for such a recent species.
More than 1500 fossil pieces were recovered from the first chamber.
The area where it was found is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Cradle of Humankind.

abschnitte.text: In 2013 two cavers crawled through narrow cracks in the **Rising Star Cave** north-west of Johannesburg. In a remote chamber, the Dinaledi Chamber, they discovered many bones. The researcher **Lee Berger** then put together a team. In 2015 the new species was described as Homo naledi.

The way to the chamber leads through a crack that is only about 18 centimetres wide at its narrowest point. Berger therefore looked for slim women researchers with climbing experience, who were called the Underground Astronauts. They recovered more than 1500 **fossil pieces** from at least 15 individuals. This is one of the largest finds of its kind in Africa.

Homo naledi was about 1.5 metres tall and slim. Its feet and legs were similar to ours, so it walked upright. The **hand** had a human-like wrist but curved fingers that were well suited to climbing. At 450 to 600 cm³, the **brain** was only about a third the size of ours.

Because of the small brain, many people first thought the species was several million years old. In 2017, however, the fossils were **dated** using various methods. They are only around 236,000 to 335,000 years old. So Homo naledi lived in Africa at the same time as early members of Homo sapiens.

How did so many bones get into the dark chamber that is so hard to reach? In 2023 Berger's team put forward the idea that Homo naledi deliberately **buried** its dead and scratched signs into the walls. Many experts think the evidence for this is not yet sufficient. The question is therefore highly **controversial**.

The Rising Star Cave lies in the area of the **Cradle of Humankind**, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999. Many important pre-humans have been found in these caves, such as Mrs Ples and Australopithecus sediba. Homo naledi shows that human evolution was not a straight path. Different human species lived side by side at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain of a living thing from earlier times.
A researcher who studies human evolution using ancient finds.
Working out how old a find is.
The genus to which modern humans and their close extinct relatives belong.

gewusst: The name of the Dinaledi Chamber means something like chamber of stars.
In 2022 Lee Berger squeezed through the narrow passage himself, after losing a lot of weight to do it.
In 2008 Lee Berger's nine-year-old son found the first bones of Australopithecus sediba in another cave in the region.

teile.einleitung: When a glacier is covered, parts of it are covered in summer with big white sheets of fleece. This is meant to protect the ice at these places from melting. In Switzerland such coverings are seen above all in ski areas and at well-known places for excursions.
wichtigste: Glacier coverings are meant to reduce the melting of ice at particular places.
The light-coloured fleece reflects a lot of solar radiation and insulates against warm air.
The melting at the covered place can go down by about half or more.
The fleece is laid out in early summer, before the strong melting begins.
In Switzerland it is above all mountain railways and ski areas that use glacier coverings.
Covering whole glaciers would be far too expensive and laborious.
Microplastics can arise through the wearing away of plastic fibres.

abschnitte.text: When a **glacier is covered**, strips of white **fleece** are laid over snow and ice and sewn together or weighted down. The fleece is a special plastic material that lets water through. The aim is to save as much snow and ice as possible at these places through the summer. The method has been used in the Alps since the beginning of the 2000s.

The light surface of the fleece **reflects** a large part of the solar radiation, rather like a white T-shirt in summer. At the same time the sheet acts like a blanket that **insulates** the ice against warm air. Dirty, grey ice, on the other hand, would take up a lot of the Sun's warmth and melt faster. That is why the winter snow under the fleece often lasts into the autumn, because the layer of snow takes up much less energy.

Measurements show that a fleece covering can reduce the melting at the covered place by about **half** or even more. It works best when it is laid out in **early summer**, while winter snow is still lying. In autumn the fleece is gathered in again. Some sheets last several summers before they have to be replaced.

In Switzerland it is above all **mountain railways** and **ski areas** that use glacier coverings. With them they protect, for example, pistes, ski lifts or the places where the glacier meets the mountain station. Also well known is the **Rhone Glacier** at the Furka Pass, where the ice grotto is protected with white sheets. From a distance the covered areas look like huge white plasters on the mountain.

Against the worldwide **loss of glaciers**, covering does not help. For large areas it would be far too expensive and laborious, and the covered areas are tiny compared with the glaciers. Besides, fine plastic fibres can come loose and get into the environment as **microplastics**. Experts therefore stress that only fewer greenhouse gases will protect the glaciers in the long term.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material of matted plastic fibres that is not woven.
The throwing back of light or radiation at a surface.
Protection that stops warmth being passed on quickly.
Tiny plastic particles that are smaller than five millimetres.
The shrinking of the glaciers, above all because of global warming.

gewusst: Under a fleece, a step several metres high can arise in the ice by the end of the summer, because everything beside it has melted away.
Laying out the heavy strips of fleece is hard manual work and often takes several days.
Light surfaces such as fresh snow throw back the greatest part of the sunlight.

teile.einleitung: The goldfish is one of the best-known ornamental fish in the world. It originally comes from China and is related to the carp. Goldfish are much cleverer than many people think, and with good care they can live to a great age.
wichtigste: The goldfish originally comes from China.
It is related to the carp and belongs to the carp family.
The wild form of the goldfish is greyish green.
Goldfish can remember things for several months.
They can learn to come to a signal for food.
With good care, goldfish live for more than 20 years.
Goldfish have no stomach.

abschnitte.text: The goldfish has the scientific name **Carassius auratus**. Most bred varieties are orange, red, yellow or white, often with spots. The wild form, by contrast, is an inconspicuous **greyish green** and therefore well camouflaged. There are many bred varieties with long veil fins, bulging eyes or a round body.

Goldfish are descended from a wild species of carp from **China**. More than a thousand years ago, people there kept strikingly coloured fish in ponds. Breeding produced more and more new forms from them. Later goldfish came to Japan and finally to **Europe**, where today they live in many garden ponds.

It is often said that goldfish can only remember something for a few seconds. That is not true, because experiments show that their **memory** lasts several months. Goldfish can learn to come to a signal such as a tap or a light for food. Some even recognise the person who feeds them.

Goldfish are **omnivores** and eat plants, insect larvae, small crustaceans and fish food. They have no **stomach**; food goes straight into the gut. That is why it is better to feed them several times a day in small portions. Too much food pollutes the water and makes the fish ill.

Goldfish need plenty of space, clean water and the company of other goldfish. A small round **bowl** is unsuitable; a large tank or a **garden pond** is better. There, with good care, they can live for more than 20 years. Goldfish can grow up to about 30 centimetres long if they have enough space.

abschnitte.titel: Never release them into the wild
abschnitte.text: You must never put goldfish into a lake, stream or pond. There they eat the spawn and larvae of native animals such as **amphibians** and churn up the bottom. Because they breed a lot, they can change entire bodies of water. In Switzerland, released goldfish are therefore considered a problem for **biodiversity**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that is kept because of its beautiful appearance.
A form of an animal that people have changed through deliberate selection.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
The variety of different animal and plant species in an area.

gewusst: Released goldfish can grow much bigger in the wild than in an aquarium and often take on their greyish green wild colour again.
Goldfish can distinguish colours well and can even see ultraviolet light.
In some countries goldfish are banned as prizes at funfairs, so that they do not suffer in small bags.

teile.einleitung: The Human Research Act, HRA for short, is a Swiss law that sets out how research involving people must be carried out. It protects the dignity, privacy and health of everyone who takes part in studies. It has applied throughout Switzerland since 2014.
wichtigste: The Human Research Act has been in force since 2014.
It regulates research into diseases and into the structure and function of the human body.
Its most important aim is to protect the dignity, privacy and health of participants.
It is based on Article 118b of the Federal Constitution.
Anyone who takes part in a study must in principle be informed and give consent.
Most research projects must be approved by a cantonal ethics committee.
Clinical trials must be entered in a public register.

abschnitte.text: The **Human Research Act** is a Swiss federal law and has applied since 1 January 2014. It lays down rules for research on people, for example when testing new medicines or studying diseases. This also includes research with blood samples, tissue or health data. It is based on **Article 118b** of the Federal Constitution. Voters approved this constitutional article in 2010.

At its heart is the protection of the people who take part in research. Their **dignity**, privacy and health are more important than the interests of science. Risks and burdens must be as small as possible and in reasonable proportion to the expected benefit. In addition, the human body must not be **commercialised**. So you may not ask for or pay money for blood, tissue or body parts.

Anyone taking part in a research project must first be **informed** in an understandable way about its aim, procedure, risks and benefits. Then the person decides freely whether to take part and can withdraw their **consent** at any time. Consent is also generally required for genetic data to be used again for research purposes. Personal data must be well protected.

In the law, children and young people are considered especially in need of protection. Research with them is only allowed if equivalent results cannot be obtained with adults. This is the case, for example, with diseases that only occur in children, or when you want to know how a medicine works in children. The parents must give consent, and the child is also asked for their opinion. If a child clearly says no, they may not take part.

Before a project may start, the responsible cantonal **ethics committee** usually checks whether it follows the rules. These committees include experts from medicine, law, ethics and other fields. For clinical trials with medicines, the therapeutic products agency **Swissmedic** must also give its approval. Clinical trials are entered in a public register so that everyone can see which studies are running. Information on this is provided by the coordination office **kofam** at the Federal Office of Public Health.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of experts who check whether research is fair and safe for the participants.
A person's voluntary agreement after being well informed.
A study that checks, for example, whether a new medicine works and is safe.
The most important law in Switzerland, on which all other laws are based.
The Coordination Office for Human Research at the Federal Office of Public Health.

gewusst: Anyone taking part in a study does not have to say why they want to drop out.
For research that could cause harm, liability or insurance for the participants must be arranged.
In Switzerland there are several cantonal and regional ethics committees, which have joined together under the name swissethics.

teile.einleitung: A glacier outburst flood is a sudden flood that happens when water dammed up in or beside a glacier drains all at once. Within a few hours, huge amounts of water can rush down into the valley. Internationally, such an event is often called by the Icelandic word jökulhlaup.
wichtigste: A glacier outburst flood happens when a glacial lake or a water pocket suddenly drains.
The Icelandic term for it is jökulhlaup, which means glacier run.
In Iceland, volcanoes such as Grímsvötn under Vatnajökull regularly trigger glacier runs.
Lake Märjelen beside the Great Aletsch Glacier used to cause floods in the Rhone Valley again and again.
The Gorner Lake in Valais drains almost every year.
The municipality of Lenk in the Simmental is affected by a lake on the Plaine Morte Glacier.
As glaciers shrink, new lakes form and the danger increases.

abschnitte.titel: What is a glacier outburst flood
abschnitte.text: In a **glacier outburst flood**, meltwater first collects in a lake at the edge of the glacier, on top of the glacier or in a cave inside the ice. Ice or moraines act like a **dam wall**. If this dam breaks, or the water suddenly finds a way under the ice, the lake drains in a short time. The flood wave often sweeps rubble, mud and trees along with it.

The word **jökulhlaup** comes from Iceland and means glacier run. Under the huge ice cap **Vatnajökull** lies the volcano **Grímsvötn**, whose heat constantly melts ice. The water collects in a lake beneath the ice and bursts out from time to time. In 1996, after a volcanic eruption, such a glacier run destroyed bridges and parts of the Ring Road in the south of Iceland.

**Lake Märjelen** is an ice-margin lake beside the Great Aletsch Glacier. In the past it drained suddenly again and again and caused floods in the Rhone Valley. That is why a tunnel was built at the end of the 19th century to lower the lake level. The **Gorner Lake** on the Gorner Glacier near Zermatt drains almost every year and is closely watched by experts.

On the flat **Plaine Morte Glacier** between Bern and Valais, a lake fills with meltwater every summer. When it drains under the ice, the water flows into the River Simme. For the municipality of **Lenk** in the Simmental, this means a risk of flooding. To reduce the risk, a channel was cut into the ice so that the lake can drain in a controlled way.

One of the worst glacier outburst floods in the Alps happened in 1892 on **Mont Blanc** in France. Hidden inside the **Tête Rousse Glacier** was a large water pocket, which suddenly burst out. The flood of water, ice and mud struck the spa town of **Saint-Gervais**. Many people lost their lives.

Because glaciers are shrinking as the climate warms, **rock basins** are being uncovered in which new lakes form. They often lie beneath steep, unstable slopes from which rock or ice can crash into the lake. Experts monitor such lakes with measuring instruments, cameras and satellite images. For protection, **relief tunnels** or channels are built to lower the lake level, and warning systems are set up.

begriffe.erklaerung: Icelandic word for a sudden glacier outburst flood.
A lake at the edge of a glacier that is dammed up by the ice.
A hollow space filled with water inside a glacier.
A tunnel through which water can drain from a lake in a controlled way.

gewusst: During a large jökulhlaup in Iceland, far more water can flow for a short time than in the Rhine at Basel.
Some glacial lakes drain through channels under the ice without anything being visible on the surface.
Lake Märjelen used to be so large that icebergs which had broken off the Aletsch Glacier floated on it.

teile.einleitung: The genetic fingerprint is a pattern from DNA that looks different in almost every person. With it, people can be identified clearly, rather as with a real fingerprint. It is used in forensics, in questions of family relationships and even in nature conservation.
wichtigste: The British researcher Alec Jeffreys developed the method in 1984.
Today, short repeating sections of DNA called STRs are mainly studied.
The number of repeats at one place differs greatly from person to person.
Because many STR sites are studied at once, a chance match is extremely unlikely.
Only identical twins have the same genetic fingerprint.
With the polymerase chain reaction invented by Kary Mullis, tiny traces of DNA can be copied.
In Switzerland, DNA analysis is used to show which wolf has been in an area.

abschnitte.text: The DNA of any two people is more than 99 per cent the same. But in some places there are big differences, and the **genetic fingerprint** uses exactly these. The result is also called a **DNA profile**. It is a kind of code made of numbers that belongs to a particular person.

The British geneticist **Alec Jeffreys** discovered the method in 1984 at the University of Leicester. He noticed that certain sections of DNA give a different pattern in every person. As early as 1985 the method helped in a real case for the first time: it proved that a boy from Ghana really was the son of a woman in Britain and could stay. Later the invention of the **polymerase chain reaction**, or PCR, by Kary Mullis revolutionised the technique, because it allows even tiny traces to be studied.

Today, **STRs** are mainly studied; these are short sections of DNA that repeat several times in a row, such as “GATA GATA GATA”. How often such a section repeats differs greatly between people. If many such places in the genetic material are studied at once, a pattern emerges that is almost unique. Only **identical twins** have the same profile, because they came from the same cell.

The police find DNA at crime scenes, for example in hairs, flakes of skin or saliva on a glass. The DNA profile from the **trace** is compared with the profiles of suspects or with a database. In Switzerland the **DNA Profiles Act** governs when such profiles may be created and stored. Since the revision of 2023, in serious crimes the prosecuting authorities may also estimate outward features such as eye and hair colour from a trace. A DNA profile can also prove that someone is innocent.

The genetic fingerprint is also used with animals. In Switzerland, experts collect droppings, hairs or saliva from killed sheep to find out which **wolf** was there. In this way they know how many wolves there are in an area and where they come from. The method also helps with bears, lynxes and in the fight against the illegal trade in protected animals.

A DNA profile is very reliable, but not every trace is proof of a crime. DNA can be transferred onto an object by a handshake, for example. Genetic information is also very personal data. That is why there are strict rules on how long profiles may be stored and who may see them, which is part of **data protection**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pattern of particular DNA features that identifies a person.
Short sections of DNA that repeat several times in a row.
A method for copying small amounts of DNA millions of times.
The science that helps to solve crimes.

gewusst: For a DNA profile, a few skin cells are often enough today.
With DNA profiles, many people wrongly convicted around the world have also been cleared after years.
Kary Mullis received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993 for inventing PCR.

teile.einleitung: Glacier melt means that glaciers lose more ice than new snow adds. Because the Earth is getting warmer, glaciers in Switzerland and all over the world are shrinking. This changes landscapes, rivers and life in the mountains.
wichtigste: The glaciers in Switzerland are getting smaller because it is getting warmer.
The cause is climate change, mainly from burning coal, oil and gas.
Since about 1850, Alpine glaciers have been retreating almost everywhere.
Where a glacier disappears, bare rock, rubble and often a new lake are left behind.
The Pizol Glacier was given a farewell ceremony in 2019.
Researchers measure every year where the glacier snout ends and how thick the ice still is.
Without glaciers, streams and rivers are short of water in hot summers.

abschnitte.text: A glacier is healthy when as much snow falls in winter as melts away in summer. If it gets warmer, more ice melts and the glacier loses mass year after year. The reason is **climate change**, meaning the worldwide warming caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide. In Switzerland it is already, on average, considerably more than 2 degrees warmer today than before industrialisation. This means the Alps are warming faster than the global average.

abschnitte.titel: How much the glaciers are shrinking
abschnitte.text: Since the end of the so-called **Little Ice Age** around 1850, Alpine glaciers have lost a large part of their ice. The hot years 2022 and 2023 were especially severe: in them the Swiss glaciers together lost about a tenth of their volume. The Great Aletsch Glacier, the longest glacier in the Alps, has become several kilometres shorter since 1850. Small glaciers such as the Pizol Glacier in the St Gallen Alps have already almost completely disappeared. In September 2019 people held a kind of farewell ceremony there to draw attention to glacier loss.

The Swiss monitoring network **GLAMOS** has been observing many glaciers for decades, some for more than a hundred years. Every year researchers measure where the **glacier snout** ends and compare it with the previous year. With poles drilled into the ice, you can see how much ice has melted away in summer. In addition there are photos, satellite images and drone flights. This creates an accurate picture of how quickly the glaciers are disappearing.

abschnitte.titel: Effects on the landscape and people
abschnitte.text: Where the ice disappears, **rock and rubble** are suddenly exposed, and new lakes form in hollows. The ground at high altitudes becomes less stable because the permafrost, which otherwise holds rocks together, is also thawing. In May 2025 a huge mass of rock and ice broke off at the Birch Glacier and buried large parts of the village of Blatten in the Lötschental. For rivers such as the Rhone and the Rhine, glaciers are important water stores. Without them, the rivers carry less water in hot, dry summers, which clearly affects farming, shipping and power stations.

abschnitte.titel: What is being done about it
abschnitte.text: At the Rhone Glacier, parts of the ice are covered with **white sheets** in summer so that the ice grotto lasts longer for visitors. The light-coloured fleeces reflect sunlight and slow down melting, but they cannot save a whole glacier. The only thing that can really help is to cut greenhouse gas emissions sharply worldwide. Switzerland has therefore set itself the goal of emitting net zero greenhouse gases by 2050. Researchers expect that even with good climate protection, a large part of today's Alpine glaciers will disappear by 2100.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lower end of a glacier, which reaches down into the valley.
The long-term change in the climate, today mainly warming caused by greenhouse gases.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
The calculation of whether a glacier has gained or lost ice in a year.

gewusst: Under some melted glaciers, old tree trunks come to light, showing that forest grew there thousands of years ago.
Light surfaces reflect sunlight, which is why dirty, dark glacier ice melts faster than fresh white snow.

teile.einleitung: Shark teeth are among the most common fossils of all. A shark loses a great many teeth during its life, and these can then turn to stone in the sea floor. Such teeth are even found in Switzerland, although there is no longer any sea here today.
wichtigste: Because a shark's skeleton is made of soft cartilage, it is mainly the teeth that remain as fossils.
A shark loses a great many teeth during its life, often thousands.
The teeth stand in several rows one behind the other and move forward as if on a conveyor belt.
Many fossil shark teeth are triangular and pointed and coloured grey, brown or black.
The prehistoric shark megalodon had teeth as big as a hand.
Shark teeth are found in Switzerland because a sea once lay over the Swiss Plateau.
Sharks existed long before the dinosaurs and also during their time.

abschnitte.text: Sharks do not have just one row of teeth but several **rows of teeth** one behind the other. At the front they bite, and behind them new teeth are waiting. If a tooth breaks off or falls out, the next one moves forward; this is called a **revolver dentition**. In this way a shark often loses thousands of teeth over its lifetime.

A shark's skeleton is made of **cartilage**, similar to our outer ear. Cartilage breaks down quickly after death and only rarely becomes fossilised. Teeth, on the other hand, are very hard and have a protective coating. That is why they are often the only thing left as a **fossil** after millions of years.

The shape reveals what a shark ate. Triangular, **serrated teeth** like those of the great white shark cut flesh, while long, thin teeth hold on to slippery fish. Fresh teeth are white. Fossil teeth, by contrast, are often grey, brown or black, because **minerals** from the ground were taken up during fossilisation.

Around 20 million years ago, a shallow sea covered large parts of today's **Swiss Plateau**. Its deposits are called **molasse**, more precisely Upper Marine Molasse. Shark teeth are found in these sandstones, for example in the cantons of Aargau, Lucerne, Bern and St Gallen. Shells and the bones of sea cows have also been found there.

**Megalodon** lived in the world's oceans about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. Its teeth could be over 15 centimetres long, as big as a child's hand. Experts estimate that the shark grew to about 15 metres long or more. It probably also hunted whales.

Fossil shark teeth are sometimes found on beaches, in gravel pits or on stream banks among small stones and sand. It is best to look after rain, when the teeth shine. In Switzerland, the cantons have rules for fossils, and on private land you need **permission**. It is best to show special finds to a natural history museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from earlier times that has turned to stone.
Flexible, firm tissue from which sharks' skeletons are made.
A set of teeth in which lost teeth are continually replaced by new ones.
Rock layers in the Swiss Plateau formed from the deposits of an ancient sea and of rivers.

gewusst: People used to think fossil shark teeth were petrified tongues and called them adders' tongues.
Sharks' skin is also covered with tiny tooth-like scales, which is why it feels as rough as sandpaper.
Sharks have existed for more than 400 million years, which is longer than trees.

teile.einleitung: Feathered dinosaurs are dinosaurs that had feathers or feather-like structures on their skin. Since the 1990s, researchers have discovered many such fossils, above all in China. They show that today's birds are the descendants of dinosaurs.
wichtigste: Many dinosaurs had feathers, not just the birds.
Sinosauropteryx was described in 1996 as the first non-bird dinosaur with feather-like structures.
Many finds come from the province of Liaoning in the northeast of China.
Microraptor had long feathers on its arms and legs and is called “four-winged”.
Even the tyrannosaur Yutyrannus, about nine metres long, had feathers.
With fossil melanosomes, the colours of some dinosaurs can be reconstructed.
Today it is regarded as certain that birds descend from theropod dinosaurs.

abschnitte.text: Feathered dinosaurs are dinosaurs in whose fossils you find impressions of **feathers** or of simple, hair-like fibres. Most belong to the **theropods**, that is, the two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus or Velociraptor. Some had only a downy coat of fibres, while others had proper feathers with a shaft and vane like today's birds. People used to picture dinosaurs as scaly giant lizards; today we know that many looked more like strange birds.

As early as 1861, **Archaeopteryx** was found in Solnhofen in Bavaria, an animal about 150 million years old with teeth, claws and feathers. In 1996 researchers described **Sinosauropteryx** from China, a small meat-eating dinosaur with a fringe of fine fibres. Microraptor had long feathers on its arms and legs and could probably glide. Yutyrannus, described in 2012, was about nine metres long and shows that large meat-eating dinosaurs could have feathers too.

Especially many feathered dinosaurs come from the province of **Liaoning** in the northeast of China. The rocks there are about 120 to 130 million years old and date from the Cretaceous. At that time, volcanic ash and fine mud in lakes buried the animals so quickly that even feathers and soft parts were preserved as impressions. Such exceptionally well preserved sites are called **fossil sites**.

Feathers contain tiny colour bodies called **melanosomes**. Their shape reveals whether a feather was black, grey or reddish brown. In this way researchers found that Anchiornis had grey feathers, black and white patterned wings and a reddish crest on its head. In Sinosauropteryx the tail was probably ringed in reddish brown and white.

In 2014 **Kulindadromeus** was described in Siberia, a small plant-eater from the group of bird-hipped dinosaurs with feather-like fibres. This suggests that perhaps very early dinosaurs already had a kind of down. In 2016 a piece of **amber** from Myanmar made headlines, with a feathered dinosaur tail trapped inside. In it the feathers are preserved in three dimensions, almost as if the animal had only just died.

The many finds show that **birds** are the descendants of theropod dinosaurs. Strictly speaking, birds are even dinosaurs themselves, namely the only ones that survived the mass extinction about 66 million years ago. Feathers probably arose at first not for flying but for warmth and for display. Only later did some species use them for **flight**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of mostly two-legged, meat-eating dinosaurs, which also includes the ancestors of birds.
Tiny bodies in feathers and hair that contain the pigment melanin.
A remain or impression of a living thing from prehistoric times that has been preserved in rock.
Petrified tree resin, in which small animals or parts of plants are sometimes trapped.
A geological period about 145 to 66 million years ago, in which many dinosaurs lived.

gewusst: Every chicken and every pigeon is a close relative of Tyrannosaurus rex.
On some Velociraptor fossils you can see small bumps on the forearm bones where large feathers were once attached.
Microraptor was about as big as a crow and, according to current knowledge, had shimmering black plumage.

teile.einleitung: A glacier mouth is a cave-like opening at the end of a glacier from which meltwater flows out. The stream that starts there is called a glacial stream. Glacier mouths look impressive, but they are dangerous because ice can come crashing down at any moment.
wichtigste: A glacier mouth is the opening at the lower end of a glacier where meltwater comes out.
The stream that flows out of the glacier mouth is called a glacial stream.
The water is often milky and cloudy because it contains fine rock flour.
The meltwater flows to the mouth through channels in and under the glacier.
Vertical shafts through which water plunges into the depths are called moulins.
In summer, a glacial stream usually carries the most water in the afternoon or early evening.
Because the ice is constantly melting, the shape of a glacier mouth changes from year to year.

abschnitte.text: A glacier is a huge river of ice that slowly flows down the valley. At its lower end, the **glacier front**, a large hole often opens in the ice. This hole is called a **glacier mouth**. Sometimes it is only small, sometimes as high as a house and shimmering bluish.

In summer, a lot of ice melts on the surface of the glacier. The water collects in streams on the ice and plunges into the depths through vertical shafts, the **moulins**. Inside and under the glacier it flows on through channels. At the glacier mouth, all the water finally comes out into the daylight.

The **glacial stream** is often grey or milky and cloudy. This comes from **rock flour**, the finest dust that the glacier grinds off the rock as it flows. That is why this water is also called glacial milk. In lakes, the rock flour slowly settles and gives some mountain lakes their turquoise green colour.

The amount of water in the glacial stream varies greatly over the course of the day. In the morning it is still cool and little water flows. In the afternoon or early evening, after many hours of sunshine, the stream carries the most water. In winter the flow is very small, and some glacier mouths almost freeze shut.

Going into a glacier mouth is extremely dangerous, because large pieces of ice can break off at any time. The stream can also swell suddenly. Meltwater and warmth constantly change the mouth: it can collapse and form again somewhere else. Well-known glacial streams in Switzerland include the young **Rhone** at the Rhone Glacier and the Massa at the Great Aletsch Glacier.

begriffe.erklaerung: An opening at the end of a glacier from which meltwater comes out.
A stream that flows out of the glacier mouth.
Very fine dust that the glacier grinds off the rock.
A vertical shaft in a glacier through which meltwater plunges into the depths.

gewusst: Many of Europe's great rivers, for example the Rhone, begin as glacial streams.
The blue glow in a glacier mouth appears because dense ice mainly lets blue light through.
Glacial streams are ice cold even in high summer, only a little above 0 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a basic rule of population genetics. It describes how common certain hereditary factors are in a large group of living things and under what conditions these frequencies do not change. With a simple formula you can work out an astonishing amount about heredity.
wichtigste: Godfrey Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg described the rule independently of each other in 1908.
Godfrey Harold Hardy was a British mathematician, Wilhelm Weinberg a German doctor.
The frequencies of the genotypes are described by the equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
One of the conditions is that no selection takes place.
With random mixing, the equilibrium is reached after just one generation.
Whether real data deviate from it is usually tested with the chi-squared test.
The rule can be used to estimate how many people carry a hereditary factor without knowing it.

abschnitte.text: Many traits are determined by a **gene**, which can come in different versions. These versions are called **alleles**, for example A and a. Every living thing has two alleles, so AA, Aa or aa; this is its **genotype**. Someone with Aa is called heterozygous, someone with AA or aa homozygous.

The frequency of allele A is called p and that of a is called q. As there are only these two, p + q = 1. In equilibrium the proportion of AA is p², of Aa is 2pq and of aa is q². Together this gives the well-known equation **p² + 2pq + q² = 1**.

Suppose 4 per cent of a group show the **recessive** trait aa. Then q² = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 0.8. The proportion of heterozygous individuals is 2 times 0.8 times 0.2, which is 0.32 or 32 per cent. If, on the other hand, p = 0.7, the proportion of AA is 0.49, which is 49 per cent.

The equilibrium only holds in an imagined, **ideal population**. It must be very large, and there must be no selection, no new mutations and no migration in or out. In addition, the hereditary factors must combine randomly from generation to generation. In nature this is never completely true, but it often is approximately.

The rule helps to estimate the number of **carriers** of a recessive hereditary disease. If a disease occurs in 1 in 2500 people, then q² = 1/2500 and q = 1/50. The carriers then make up about 2pq, that is, roughly 1 in 25 people. They are healthy themselves and usually know nothing about their hereditary factor.

The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium serves as a **null model**, that is, as a comparison for the case in which nothing happens. If real counts deviate clearly, a factor of evolution such as selection or migration is probably at work. Whether the deviation is due to chance is tested with the **chi-squared test**. In this way the rule becomes a tool for making evolution measurable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A version of a gene, for example for a particular flower colour.
The combination of the two alleles that a living thing has for a gene.
A group of living things of the same species that live in the same area.
An allele that only shows when it is present twice.
A process in which certain traits are passed on more often than others.

gewusst: Hardy wrote his explanation as a short letter to a journal, because he thought the question was fairly simple.
Weinberg's contribution was overlooked for decades, which is why the rule was long called simply Hardy's law.
A rare trait hides much more often in heterozygous people than in people in whom it is visible.

teile.einleitung: A habit is a behaviour that we have repeated so often that it runs almost automatically. Brushing your teeth, the way to school or putting on your shoes are typical examples. Habits take a load off our brain, but they can also be stubborn when we want to get rid of them.
wichtigste: Habits run almost automatically and so take a load off the brain.
The habit loop consists of a cue, a routine and a reward.
The basal ganglia in the brain play an important part in habits.
In a study by Phillippa Lally in 2009 it took about 66 days on average for a new behaviour to become a habit.
The idea that a habit arises in 21 days goes back to Maxwell Maltz, but it is not proven.
If-then plans help in building up new habits.
