To get rid of an unwanted habit, it often helps to change the cue in your surroundings.

abschnitte.text: A **habit** is a behaviour that we carry out in a particular situation almost without thinking. At the beginning you still have to concentrate consciously, for instance when tying your shoes. After many repetitions it goes as if by itself, and people speak of an **automatic** behaviour. Experts estimate that a large part of our daily actions consists of habits.

In habits the **basal ganglia** play an important part, a group of nerve cell clusters deep inside the brain. When a behaviour is often repeated, they increasingly take over the control. The cerebral cortex, which is responsible for conscious thinking, is thereby **relieved**. In this way our head is free for other things, for example for a conversation while cycling.

Many experts describe habits with a **habit loop** made of three parts. First comes a **cue**, such as the ringing of the alarm clock. Then follows the **routine**, that is, the behaviour itself, for example getting up and brushing your teeth. At the end there is a reward, such as a fresh feeling in the mouth, and the brain notes that the behaviour is worth it.

You often hear that a new habit arises in **21 days**. This idea goes back to the American surgeon Maxwell Maltz, but it is not scientifically proven. In a study by the British psychologist **Phillippa Lally** in 2009 it took about 66 days on average for a new behaviour to run automatically. Depending on the person and the behaviour, the time lay between a few weeks and several months.

So-called **if-then plans** are helpful, for example: “When I come home from school, I drink a glass of water.” In this you link the new behaviour with a fixed situation. It also helps to start small and to practise regularly. Anyone who wants to get rid of an unwanted habit does best to change the **cue**, for instance by putting the mobile phone in another room while studying.

Related to habit is **habituation**, getting used to a stimulus. Anyone sitting next to a ticking clock stops hearing the ticking after a while. The brain blocks out stimuli that always stay the same and have no meaning. In this way we can concentrate on what is new and important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sequence that you always carry out in the same way.
A situation or stimulus that starts a particular behaviour.
Groups of nerve cells deep in the brain that help to control movements and habits.
Getting used to a stimulus that always stays the same.
A resolution that firmly links a behaviour to a particular situation.

gewusst: According to Lally's study, anyone who misses a day does not lose all their progress at once.
Many people brush their teeth in the same order every day without noticing it.
Animals form habits too, such as cows that walk to the barn by themselves in the evening.

teile.einleitung: The Nobel Peace Prize is one of the most famous awards in the world. It honours people and organisations that have done especially much for peace, human rights and understanding between people. Unlike all the other Nobel Prizes, it is awarded not in Sweden but in Norway.
wichtigste: The Nobel Peace Prize goes back to the will of Alfred Nobel.
A committee of the Norwegian parliament chooses the prizewinners.
The prize is presented in the city hall of Oslo.
The first prize went in 1901 partly to the Swiss Henry Dunant.
Malala Yousafzai received it at the age of 17 as the youngest Nobel laureate.
Martin Luther King was honoured in 1964 for his non-violent struggle.
In 2024 it went to the Japanese organisation Nihon Hidankyo, and in 2025 to María Corina Machado.

abschnitte.text: The Swedish inventor **Alfred Nobel** became very rich from dynamite and died in 1896. In his will he decided that his fortune should be used each year for prizes for the most important achievements of humankind. For the peace prize he named a committee of the **Norwegian parliament**, the Storting. At that time Sweden and Norway were joined in a union; why Nobel chose Norway in particular is not known for certain.

The **Norwegian Nobel Committee** consists of five members. Nominations may be submitted by members of parliament, professors and former prizewinners, for example. The prize is awarded every year on **10 December**, the day Alfred Nobel died. The ceremony takes place in the **city hall of Oslo**, and the winners receive a gold medal, a certificate and prize money.

The very first Nobel Peace Prize went in 1901 to the Genevan **Henry Dunant**, the founder of the Red Cross, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. As early as 1902 the prizes went to the Swiss Élie Ducommun and Albert Gobat. The **International Committee of the Red Cross**, based in Geneva, received the prize three times: in 1917, 1944 and 1963. Several UN organisations in Geneva have also been honoured.

The US civil rights leader **Martin Luther King** received the prize in 1964 for his non-violent struggle against racial segregation. In 1993 Nelson Mandela and Frederik de Klerk were honoured for ending **apartheid** in South Africa. The German journalist Carl von Ossietzky was given the prize for 1935 while he was imprisoned in a concentration camp. The Pakistani **Malala Yousafzai**, who campaigns for girls' right to education, was the youngest prizewinner at the age of 17.

In 2024 the Japanese organisation **Nihon Hidankyo** received the prize, an association of people who survived the atomic bombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It campaigns for nuclear weapons never to be used again. In 2025 the prize went to **María Corina Machado** from Venezuela for her work for democracy. In some years, above all during the world wars, no peace prize was awarded at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: A written statement of what should happen to someone's property after their death
The parliament of Norway
The former policy of strict separation of black and white people in South Africa
The group of five people who choose the peace prizewinner

gewusst: Henry Dunant, the first prizewinner, was living at the time in poverty and almost forgotten in a hospital in Heiden in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
The Nobel Peace Prize is the only Nobel Prize that can also be awarded to organisations.
The committee keeps the names of those nominated for the prize secret for 50 years.

teile.einleitung: Gore-Tex is a well-known material for raincoats, shoes and gloves. It is waterproof and yet lets sweat out as water vapour. The secret is a wafer-thin membrane with billions of tiny pores.
wichtigste: Gore-Tex is waterproof and breathable at the same time.
The classic membrane is made of expanded PTFE, a plastic.
Bob Gore discovered expanded PTFE in 1969.
The company W. L. Gore & Associates was founded in 1958 by Bill and Vieve Gore.
The pores are about 20,000 times smaller than a drop of water, but bigger than water vapour particles.
The same plastic is also found in the coating of many frying pans.
PTFE belongs to the controversial PFAS, which is why there are now also membranes made of other materials.

abschnitte.text: **Gore-Tex** is a brand name for waterproof and breathable textiles. Its heart is a very thin **membrane** that is glued in between the outer fabric and the lining. It is found in raincoats, walking boots, gloves and ski trousers. When you are out and about, it keeps you dry from the outside, and on the inside you sweat less in your own steam. This is especially practical for mountain sports, hiking and outdoor work.

The membrane has billions of tiny **pores** per square centimetre. According to the manufacturer, these pores are around 20,000 times smaller than a drop of water, which is why rain cannot get through. At the same time they are much larger than individual **water vapour particles**, so sweat can escape outwards as vapour. This property is called **breathable**. For this to work, the outside of the jacket must be clean and let water bead off well.

The classic membrane is made of **PTFE**, which stands for polytetrafluoroethylene. The chemist Roy Plunkett discovered this plastic by chance in 1938. It became known under the name Teflon, for example as the non-stick coating of frying pans. PTFE is very smooth, withstands heat and is attacked by almost no other substance. Gore-Tex uses a special, stretched form of it, known as expanded PTFE.

Bill and Vieve Gore founded the company **W. L. Gore & Associates** in the USA in 1958. In 1969 their son **Bob Gore** discovered that heated PTFE can be pulled apart in a flash without tearing. This creates a material full of tiny holes that still stays strong. In the 1970s the first rainwear with this membrane came onto the market. Expanded PTFE materials are also used in medicine, for example for artificial blood vessels.

PTFE belongs to the **PFAS**, a large group of artificial substances that hardly break down in nature. When some PFAS are produced, substances get into the environment that can build up in water, soil and living things. That is why the manufacturer now also offers membranes made of a different plastic without PFAS. If you want to use a performance jacket for a long time, you should wash it according to the instructions and repair it instead of throwing it away. That saves raw materials and protects the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very thin layer that lets some substances through and not others.
Describes a material that lets water vapour pass from the inside to the outside.
Polytetrafluoroethylene, a very smooth and heat-resistant plastic.
A group of artificial substances that are very long-lasting and can build up in the environment.

gewusst: According to the manufacturer, a single square centimetre of Gore-Tex membrane has around 1.4 billion pores.
Bob Gore found expanded PTFE because, after a long time of pulling slowly, he grew impatient and tried it once with a quick, sharp jerk.

teile.einleitung: Homo floresiensis was a small human species that lived on the island of Flores in Indonesia. Adults were only about one metre tall, which is why the species got the nickname “hobbit”. Its discovery in 2003 greatly surprised researchers studying human origins.
wichtigste: Homo floresiensis was discovered in 2003 in the Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores.
The most important skeleton is called LB1 and belonged to an adult who was only about one metre tall.
Because of its small size, the species is often called the “hobbit”.
According to the new dating of 2016, the bones from Liang Bua are about 100,000 to 60,000 years old.
Many experts believe that Homo floresiensis is descended from Homo erectus.
The small size is often explained by island dwarfism.
Most experts have rejected the early suggestion that LB1 was a sick modern human.

abschnitte.text: In 2003, Australian and Indonesian researchers were digging in the limestone cave **Liang Bua** on the island of Flores. There they found the almost complete skeleton of a very small human. It was given the designation **LB1**. In 2004 the find was described as a new human species with the name Homo floresiensis, meaning “human from Flores”.

LB1 was only about one metre tall, smaller than most six-year-olds today. Its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's and much smaller than ours. The arms were long in proportion, and the feet fairly large. Despite the small brain, **stone tools** were found in the cave that probably belonged to this human species.

At that time special animals lived on Flores: dwarf relatives of elephants called **Stegodon**, giant rats and Komodo dragons. The small humans apparently hunted or butchered such animals. Many experts explain their size by **island dwarfism**: on islands with little food, large animal species become smaller over many generations. According to a widespread hypothesis, the hobbits are descended from Homo erectus, which had somehow reached the island.

At first the bones were thought to be very young, only about 18,000 years old. In 2016 a **new dating** showed that the skeletal remains from Liang Bua are about 100,000 to 60,000 years old. In the same year, fossils of small early humans around 700,000 years old were published from the **Mata Menge** site on Flores. So the small humans lived on the island for a very long time.

Shortly after the find, some researchers argued that LB1 was a modern human with a disease called **microcephaly**, in which the head stays too small. However, further bone finds from several individuals and detailed studies speak against this. Today most experts regard Homo floresiensis as a species of its own. How exactly it is related to other human species is still being researched.

begriffe.erklaerung: Petrified or very old remains of a living thing.
When animal species on islands become smaller over many generations because there is little food and space.
An early human species that left Africa more than a million years ago.
Working out how old a find is.

gewusst: The nickname “hobbit” comes from the small beings in the books by J. R. R. Tolkien.
On Flores there were not only small humans but also small relatives of elephants, yet giant rats.
To reach Flores, the ancestors of these humans had to cross the sea, because the island was never connected to the mainland.

teile.einleitung: Hail is precipitation made of ice pellets that fall from thunderclouds. The pellets can be as small as peas or as big as golf balls. Every year, heavy hail causes a lot of damage in Switzerland to cars, roofs and fields.
wichtigste: Hail consists of ice pellets and falls from thunderclouds.
In the cloud, a hailstone is whirled upwards several times and grows layer by layer.
Hailstones can sometimes become as big as a golf ball.
Heavy hail can damage cars, roofs and fields.
Farmers protect fruit trees with hail nets.
Small, soft ice pellets that often fall in spring are called graupel.
When it hails heavily, you should go under a roof.

abschnitte.text: Hail forms in large, tall **thunderclouds**, the cumulonimbus clouds. Inside them there are strong updraughts that carry water droplets high up, where it is freezing cold. There they freeze into small grains of ice. The grains fall, are whirled up again and collect new layers of ice. Only when they are too heavy do they fall to the ground as **hailstones**.

People usually speak of hail from a diameter of about five millimetres. Smaller, soft and white pellets are called **graupel**; they often fall in cool weather in spring. If you cut open a large hailstone, you often see layers like those of an onion. The stronger the updraughts, the bigger the stones can become, sometimes as big as a golf ball or even bigger.

Large hailstones fall at high speed and can dent cars and smash windows and roof tiles. In a few minutes they can destroy fields of grain, vegetables or vines. For farmers this can cost a whole harvest. That is why many of them take out **hail insurance**.

Switzerland is one of the countries in Europe with relatively a lot of hail, especially in summer. Areas often affected include the edge of the Pre-Alps, the Swiss Plateau and Ticino. In summer 2021, violent hailstorms caused great damage in several regions of Switzerland. Fruit growers stretch **hail nets** over their trees to protect the fruit.

When a thunderstorm with hail is approaching, it is best to go straight under a roof or into a building. Hailstones can injure people and animals. If possible, put a car in a garage. The weather service **MeteoSwiss** warns of severe thunderstorms in its app, so that you can protect yourself in time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pellet of ice from a thundercloud, usually from about five millimetres in size.
Small, soft ice pellets, smaller than hail.
Air that flows strongly upwards, for example in a thundercloud.
A net stretched over fruit trees to protect the fruit from hail.

gewusst: The largest hailstone measured so far fell in South Dakota in the USA in 2010 and had a diameter of around 20 centimetres.
The Swiss Hail Insurance company was founded as early as 1880.
A hailstorm often lasts only a few minutes in one place, but can cause enormous damage.

teile.einleitung: The glacier tongue is the lower, elongated part of a glacier, which reaches down into the valley like a tongue. Here more ice melts than is added. At the glacier tongue you can see especially clearly how much the glaciers in the Alps are shrinking.
wichtigste: The glacier tongue is the lower part of a glacier that reaches down the valley.
It lies in the ablation zone, where more ice melts than forms.
The very front end of the glacier tongue is called the glacier front.
In summer there is bare ice on the tongue, because the winter snow has melted away.
If a glacier loses more ice than it gains over several years, the tongue retreats and becomes thinner.
A glacial lake often forms in front of a retreating tongue.
If the tongue ends in a lake or the sea, icebergs break off.

abschnitte.text: A glacier has two parts. At the top, in the **accumulation zone**, more snow falls than melts in summer, and over time this turns into ice. Further down lies the **ablation zone**, where more ice melts in summer than is added. The boundary between them is called the equilibrium line. The glacier tongue is the largest part of the ablation zone.

Under its own weight the ice flows slowly downhill, often only a few dozen to a hundred metres a year. In the valley it becomes a long, narrow tongue. In summer you can see **bare ice** on it with crevasses and stones, because the winter snow has melted away there. The very front end is called the **glacier front**, and a glacier mouth often opens there.

Whether a tongue grows or shrinks depends on how much snow falls and how warm the summers are. Since the end of the so-called Little Ice Age around 1850, the Alpine glaciers have been retreating. Because of **climate change** this is happening especially fast today. The tongues are becoming shorter and thinner, and moraines and bare rock are left behind in front of them.

The longest glacier tongue in the Alps belongs to the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais. The Lower Grindelwald Glacier in the Bernese Oberland used to reach almost to the village of Grindelwald; today it has retreated a long way. At the Rhone Glacier, a glacial lake has formed in front of the tongue. At the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine, signs along the path show where the tongue ended in earlier years.

When a tongue retreats, it often leaves a hollow that fills with meltwater, and so a **glacial lake** forms. If a tongue reaches into a lake or the sea, large pieces of ice break off; this is called **calving**. That is how icebergs form, for example in Greenland or Antarctica. Glacial lakes can also become dangerous if a dam of ice or rubble suddenly breaks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lower part of the glacier where more ice melts than forms.
The upper part of the glacier where snow builds up and turns into ice.
The very front end of the glacier tongue.
A ridge of stones and rubble left behind by a glacier.
Pieces of ice breaking off when a glacier ends in water.

gewusst: At the Lower Grindelwald Glacier, ice used to be quarried and was even sold as far away as Paris.
On some glaciers, parts of the tongue are covered with white sheets in summer so that they melt more slowly.
The ice at the tip of a long glacier tongue is often hundreds of years old.

teile.einleitung: Glaciers look like frozen rivers of ice, but in reality they are constantly in motion. Under their own weight they flow slowly down the valley, mostly a few metres to a few hundred metres a year. This movement shapes crevasses, ice towers and whole valleys.
wichtigste: A glacier moves down the valley because of its own weight.
At the surface the ice flows fastest in the middle of the valley.
In basal sliding the glacier slides over the rock on a film of water.
Deep crevasses arise through stresses in the ice.
If a glacier flows over a steep rock step, ice towers form, the seracs.
Glaciers leave behind glacial striations and U-shaped trough valleys.
Most Alpine glaciers move a few metres to a few hundred metres a year.

abschnitte.text: Glacier ice is solid, but under great pressure it can slowly deform like a very stiff dough. Gravity pulls the heavy mass of ice downhill. Inside it the ice crystals shift a little against each other, and this is called **internal deformation**. The thicker and steeper a glacier is, the faster it flows.

Often there is a thin layer of **meltwater** under the glacier. On this the ice slides over the rock beneath, and people speak of **basal sliding**. In early summer, when a lot of meltwater seeps downwards, a glacier can therefore suddenly become faster. If the glacier is frozen to the ground, there is hardly any sliding.

abschnitte.titel: Fast in the middle, slow at the edge
abschnitte.text: On the valley sides and at the bottom, **friction** on the rock slows the ice down. That is why at the surface a valley glacier flows fastest in the **middle**, rather like a river. The Swiss natural scientist **Louis Agassiz** proved this in the 1840s on the Unteraar Glacier. He drove a row of stakes across the glacier and saw how the row bent forwards with time.

Because the ice moves at different speeds in different places, stresses arise. At the surface, where the ice is brittle, it tears open, and so **crevasses** arise. If the glacier flows over a steep rock step, it breaks up into an **icefall** with wobbly ice towers, the **seracs**. For mountaineers, crevasses and seracs are especially dangerous.

Stones that are frozen into the ice act like sandpaper on the rock beneath. In this way smoothly polished rocks arise with fine scratches, the **glacial striations**. Big glaciers gouge broad, **U-shaped trough valleys** out of narrow river valleys. A well-known example is the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland.

A **valley glacier** such as the Aletsch Glacier flows as a long tongue through a valley. A **cirque glacier** fills only a hollow under a mountain summit and forms no long tongue. Besides these there are hanging glaciers that cling to steep mountain sides. Today researchers measure the movement very precisely with GPS devices and satellite pictures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sliding of a glacier on a film of water over the rock floor.
A deep crack in the glacier ice.
An ice tower that arises when a glacier breaks over a steep step.
A broad, U-shaped valley that a glacier has gouged out.

gewusst: Objects that fall into a glacier sometimes reappear only decades later further down at the glacier tongue.
Crevasses can be several dozen metres deep and are often hidden by a thin bridge of snow.
Some glaciers in Greenland flow several kilometres a year and are among the fastest in the world.
